knowledge_statements.statement_title: Approximation and fully polynomial scheme regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General scheme definitions for optimization problems with nonnegative weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal P\) be an optimization problem with nonnegative weights. An approximation scheme is an algorithm \(A(I,\epsilon)\), with \(\epsilon>0\), such that for each fixed \(\epsilon\), \(A\) is a \((1+\epsilon)\)-factor polynomial-time approximation algorithm. An asymptotic approximation scheme is a pair \((A,A')\), where \(A'\) computes \(c_\epsilon\) from \(\epsilon\) in polynomial time and \(A\) returns a feasible solution satisfying \[\frac{1}{1+\epsilon}\operatorname{OPT}(I)-c_\epsilon\le A(I,\epsilon)\le(1+\epsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(I)+c_\epsilon,\] with running time polynomial in \(\operatorname{size}(I)\) for each fixed \(\epsilon\). Either scheme is fully polynomial when its running time and the maximum encoded size of every number occurring in its computation are polynomially bounded in \(\operatorname{size}(I)+\operatorname{size}(\epsilon)+1/\epsilon\); for the asymptotic variant, \(c_\epsilon\) must also be polynomially bounded in \(1/\epsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial-time approximation scheme provides a (1+epsilon)-approximation for every fixed positive epsilon. An asymptotic scheme may additionally use an epsilon-dependent additive constant. Fully polynomial variants impose joint polynomial bounds in the input and accuracy parameters on runtime and intermediate-number sizes, with an additional polynomial bound on the asymptotic constant.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal P\text{ is an optimization problem with nonnegative weights}
I\text{ is an instance of }\mathcal P
\epsilon>0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\text{ satisfies the stated approximation guarantee and the complexity bounds defining its scheme regime}

source_evidence.locator: Approximation Algorithms / 16.4. Approximation Schemes / Definition 16.25

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Factor Approximation Algorithm and Performance Ratio
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a symmetric multiplicative objective-value guarantee for optimization problems with nonnegative weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal P\) be an optimization problem with nonnegative weights and let \(k\ge 1\). A polynomial-time algorithm \(A\) for \(\mathcal P\) is a \(k\)-factor approximation algorithm if, for every instance \(I\) of \(\mathcal P\), \[\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{OPT}(I)\le A(I)\le k\operatorname{OPT}(I).\] The value \(k\) is also called the performance ratio or performance guarantee of \(A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an optimization problem with nonnegative weights and k at least 1, a k-factor approximation algorithm runs in polynomial time and returns, on every instance, an objective value between 1/k times and k times the optimum. The value k is also called its performance ratio or performance guarantee.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal P\) is an optimization problem with nonnegative weights.
\(A\) is a polynomial-time algorithm for \(\mathcal P\).

source_evidence.locator: Approximation Algorithms / 16. Approximation Algorithms / Definition 16.2

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalence of ordinary and asymptotic approximation schemes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The equivalence requires polynomial-time recognition and exact solution of every fixed bounded-optimum regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal P\) be an optimization problem with nonnegative weights. Assume that for every fixed constant \(k\), there is a polynomial-time algorithm that decides whether an instance \(I\) has \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\le k\) and, when it does, returns an optimum solution. Then \[\mathcal P\text{ has an approximation scheme}\iff\mathcal P\text{ has an asymptotic approximation scheme}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If, for every fixed bound, instances whose optimum does not exceed that bound can be recognized and solved optimally in polynomial time, then a nonnegatively weighted optimization problem has an ordinary approximation scheme exactly when it has an asymptotic approximation scheme.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal P\text{ is an optimization problem with nonnegative weights}
\forall k\text{ fixed},\ \exists\text{ a polynomial-time algorithm deciding }\operatorname{OPT}(I)\le k\text{ and returning an optimum solution when the answer is yes}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal P\text{ has an approximation scheme}\iff\mathcal P\text{ has an asymptotic approximation scheme}

source_evidence.locator: Approximation Algorithms / 16.4. Approximation Schemes / Theorem 16.27

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Encoded-accuracy polynomial approximation implies exact solvability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to NP optimization problems whose objective function takes nonnegative integer values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal P\) be an NP optimization problem whose objective function takes values in \(\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\). Suppose that, given any instance \(I\) and any \(\epsilon>0\), an algorithm \(A\) returns a feasible solution satisfying \[\frac{1}{1+\epsilon}\operatorname{OPT}(I)\le A(I,\epsilon)\le(1+\epsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(I),\] and its running time is bounded by a polynomial in \(\operatorname{size}(I)+\operatorname{size}(\epsilon)\). Then \(\mathcal P\) can be solved exactly in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an NP optimization problem with nonnegative integer objective values, a multiplicative approximation algorithm whose running time is polynomial in the encoded lengths of both the instance and epsilon yields an exact polynomial-time algorithm.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal P\text{ is an NP optimization problem}
c(S)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\text{ for every feasible solution }S
\forall I\;\forall\epsilon>0:\ A(I,\epsilon)\text{ is feasible and satisfies the stated bounds}
T_A(I,\epsilon)\le\operatorname{poly}(\operatorname{size}(I)+\operatorname{size}(\epsilon))
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal P\text{ is exactly solvable in polynomial time}

children.title: Multiplicative Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Ratio-based quality regimes for minimization and maximization.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero and Sign Boundary for Ratio Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessity of the positive-optimum convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The ratio \(A(I)/\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) is undefined when \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)=0\). For minimization with \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)<0\) and \(\rho>1\), even the optimum fails \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\le\rho\operatorname{OPT}(I)\). Thus the standard factor inequalities do not express relative closeness for unrestricted-sign objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero optima make ratios undefined, while negative optima invalidate the conventional factor inequalities.
assumptions_latex: The conventional minimization inequality is \(A(I)\le\rho\operatorname{OPT}(I)\).
\(\rho>1\) in the negative-optimum example.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A positivity convention or another normalized error measure is required.
knowledge_statements.title: Zero and Sign Boundary for Ratio Guarantees

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transitivity through an intermediate nonnegative benchmark.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(x\le\alpha y\) and \(y\le\beta z\), then \(x\le\alpha\beta z\). Dually, if \(x\ge y/\alpha\) and \(y\ge z/\beta\), then \(x\ge z/(\alpha\beta)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Successive multiplicative losses compose by multiplying their factors.
assumptions_latex: \(\alpha,\beta\ge1\).
The comparisons have consistent orientation.
knowledge_statements.title: Composition of Multiplicative Comparisons

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative-Error Form of a Multiplicative Guarantee
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent relative-deviation formulations for positive optima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For minimization with \(0<\operatorname{OPT}(I)\le A(I)\), \(A(I)\le\rho\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) is equivalent to \((A(I)-\operatorname{OPT}(I))/\operatorname{OPT}(I)\le\rho-1\). For maximization with \(0<A(I)\le\operatorname{OPT}(I)\), \(A(I)\ge\operatorname{OPT}(I)/\rho\) is equivalent to \((\operatorname{OPT}(I)-A(I))/\operatorname{OPT}(I)\le1-1/\rho\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For positive optima, factor guarantees are equivalent to orientation-specific relative-error bounds.
assumptions_latex: The optimum and returned value are positive and ordered in the stated optimization direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed factor and relative-error inequalities are equivalent.
knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Error Form of a Multiplicative Guarantee
Multiplicative Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard ratio guarantee for nonnegative minimization or maximization objectives with positive optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A(I)\) be the objective value of a feasible solution returned on instance \(I\), and suppose \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)>0\). For \(\rho\ge 1\), \(A\) has a \(\rho\)-multiplicative guarantee if, for every instance \(I\),
\[
A(I)\le \rho\operatorname{OPT}(I)
\]
in a minimization problem, or
\[
A(I)\ge \operatorname{OPT}(I)/\rho
\]
in a maximization problem. The guarantee is uniform when the same \(\rho\) applies to every instance in the problem class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multiplicative guarantee bounds the algorithmic value by a fixed factor of the positive optimum, with the inequality oriented according to minimization or maximization.
assumptions_latex: \(A(I)\) is the value of a feasible output.
\(\operatorname{OPT}(I)>0\).

notation.meaning: Optimal objective value of instance I.
Objective value returned by algorithm A.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard definition of a multiplicative approximation ratio

children.title: Objective-Deviation Guarantee Classes
children.top_down_role: Quality regimes based on objective-value deviation.

children.title: Additive Error Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Objective-quality guarantees expressed through additive deviation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Why bounded additive error need not imply a uniform factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For minimization, instances with \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)=t>0\) and feasible returned value \(A(I)=t+C\) satisfy additive error \(C\), while their factor \(1+C/t\) diverges as \(t\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded additive error can have an unbounded ratio when positive optima approach zero.
assumptions_latex: The instance class permits positive optimal values arbitrarily close to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No finite uniform multiplicative factor follows from the additive bound alone.
knowledge_statements.title: Vanishing-Optimum Relative-Quality Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conversion Between Additive and Multiplicative Error
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Instancewise conversion using a positive optimum as scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)>0\), a minimization bound \(A(I)\le\operatorname{OPT}(I)+\varepsilon(I)\) implies factor \(1+\varepsilon(I)/\operatorname{OPT}(I)\). A maximization bound \(A(I)\ge\operatorname{OPT}(I)-\varepsilon(I)>0\) implies factor \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)/(\operatorname{OPT}(I)-\varepsilon(I))\). Conversely, factor \(\rho\) implies additive error at most \((\rho-1)\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) for minimization and \((1-1/\rho)\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) for maximization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Additive and multiplicative errors convert through the positive optimum, with orientation-specific formulas.
assumptions_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)>0\).
For maximization additive-to-factor conversion, \(\varepsilon(I)<\operatorname{OPT}(I)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed instancewise factor and additive bounds hold.
knowledge_statements.title: Conversion Between Additive and Multiplicative Error
Additive Error Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Instance-dependent additive deviation from the optimal objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\varepsilon:\mathcal I\to[0,\infty)\). A feasible-output algorithm \(A\) has additive error at most \(\varepsilon\) if, for every instance \(I\in\mathcal I\),
\[
A(I)\le \operatorname{OPT}(I)+\varepsilon(I)
\]
in a minimization problem, or
\[
A(I)\ge \operatorname{OPT}(I)-\varepsilon(I)
\]
in a maximization problem. Equivalently, feasibility and optimality imply
\[
\lvert A(I)-\operatorname{OPT}(I)\rvert\le\varepsilon(I).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An additive guarantee limits objective deviation from optimum by a nonnegative error allowance that may depend on the instance.
assumptions_latex: \(A(I)\) is the value of a feasible output.
\(\varepsilon:\mathcal I\to[0,\infty)\).

notation.meaning: Permitted additive error on instance I.

children.title: Absolute Approximation Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Absolute approximation regimes for objective values.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Discrete-Gap Exactness from an Absolute Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact recovery when attainable objective values have a uniform positive separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose distinct attainable objective values on every instance differ by at least \(\Delta>0\). If a feasible-output algorithm satisfies \(|A(I)-\operatorname{OPT}(I)|\le C\) uniformly with \(C<\Delta\), then \(A(I)=\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) for every instance. In particular, an integer-valued objective and \(C<1\) force exact optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An absolute error smaller than the minimum attainable-value gap forces exactness.
assumptions_latex: Distinct attainable values differ by at least \(\Delta>0\).
\(C<\Delta\).
The returned solution is feasible.

notation.meaning: Uniform separation of distinct attainable objective values.

knowledge_statements.title: Discrete-Gap Exactness from an Absolute Bound
Absolute Approximation Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform absolute-error guarantee independent of instance scale; terminology requires source confirmation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A feasible-output algorithm \(A\) has an absolute approximation guarantee \(C\) on an instance class \(\mathcal I\) if \(C\ge0\) is independent of the instance and
\[
\sup_{I\in\mathcal I}\left\lvert A(I)-\operatorname{OPT}(I)\right\rvert\le C.
\]
Thus the allowed objective deviation is uniformly bounded even when objective magnitudes vary across \(\mathcal I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An absolute guarantee bounds objective error by one constant over the entire instance class, independently of objective magnitude.
assumptions_latex: \(A(I)\) is the value of a feasible output.
\(C\ge0\) is independent of \(I\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: uniform additive-error interpretation selected from the local objective-deviation path

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a uniform additive objective-value guarantee for an optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An absolute approximation algorithm for an optimization problem \(\mathcal P\) is a polynomial-time algorithm \(A\) for which there exists a constant \(k\) such that, for every instance \(I\) of \(\mathcal P\), \[\lvert A(I)-\operatorname{OPT}(I)\rvert\le k.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An absolute approximation algorithm is a polynomial-time algorithm whose objective value differs from the optimum by at most a fixed constant on every instance.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal P\) is an optimization problem.
\(A\) is a polynomial-time algorithm for \(\mathcal P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists k\in\mathbb R\;\forall I\in\operatorname{Inst}(\mathcal P):\lvert A(I)-\operatorname{OPT}(I)\rvert\le k.\)

source_evidence.locator: Approximation Algorithms / 16. Approximation Algorithms / Definition 16.1

children.title: Scale-Sensitivity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Dependence of deviation-based guarantees on objective scaling and normalization.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normalization Requirement for Cross-Instance Additive Claims
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparability condition for numerical deviations across differently scaled instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under instance-dependent positive rescaling \(v\mapsto c(I)v\), preserving the semantic tolerance requires \(\varepsilon(I)\mapsto c(I)\varepsilon(I)\). Leaving its numerical value unchanged defines a different guarantee. Thus cross-instance numerical additive or absolute tolerances require a declared common unit or normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cross-instance additive tolerances require common units or an explicit scale-dependent transformation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A scale convention is necessary for invariant interpretation of numerical additive bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Normalization Requirement for Cross-Instance Additive Claims

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Behavior under adding a common baseline to all feasible objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Replace every objective value on instance \(I\) by \(v_b=v+b(I)\). Then \(A_b(I)-\operatorname{OPT}_b(I)=A(I)-\operatorname{OPT}(I)\), so additive error is unchanged. The ratio becomes \((A(I)+b(I))/(\operatorname{OPT}(I)+b(I))\) when defined and can be arbitrarily distorted, become undefined, or violate positivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a common baseline preserves objective differences but can arbitrarily alter or invalidate approximation ratios.
assumptions_latex: The same \(b(I)\) is added to every feasible objective value of instance \(I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Additive deviations are translation invariant; multiplicative factors generally are not.

notation.meaning: Instancewise baseline added to all feasible objective values.

knowledge_statements.title: Translation Sensitivity of Multiplicative Ratios
Scale-Sensitivity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Behavior of additive and multiplicative guarantees under positive objective rescaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Replace every objective value by \(c\) times that value, where \(c>0\). Then \(A_c(I)=cA(I)\) and \(\operatorname{OPT}_c(I)=c\operatorname{OPT}(I)\). A multiplicative factor \(\rho\) is unchanged by this transformation. An additive bound \(\varepsilon(I)\), however, becomes \(c\varepsilon(I)\). Consequently, a fixed numerical absolute bound \(C\) is not invariant under arbitrary rescaling unless \(C=0\) or the admissible scale is normalized.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplicative ratios survive positive rescaling, whereas additive errors scale with the objective; fixed absolute errors therefore require a chosen normalization.
assumptions_latex: \(A_c(I)=cA(I)\) and \(\operatorname{OPT}_c(I)=c\operatorname{OPT}(I)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Multiplicative factors are scale invariant, while additive bounds transform as \(\varepsilon\mapsto c\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Algorithmic and optimal values after rescaling.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct algebraic scaling law for ratio and additive guarantees

children.title: Asymptotic Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Large-instance guarantees separated from bounded residual effects.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Asymptotic Ratio Need Not Bound the Absolute Ratio
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that bounded-optimum residual instances can have unbounded ordinary ratios.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a minimization instance family \(\{J_k:k\ge1\}\cup\{I_m:m\ge1\}\) with \(\operatorname{OPT}(J_k)=1\), \(A(J_k)=k\), and \(\operatorname{OPT}(I_m)=A(I_m)=m\). Then \(R_A^\infty=1\), while \(\sup_I R_A(I)=\infty\) because \(R_A(J_k)=k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An algorithm can be asymptotically exact while having an unbounded ordinary worst-case ratio on bounded-optimum instances.
assumptions_latex: k,m\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}.
All displayed algorithmic and optimal values are positive.
knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Ratio Need Not Bound the Absolute Ratio

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Threshold Characterization of an Asymptotic Ratio
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantified equivalent of the seeded limsup definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(R_A^\infty\) defined over instances with unbounded \(\operatorname{OPT}\), the inequality \(R_A^\infty\le\rho\) holds if and only if, for every \(\delta>0\), there exists \(N_\delta\) such that \(R_A(I)\le\rho+\delta\) whenever \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\ge N_\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An asymptotic ratio at most rho is equivalent to eventually bounding every sufficiently large-optimum instance by rho plus arbitrary positive slack.
assumptions_latex: R_A(I)\ge1\text{ is defined for every instance}.
\operatorname{OPT}\text{ is unbounded over the instance class}.

notation.meaning: Optimum threshold associated with slack delta.

knowledge_statements.title: Threshold Characterization of an Asymptotic Ratio
Asymptotic Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case symmetric ratio after excluding instances with bounded optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a problem with \(A(I)>0\) and \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)>0\), define
\[
R_A(I)=\max\left\{\frac{A(I)}{\operatorname{OPT}(I)},\frac{\operatorname{OPT}(I)}{A(I)}\right\}.
\]
If optimal values are unbounded over the instance class \(\mathcal I\), define the asymptotic approximation ratio by
\[
R_A^{\infty}=\lim_{N\to\infty}\sup\left\{R_A(I):I\in\mathcal I,\ \operatorname{OPT}(I)\ge N\right\}.
\]
Algorithm \(A\) has asymptotic guarantee \(\rho\) when \(R_A^{\infty}\le\rho\); instances with bounded optimal value do not determine this ratio.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An asymptotic guarantee bounds the worst approximation ratio among instances whose optimal values grow without bound, ignoring bounded residual effects.
assumptions_latex: \(A(I)>0\) and \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)>0\) for every \(I\in\mathcal I\).
Optimal values are unbounded over \(\mathcal I\).

notation.meaning: Symmetric approximation ratio on instance I.
Lower threshold on the optimal value.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: limsup formulation of an asymptotic approximation ratio

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Asymptotic approximation factor and approximation ratio
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General performance definitions for optimization problems with nonnegative weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal P\) be an optimization problem with nonnegative weights. A polynomial-time algorithm \(A\) is an asymptotic \(k\)-factor approximation algorithm if there exists a constant \(c\), independent of the instance, such that for every instance \(I\), \[\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{OPT}(I)-c\le A(I)\le k\operatorname{OPT}(I)+c.\] The algorithm then has asymptotic performance ratio \(k\). The approximation ratio, respectively asymptotic approximation ratio, of \(\mathcal P\) is the infimum of all \(k\) for which an approximation algorithm, respectively asymptotic approximation algorithm, exists, and is \(\infty\) when no such algorithm exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An asymptotic k-factor algorithm runs in polynomial time and attains factor k up to one instance-independent additive constant. A problem's ordinary or asymptotic approximation ratio is the infimum of the achievable factors in the corresponding regime, or infinity if none exists.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal P\text{ is an optimization problem with nonnegative weights}
A\text{ is a polynomial-time algorithm}

source_evidence.locator: Approximation Algorithms / 16.4. Approximation Schemes / Definition 16.24

children.title: Instance-Sensitive Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Guarantees indexed by numerical or structural instance parameters.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between pointwise parameter guarantees and a class-wide constant factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\sup_{I\in\mathcal I}g(\kappa(I))=\infty\), the parameter-indexed inequalities alone imply no finite \(\rho\) satisfying the corresponding multiplicative inequality on every \(I\in\mathcal I\), even when every individual \(g(\kappa(I))\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pointwise finite factors need not yield a constant-factor guarantee when their class-wide supremum is unbounded.
assumptions_latex: The only supplied quality bounds are the factors \(g(\kappa(I))\).
\(\sup_{I\in\mathcal I}g(\kappa(I))=\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No finite uniform factor follows from these bounds alone.
knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded-Parameter Uniformity Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent representation by ordinary guarantees on parameter strata.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(k\in K\), let \(\mathcal I_k=\{I\in\mathcal I:\kappa(I)=k\}\). The factor \(g(\kappa(I))\) holds exactly when factor \(g(k)\) holds on every nonempty \(\mathcal I_k\). If \(\rho=\sup_{I\in\mathcal I}g(\kappa(I))<\infty\), the algorithm consequently has uniform factor \(\rho\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An instance-sensitive guarantee is a family of ordinary guarantees on parameter strata; a finite worst stratum factor gives a uniform guarantee.
assumptions_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)>0\) for all \(I\in\mathcal I\).
\(g:K\to[1,\infty)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stratumwise and instance-indexed formulations are equivalent, and finite \(\rho\) yields a uniform \(\rho\)-guarantee.

notation.meaning: Worst parameter-indexed factor over the class.

knowledge_statements.title: Stratumwise Representation and Uniformization
Instance-Sensitive Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximation quality expressed through a numerical or structural instance parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal I\) be an instance class, let \(\kappa:\mathcal I\to K\) be an instance parameter, and let \(g:K\to[1,\infty)\). Suppose \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)>0\) for every \(I\in\mathcal I\). A feasible-output algorithm \(A\) has the instance-sensitive multiplicative guarantee \(g\circ\kappa\) if every minimization instance satisfies
\[
A(I)\le g(\kappa(I))\operatorname{OPT}(I),
\]
or every maximization instance satisfies
\[
A(I)\ge \operatorname{OPT}(I)/g(\kappa(I)).
\]
The bound is informative when variation in \(\kappa(I)\) yields stronger factors than a single worst-case constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An instance-sensitive guarantee makes the approximation factor depend explicitly on a numerical or structural parameter of each instance.
assumptions_latex: \(\kappa:\mathcal I\to K\).
\(g:K\to[1,\infty)\).
\(\operatorname{OPT}(I)>0\) for every \(I\in\mathcal I\).

notation.meaning: Approximation factor as a function of the parameter.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: parameter-indexed refinement of the standard approximation ratio

children.title: Randomized Guarantee Models
children.top_down_role: Probability-sensitive interpretations of solution quality and running time.

children.title: Randomized Quality Confidence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Expected-quality and controlled-failure regimes.

children.title: Expected-Quality Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Approximation quality assessed through expected objective performance.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Expectation Does Not Control Rare Bad Outcomes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation between a fixed expected factor and tail quality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\rho>1\). For any \(M>\rho\), let a minimization algorithm with \(\operatorname{OPT}=1\) return \(M\) with probability \(p=(\rho-1)/(M-1)\) and \(1\) otherwise. Then \(\mathbb E[A]=\rho\), yet an arbitrarily poor value \(M\) occurs with positive probability. Hence an expected \(\rho\)-guarantee does not imply the same threshold on every run or with an arbitrarily prescribed failure probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed good expected factor can coexist with rare arbitrarily poor outputs.
assumptions_latex: Both outcomes are feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Expected quality alone supplies no matching per-run or arbitrary-confidence guarantee.
knowledge_statements.title: Expectation Does Not Control Rare Bad Outcomes

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence of a Seed Meeting the Expected Threshold
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic existential consequence of an expectation guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If an integrable random objective value \(X\) satisfies \(\mathbb E[X]\le B\), some seed satisfies \(X\le B\). If \(\mathbb E[X]\ge B\), some seed satisfies \(X\ge B\). This does not itself provide an efficient procedure for finding such a seed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An expected guarantee ensures existence of a seed meeting the expected threshold but does not automatically derandomize the algorithm.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A seed meeting the corresponding threshold exists.

notation.meaning: Random returned objective value for a fixed instance.

knowledge_statements.title: Existence of a Seed Meeting the Expected Threshold
Expected-Quality Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximation quality averaged over an algorithm's internal randomness for each fixed instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A(I;\omega)\) be the feasible objective value produced on instance \(I\) using internal random seed \(\omega\). Assume \(A(I;\omega)\) is integrable and \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)>0\). For \(\rho\ge1\), an expected-quality guarantee requires
\[
\mathbb E_{\omega}[A(I;\omega)]\le \rho\operatorname{OPT}(I)
\]
for every minimization instance, or
\[
\mathbb E_{\omega}[A(I;\omega)]\ge \operatorname{OPT}(I)/\rho
\]
for every maximization instance. The expectation is over internal randomness with \(I\) fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An expected-quality guarantee bounds the mean objective value over the algorithm's random choices for every fixed instance.
assumptions_latex: \(A(I;\omega)\) is feasible for every relevant \(\omega\).
\(A(I;\omega)\) is integrable.
\(\operatorname{OPT}(I)>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The expected returned value satisfies the stated \(\rho\)-factor inequality.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard expectation-based randomized approximation guarantee

children.title: High-Probability Quality Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Approximation quality under explicitly controlled failure probability.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinction between per-instance confidence and one seed working for all instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The statement \(\forall I,\Pr_\omega(E(I,\omega))\ge1-\delta\) does not imply \(\Pr_\omega(\forall I,E(I,\omega))\ge1-\delta\). With two equiprobable seeds and two instances, let each seed succeed on exactly one instance. Each fixed instance succeeds with probability \(1/2\), while no seed succeeds on both.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: High probability for every fixed instance does not mean that one seed works simultaneously for all instances.
assumptions_latex: The counterexample uses the same seed distribution for both instances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The probability operator and universal instance quantifier cannot be interchanged without additional control.

notation.meaning: Quality event for instance I and seed omega.

knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise Versus Uniform Quantifier Boundary
High-Probability Quality Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Per-instance approximation guarantee with an explicit failure probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(\rho\ge1\) and \(\delta\in[0,1]\). Suppose \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)>0\). A randomized feasible-output algorithm has a high-probability quality guarantee if, for every fixed instance \(I\),
\[
\Pr_{\omega}\!\left[A(I;\omega)\le\rho\operatorname{OPT}(I)\right]\ge1-\delta
\]
for minimization, or
\[
\Pr_{\omega}\!\left[A(I;\omega)\ge\operatorname{OPT}(I)/\rho\right]\ge1-\delta
\]
for maximization. The probability is taken only over the algorithm's internal randomness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each fixed instance, the requested approximation factor holds with probability at least one minus the declared failure probability.
assumptions_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)>0\).
\(A(I;\omega)\) is feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The \(\rho\)-quality event has probability at least \(1-\delta\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard per-instance high-probability approximation definition

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Simultaneous Quality by a Union Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proposed finite-event confidence allocation; canonically owned by Tail-Failure Calibration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\Pr(E_j)\ge1-\delta_j\) for \(j=1,\ldots,m\), then \(\Pr(\bigcap_jE_j)\ge1-\sum_j\delta_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A union bound combines finitely many confidence guarantees.
assumptions_latex: \(m<\infty\).
All events belong to the same probability experiment.

children.title: Tail-Failure Calibration
children.top_down_role: Tradeoffs between quality thresholds, confidence levels, and repeated trials.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Runtime overhead of independent best-of-run amplification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If one run takes time \(T(I)\), then \(m\) sequential independent runs plus best-value selection take \(O(mT(I)+m)\) time. For fixed \(\delta_0\in(0,1)\), reducing failure to \(\delta\) requires \(m=\Theta(\log(1/\delta))\), so \(T_{\mathrm{amp}}(I,\delta)=O(T(I)\log(1/\delta)+\log(1/\delta))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent amplification multiplies runtime by a number of trials logarithmic in inverse target failure.
assumptions_latex: Runs are sequential and independently randomized.
One run costs \(T(I)\).
\(\delta_0\) is a fixed constant in \((0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The amplification overhead is logarithmic in \(1/\delta\).
knowledge_statements.title: Repetition Cost of Confidence Amplification

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independence boundary for repeated-trial amplification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If all \(m\) trials reuse the same random seed and therefore have the same success indicator with failure probability \(\delta_0\), the combined best-of-run procedure fails with probability \(\delta_0\), not \(\delta_0^m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Perfectly correlated trials provide no confidence amplification despite identical marginal guarantees.
assumptions_latex: All trial success indicators are identical.
Each trial has marginal failure probability \(\delta_0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Correlation Prevents Exponential Amplification

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordering of tail guarantees as the accepted threshold changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For minimization, \(F(q)=\Pr[A(I;\omega)>q]\) is nonincreasing in \(q\). For maximization, \(F(q)=\Pr[A(I;\omega)<q]\) is nondecreasing in \(q\). Thus relaxing a quality threshold cannot worsen its confidence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stricter quality thresholds cannot have lower failure probability solely by threshold inclusion.
assumptions_latex: The instance and random-output distribution are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Failure probability is monotone in the threshold with the stated orientation.
knowledge_statements.title: Monotone Quality-Confidence Tradeoff

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous calibration of finitely many quality events without independence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\Pr(E_j)\ge1-\delta_j\) for \(j=1,\ldots,m\), then \(\Pr(\bigcap_{j=1}^mE_j)\ge1-\sum_{j=1}^m\delta_j\). Thus assigning failure budget \(\delta/m\) to each event yields simultaneous validity at least \(1-\delta\). Independence is unnecessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A union bound allocates a total failure budget among finitely many required quality claims.
assumptions_latex: \(m<\infty\).
All events are measured under the same probability experiment.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Confidence-Budget Allocation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degraded quality thresholds obtainable from expectation alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For minimization, let \(X=A(I;\omega)\ge0\) and suppose \(\mathbb E[X]\le\rho\operatorname{OPT}(I)\). Then for every \(\lambda>1\), \(\Pr[X>\lambda\rho\operatorname{OPT}(I)]\le1/\lambda\). For maximization, if additionally \(0\le X\le\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) and \(\mathbb E[X]\ge\operatorname{OPT}(I)/\rho\), then for \(0\le\theta<1/\rho\), \(\Pr[X\ge\theta\operatorname{OPT}(I)]\ge(1/\rho-\theta)/(1-\theta)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expectation yields only degraded-threshold tail guarantees, with the maximization conversion requiring bounded nonnegative outputs.
assumptions_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)>0\).
For minimization, \(X\ge0\).
For maximization, \(0\le X\le\operatorname{OPT}(I)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed failure and success probability bounds hold.

notation.meaning: Random returned objective value for a fixed instance.
Relaxed minimization and maximization quality thresholds.

knowledge_statements.title: Expectation-to-Tail Calibration
Tail-Failure Calibration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent repetition calibrates failure probability while preserving a fixed target quality threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose one randomized run meets a fixed quality threshold with probability at least \(1-\delta_0\), where \(0<\delta_0<1\). Run the algorithm independently \(m\) times and return the best objective value, using the minimum for minimization and the maximum for maximization. All runs fail only if every individual run fails, so
\[
\Pr[\text{combined failure}]\le\delta_0^m.
\]
To obtain failure probability at most \(\delta\in(0,1)\), it suffices to choose
\[
m\ge\left\lceil\frac{\log\delta}{\log\delta_0}\right\rceil.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent repetition and selection of the best result reduce a per-run failure probability exponentially in the number of runs.
assumptions_latex: The \(m\) runs are mutually independent.
Each run fails the same quality threshold with probability at most \(\delta_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After \(m\) runs, failure probability is at most \(\delta_0^m\), hence at most \(\delta\) for the displayed choice of \(m\).

children.title: Runtime-Quality Randomness Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Separation between randomness in running time and randomness in quality.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Randomized, Las Vegas, Monte Carlo, One-Sided-Error, and Nondeterministic Algorithms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for algorithms represented by finite random-bit strings on each input.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:S\to T\), \(k:S\to\mathbb Z_+\), and \(g:\{s\#r:s\in S,\ r\in\{0,1\}^{k(s)}\}\to T\). The map \(g\) is a randomized algorithm for \(f\). It is Las Vegas if \(g(s\#r)=f(s)\) for every \(s\) and \(r\). It is Monte Carlo if \(\inf_{s\in S}2^{-k(s)}|\{r:g(s\#r)=f(s)\}|>0\). When \(T=\{0,1\}\), it has one-sided error if \(f(s)=0\) implies \(g(s\#r)=0\) for every \(r\); it is nondeterministic if, additionally, every \(s\) with \(f(s)=1\) has some \(r\) satisfying \(g(s\#r)=1\). Running time is measured as a function of \(\operatorname{size}(s)\), so a polynomial-time randomized algorithm can read only polynomially many random bits.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A randomized algorithm receives an input and an input-dependent finite random-bit string. A Las Vegas algorithm is correct for every random string. A Monte Carlo algorithm has a uniformly positive probability of correctness over all inputs. For decision problems, one-sided error forbids acceptance of no-instances; the nondeterministic model additionally requires at least one accepting random string for every yes-instance. Polynomial running time permits reading only polynomially many random bits.
assumptions_latex: f:S\to T
k:S\to\mathbb Z_+
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The stated conditions define the randomized, Las Vegas, Monte Carlo, one-sided-error, and nondeterministic regimes.}

source_evidence.locator: NP-Completeness / 15.3. P and NP / Definition 15.13

knowledge_statements.title: Randomized, Las Vegas, Monte Carlo, One-Sided-Error, and Nondeterministic Algorithms

directory_assessment.rationale: The available taxonomy owns approximation-specific randomness, but the extract requires a general complexity-theoretic container for randomized and nondeterministic computation.

children.title: Las Vegas Approximation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Approximation settings with certified output quality but randomized running time.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion of a trial procedure with verifiable success into a Las Vegas approximation algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose each independent execution of a randomized trial is accepted with probability at least \(p>0\), and a deterministic verifier accepts exactly when the trial supplies a valid certificate that its output is feasible and \(\rho\)-approximate. Repeatedly run the trial and return the first accepted output. The returned solution is always feasible and \(\rho\)-approximate, termination occurs almost surely, and the number \(N\) of trials satisfies
\[\Pr[N>t]\le(1-p)^t,\qquad \mathbb E[N]\le1/p.\]
If the trial-plus-verification costs are independent and identically distributed across attempts, integrable, and have expectation at most \(R\), then the expected total runtime is at most \(R/p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeat independent trials until a sound certificate verifier accepts; output quality becomes certain while the trial count has a geometric tail.
assumptions_latex: Independent trials have acceptance probability at least \(p>0\).
The verifier has no false acceptances and accepts every trial carrying the declared valid certificate.
Trial-plus-verification cost pairs are independent and identically distributed across attempts and have expectation at most \(R\).

notation.meaning: Number of trials through the first accepted output.
Lower bound on one-trial acceptance probability.
Expected cost of one trial together with verification.

knowledge_statements.title: Restart-Until-Certified Las Vegas Conversion

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Universal tail consequence of a finite expected Las Vegas runtime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For any nonnegative Las Vegas runtime \(T\) with \(\mathbb E[T]\le M\), Markov's inequality gives
\[\Pr[T>M/\delta]\le\delta\qquad(0<\delta<1).\]
Thus expected polynomial time supplies a polynomial cutoff for every fixed failure probability, but does not by itself imply an exponentially decreasing runtime tail.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite expected runtime gives an inverse-linear tail bound, not an exponential tail without additional structure.
assumptions_latex: \(T\ge0\) almost surely.
\(\mathbb E[T]\le M<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.title: Expected-Runtime Tail Bound
Las Vegas Approximation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Random runtime with an approximation guarantee holding on every terminating execution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A(I;\omega)\) be the objective value returned on instance \(I\), let \(T(I;\omega)\) be its runtime, and suppose \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)>0\). A randomized approximation algorithm is Las Vegas with factor \(\rho\ge1\) if, for every \(I\), it terminates almost surely and every terminating execution returns a feasible solution satisfying
\[
A(I;\omega)\le\rho\operatorname{OPT}(I)
\]
for minimization, or
\[
A(I;\omega)\ge\operatorname{OPT}(I)/\rho
\]
for maximization. It is expected-polynomial Las Vegas if there is a polynomial \(p\) such that
\[
\mathbb E_{\omega}[T(I;\omega)]\le p(|I|)
\]
for every encoded instance \(I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Las Vegas approximation algorithm always meets its feasibility and quality guarantees on termination; in the expected-polynomial regime, only its runtime is random and its expected runtime is polynomial.
assumptions_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)>0\).
The algorithm terminates almost surely.
\(T(I;\omega)\) is integrable in the expected-polynomial regime.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Quality holds on every terminating execution, and \(\mathbb E_{\omega}[T(I;\omega)]\le p(|I|)\) in the expected-polynomial regime.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Las Vegas classification specialized to approximation quality

children.title: Monte Carlo Approximation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Approximation settings permitting controlled uncertainty in output quality or feasibility.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Amplification when all runs are feasible and their objective values can be ordered.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If one run takes at most \(T(n)\), always returns a feasible solution, and is a \(\rho\)-approximation with probability at least \(1-\delta\), then \(r\) independent runs followed by selecting the best objective value take at most \(rT(n)\) and fail with probability at most \(\delta^r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent repetition and best-output selection reduce failure probability exponentially while increasing runtime linearly.
assumptions_latex: \(r\in\mathbb N\).
Runs use independent random bits.
Every run returns a feasible solution, and objective values can be compared.
knowledge_statements.title: Independent-Repetition Amplification

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Expectation Does Not Preserve the Same Approximation Factor
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between expected-value and high-probability approximation guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\rho>1\), \(q\in(0,1)\), and \(\operatorname{OPT}=1\). A feasible minimization output taking value \(1\) with probability \(1-q\) and value \(1+(\rho-1)/q\) with probability \(q\) satisfies \(\mathbb E[A]=\rho\), but exceeds \(\rho\operatorname{OPT}\) with probability \(q\). In general Markov's inequality yields only \(\Pr[A\le(\rho/\eta)\operatorname{OPT}]\ge1-\eta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An expected rho-approximation need not be a high-probability rho-approximation; obtaining confidence from expectation generally worsens the factor.
assumptions_latex: The problem is nonnegative minimization.

notation.meaning: Probability of the bad output in the counterexample.
Target failure probability in the Markov bound.

knowledge_statements.title: Expectation Does Not Preserve the Same Approximation Factor
Monte Carlo Approximation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case bounded runtime with approximation quality permitted to fail probabilistically.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A(I;\omega)\) be the objective value returned on instance \(I\), and suppose \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)>0\). A randomized approximation algorithm is Monte Carlo with factor \(\rho\ge1\) and failure bound \(\delta\in[0,1]\) if every execution halts within \(p(|I|)\) steps for some polynomial \(p\), returns a feasible solution, and satisfies
\[
\Pr_{\omega}\!\left[A(I;\omega)\le\rho\operatorname{OPT}(I)\right]\ge1-\delta
\]
for minimization, or
\[
\Pr_{\omega}\!\left[A(I;\omega)\ge\operatorname{OPT}(I)/\rho\right]\ge1-\delta
\]
for maximization. Randomness may affect whether the quality threshold is met, but not the worst-case runtime bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Monte Carlo approximation algorithm has a worst-case polynomial runtime bound, while its stated approximation quality may fail with controlled probability.
assumptions_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)>0\).
Every execution halts within \(p(|I|)\) steps and returns a feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The \(\rho\)-quality event occurs with probability at least \(1-\delta\) within worst-case polynomial time.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Monte Carlo classification specialized to approximation quality

children.title: Runtime–Quality Randomness Boundary
children.top_down_role: Placement of randomized uncertainty across running time, quality, and success probability.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reverse conversion when successful approximation outputs are exactly recognizable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose independent bounded-time runs succeed with probability at least \(p>0\), and a polynomial-time verifier accepts exactly the outputs satisfying the declared feasibility and \(\rho\)-quality condition. Repeating until acceptance terminates almost surely, returns only certified \(\rho\)-approximations, and has expected runtime at most \((T(n)+V(n))/p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exactly verifiable Monte Carlo success can be converted to Las Vegas behavior by independent restart.
assumptions_latex: Independent runs succeed with probability at least \(p>0\).
The verifier is sound and complete for the declared success event.
A run and verification take at most \(T(n)\) and \(V(n)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Verified Restart Conversion

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the Monte Carlo-to-Las Vegas conversion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A guarantee \(\Pr[Q(I,\omega)]\ge p>0\) does not alone justify repeat-until-success: when \(Q\), such as an optimum-relative quality event, cannot be recognized from the run and its output, the procedure has no sound stopping rule that accepts exactly successful runs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive success probability is insufficient for restart conversion unless success is recognizable or certified.
assumptions_latex: No sound and complete verifier for \(Q\) is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pr[Q]\ge p>0\text{ alone does not imply a Las Vegas restart conversion}.
knowledge_statements.title: Unrecognizable Success Blocks Generic Restart

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Las Vegas Truncation with a Feasible Fallback
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion to the seeded Monte Carlo regime, which requires every run to return a feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a Las Vegas procedure returns a feasible \(\rho\)-approximation upon termination and has expected runtime at most \(T(I)\). Stop it after \(cT(I)\) steps, where \(c>1\), and on timeout return an available feasible fallback solution. The resulting procedure has worst-case bounded runtime and its \(\rho\)-quality event fails with probability at most \(1/c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Truncating a Las Vegas approximation and returning a feasible fallback on timeout gives a Monte Carlo approximation with timeout probability at most one over c.
assumptions_latex: The expected-time bound holds for each fixed instance.
Every normal termination returns a feasible \(\rho\)-approximation.
A feasible fallback can be produced within the stated worst-case bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Las Vegas Truncation with a Feasible Fallback
Runtime–Quality Randomness Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between unconditional quality with random runtime and bounded runtime with probabilistic quality failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a randomized approximation procedure on each fixed instance, distinguish its runtime guarantee from its feasibility and quality guarantee. In the Las Vegas regime, every terminating execution satisfies the declared feasibility and quality requirements, termination occurs almost surely, and runtime may have an unbounded tail subject to an expected-time bound. In the Monte Carlo regime, every execution obeys a worst-case runtime bound, while the declared quality event may fail with probability at most \(\delta>0\). If neither almost-sure termination with unconditional output quality nor worst-case bounded runtime with a quantified quality-failure probability is established, neither classification follows; runtime and quality tails must be reported separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Las Vegas algorithms preserve output quality while permitting a random runtime tail; Monte Carlo algorithms bound runtime while allowing quantified quality failure. Other combinations require separate runtime and quality guarantees.
assumptions_latex: Runtime and quality are evaluated for every fixed input instance.
\(\delta>0\) denotes an allowed quality-failure probability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Unconditional quality on termination with almost-sure termination characterizes the stated Las Vegas regime, whereas worst-case bounded runtime with possible quality failure characterizes the stated Monte Carlo regime.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: conventional runtime-versus-correctness distinction applied to approximation quality

children.top_down_role: Approximation tradeoffs involving two performance or feasibility criteria.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Separate Existential Guarantees Are Not Simultaneous
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifier boundary for a genuine bicriteria output.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The claims \(\exists x\,[f(x)\le\alpha B]\) and \(\exists y\,[g(y)\le\beta C]\) do not imply one \(z\) satisfying both. With only objective pairs \((1,M)\) and \((M,1)\), each unit coordinate is separately attainable, but no output attains \((1,1)\) when \(M>1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One returned solution must satisfy both bicriteria bounds; two separately good solutions do not suffice.
assumptions_latex: Both coordinates are minimized.

notation.meaning: Large loss in the coordinate not optimized by a solution.

knowledge_statements.title: Separate Existential Guarantees Are Not Simultaneous

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dominance and incomparability of guarantee pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An \((\alpha,\beta)\)-guarantee implies every \((\alpha',\beta')\)-guarantee with \(\alpha'\ge\alpha\) and \(\beta'\ge\beta\). Pairs with \(\alpha_1<\alpha_2\) but \(\beta_1>\beta_2\) are incomparable without an external scalarization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bicriteria guarantee pairs are ordered coordinatewise and generally are not totally ordered.
assumptions_latex: Both coordinates are minimization-style loss factors.
The benchmark and constraint normalization are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The guarantee region is upward closed under the product order}.
knowledge_statements.title: Product Order of Bicriteria Guarantees

assumptions_latex: The problem is a nonnegative minimization problem with original feasible set \(X(I)=\{x\in X_0(I):g_j(x)\le b_j(I),\ 1\le j\le m\}\).
The original optimum \(\mathrm{OPT}(I)=\min_{x\in X(I)}f_I(x)\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm simultaneously controls objective loss and feasibility violation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicative objective-and-violation convention for nonnegative minimization problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For factors \(\alpha,\beta\ge 1\), a polynomial-time algorithm is an \((\alpha,\beta)\)-bicriteria approximation if, on every instance \(I\), it returns \(x\in X_0(I)\) satisfying
\[
f_I(x)\le \alpha\,\mathrm{OPT}(I)
\quad\text{and}\quad
g_j(x)\le \beta b_j(I)\quad(1\le j\le m).
\]
The first coordinate measures objective degradation relative to the unrelaxed optimum, while the second bounds the simultaneous multiplicative relaxation of every constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bicriteria algorithm approximates the original optimum while bounding how much every feasibility constraint may be violated.

children.title: Multicriteria Approximation
children.top_down_role: Approximation tradeoffs involving multiple simultaneous criteria.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weighted Sums Miss Unsupported Pareto Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limit of positive weighted-sum scalarization in discrete objective sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For minimization vectors \(a=(0,2)\), \(b=(1,3/2)\), and \(c=(2,0)\), all three are Pareto-optimal. For \(b\) to be no worse than \(a\) under \(w_1f_1+w_2f_2\) requires \(w_1\le w_2/2\), while being no worse than \(c\) requires \(w_1\ge3w_2/2\). Hence no \(w_1,w_2>0\) selects \(b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A discrete Pareto-optimal point need not optimize any strictly positive weighted sum.
assumptions_latex: Both objectives are minimized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Pareto optimality does not imply positive-weighted-sum optimality}.
knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Sums Miss Unsupported Pareto Points

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coordinatewise Ideal Values May Be Jointly Unattainable
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary on using separate single-objective optima as one benchmark vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B_i=\min_{x\in X}f_i(x)\). The vector \(B\) need not be attained by one solution. For feasible objective vectors \((1,M)\) and \((M,1)\), the ideal vector is \((1,1)\), but every solution loses a factor \(M\) in one coordinate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The vector of separate objective optima can be infeasible as a joint target.
assumptions_latex: All objectives are minimized.
knowledge_statements.title: Coordinatewise Ideal Values May Be Jointly Unattainable

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise order governing simultaneous guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If one solution satisfies \(f_i(x)\le\alpha_iB_i\) for all \(i\), it satisfies every factor vector \(\boldsymbol\alpha'\ge\boldsymbol\alpha\) coordinatewise. Thus attainable factor vectors form an upward-closed set that may have mutually incomparable minimal elements.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multicriteria factor vectors are ordered coordinatewise and need not have a single best element.
assumptions_latex: The objective directions and benchmark vector are fixed.
\(\boldsymbol\alpha'\ge\boldsymbol\alpha\) coordinatewise.
knowledge_statements.title: Product-Order Monotonicity of Multicriteria Factors

assumptions_latex: Each instance \(I\) has feasible set \(X(I)\) and nonnegative minimization objectives \(f_1,\ldots,f_k\).
A benchmark vector \(B(I)\in\mathbb R_+^k\) is specified for the guarantee.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every objective coordinate satisfies its stated approximation factor simultaneously.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard simultaneous coordinatewise approximation convention
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise multiplicative guarantees for finitely many nonnegative minimization criteria.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\boldsymbol\alpha\in[1,\infty)^k\), a polynomial-time algorithm is a multicriteria \(\boldsymbol\alpha\)-approximation relative to \(B\) if, for every instance \(I\), it returns some \(x\in X(I)\) such that
\[
f_i(x)\le \alpha_i B_i(I)\qquad(1\le i\le k).
\]
All inequalities must hold for the same returned solution. The benchmark may be a prescribed target, a coordinatewise lower bound, or the objective vector of a designated comparison solution, but its meaning must be fixed by the problem formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multicriteria approximation returns one feasible solution satisfying a separate approximation guarantee for every objective coordinate.
knowledge_statements.title: Multicriteria Approximation

children.title: Approximate Pareto Frontiers
children.top_down_role: Navigation of representative tradeoff sets for competing criteria.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Pareto Frontiers Can Be Exponential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-objective family with exponentially many nondominated vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in\{0,\ldots,2^n-1\}\), minimize \(f_1(x)=x+1\) and \(f_2(x)=2^n-x\). If \(x<y\), then \(f_1(x)<f_1(y)\) and \(f_2(x)>f_2(y)\); therefore all \(2^n\) objective vectors are Pareto-optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even with two objectives and n-bit solutions, an exact Pareto frontier can contain exponentially many vectors.
assumptions_latex: Both objectives are minimized.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Pareto Frontiers Can Be Exponential

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero Coordinates Require Exact or Additive Treatment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of purely multiplicative Pareto coverage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a covered solution has \(f_i(y)=0\), multiplicative coverage requires \(f_i(x)\le(1+\varepsilon)f_i(y)=0\). Thus geometric discretization requires positive values, separate treatment of zeros, or an explicitly additive tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplicative Pareto coverage cannot soften a zero objective coordinate.
assumptions_latex: Objectives are nonnegative and minimized.
\(f_i(y)=0\) for some covered vector.
knowledge_statements.title: Zero Coordinates Require Exact or Additive Treatment

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fixed-Dimension Approximate Pareto Sets and the Gap Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard construction principle for multiplicative approximate Pareto sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed \(k\) and positive rational minimization objectives of polynomially bounded encoding length, an \(\varepsilon\)-approximate Pareto set of size polynomial in the input length and \(1/\varepsilon\) exists. Such sets can be constructed in corresponding polynomial time when the associated gap problem is polynomial-time solvable: given \(b\in\mathbb Q_+^k\), either produce \(x\) with \(f(x)\le b\) or certify that no feasible \(x\) satisfies \(f(x)\le b/(1+\varepsilon)\), coordinatewise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a fixed number of positive rational objectives, approximate Pareto sets have polynomial size, and an approximate gap routine provides the generic construction route.
assumptions_latex: The number of objectives \(k\) is fixed.
Objective values are positive rationals with polynomially bounded encoding length.
Complexity is polynomial in the input length and \(1/\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |S_\varepsilon|\le\operatorname{poly}(|I|,1/\varepsilon),\quad\text{and a polynomial gap routine yields polynomial construction}.

notation.meaning: Target objective vector for the gap problem.

assumptions_latex: The feasible set \(X(I)\) has nonnegative minimization objectives \(f_1,\ldots,f_k\).
The accuracy parameter satisfies \(\varepsilon>0\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite multiplicative coverage of the Pareto frontier in minimization form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A finite set \(S_\varepsilon\subseteq X(I)\) is an \(\varepsilon\)-approximate Pareto frontier if, for every \(y\in X(I)\), there exists \(x\in S_\varepsilon\) satisfying
\[
f_i(x)\le(1+\varepsilon)f_i(y)\qquad(1\le i\le k).
\]
Thus every feasible objective vector, and hence every Pareto-optimal vector, is weakly dominated after coordinatewise multiplication by \(1+\varepsilon\). An algorithmic approximate frontier additionally requires that \(S_\varepsilon\) be generated in time polynomial in the input length and the stated accuracy encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An approximate Pareto frontier is a finite feasible set that multiplicatively covers every feasible objective vector in all coordinates.
knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Pareto Frontiers

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Original and Augmented Optima Are Different Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes resource augmentation from ordinary approximation on the augmented instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For minimization with \(X_I(b)\subseteq X_I((1+\delta)b)\), one has \(\operatorname{OPT}_I((1+\delta)b)\le\operatorname{OPT}_I(b)\). Hence \(f_I(x)\le\alpha\operatorname{OPT}_I((1+\delta)b)\) implies \(f_I(x)\le\alpha\operatorname{OPT}_I(b)\), but the converse need not hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximating the augmented optimum is stronger than comparing an augmented-resource output with the original-resource optimum.

The feasible regions are nested under augmentation.
\(\delta\ge0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If an algorithm has an \((\alpha,\delta)\) guarantee relative to \(\operatorname{OPT}_I(b)\), then it also has an \((\alpha',\delta')\) guarantee for \(\alpha'\ge\alpha\) and \(\delta'\ge\delta\), provided \(b\le b'\) implies \(X_I(b)\subseteq X_I(b')\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A guarantee remains valid after allowing more resources or a weaker objective factor when resource feasibility is monotone.
assumptions_latex: \(\alpha'\ge\alpha\), \(\delta'\ge\delta\).
Resource vectors use componentwise order.
Resource-feasible regions are monotone.

assumptions_latex: The original feasible region is \(X_I(b)=\{x\in X_0(I):g_j(x)\le b_j,\ 1\le j\le m\}\).
The problem is minimization and \(\mathrm{OPT}_I(b)=\min_{x\in X_I(b)}f_I(x)\) is finite.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform multiplicative augmentation of packing-style resource bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\delta\ge0\) and \(\alpha\ge1\), an algorithm has an \((\alpha,\delta)\) resource-augmented guarantee if, for every instance \(I\) and resource vector \(b\ge0\), it returns \(x\in X_I((1+\delta)b)\) satisfying
\[
f_I(x)\le\alpha\,\mathrm{OPT}_I(b).
\]
The comparison solution receives only the original resources \(b\), whereas the algorithm may use the componentwise augmented vector \((1+\delta)b\). Running time must be polynomial in the ordinary instance encoding for fixed guarantee parameters.

children.title: Constraint-Violation Guarantees

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalization boundary for multiplicative and additive violation conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(g_j(x)\le b_j\), the multiplicative allowance \(g_j(x)\le\beta_jb_j\) permits no positive excess when \(b_j=0\). Positive rescaling to \(cg_j(x)\le cb_j\) preserves \(\beta_j\), whereas an additive allowance must change from \(\Delta_j\) to \(c\Delta_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplicative violation does not relax a zero bound, while additive violation depends on the chosen constraint scale.
assumptions_latex: The rescaled inequality represents the same original constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Multiplicative and additive violation have different zero-bound and normalization behavior}.
knowledge_statements.title: Zero Bounds and Constraint Scaling

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise weakening of objective and violation bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f_I(x)\le\alpha\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) and \(g_j(x)\le\beta_jb_j+\Delta_j\) for every \(j\), the same output satisfies every guarantee with \(\alpha'\ge\alpha\), \(\beta'_j\ge\beta_j\), and \(\Delta'_j\ge\Delta_j\), provided the same benchmark and normalization are retained and the relevant right-hand sides are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Valid objective and violation bounds remain valid when any allowance is weakened coordinatewise.
assumptions_latex: The benchmark and constraint normalization are unchanged.
\(\alpha'\ge\alpha\), \(\boldsymbol\beta'\ge\boldsymbol\beta\), and \(\boldsymbol\Delta'\ge\boldsymbol\Delta\).

assumptions_latex: The original feasible set is \(X(I)=\{x\in X_0(I):g_j(x)\le b_j,\ 1\le j\le m\}\).
The objective is nonnegative minimization with finite value \(\mathrm{OPT}(I)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\alpha\ge1\) and \(\boldsymbol\beta\in[1,\infty)^m\), an algorithm has an \((\alpha,\boldsymbol\beta)\) constraint-violation guarantee if it returns \(x\in X_0(I)\) such that
\[
f_I(x)\le\alpha\,\mathrm{OPT}(I)
\quad\text{and}\quad
g_j(x)\le\beta_jb_j\qquad(1\le j\le m).
\]
The vector form permits different relaxation limits for different constraints. Additive guarantees instead replace the second inequality by \(g_j(x)\le b_j+\Delta_j\), with the scale of each \(\Delta_j\) specified by the problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constraint-violation guarantee bounds objective degradation and the allowed excess in each original feasibility constraint.

children.title: Relaxation-Budget Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Quality changes induced by varying the permitted feasibility relaxation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary requiring the comparison benchmark to remain fixed across budgets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Nested permitted-output sets do not imply monotonicity for ratios whose denominator changes with \(\delta\). In minimization, \(\operatorname{OPT}_{I,b}(\delta)\) may decrease as relaxation grows, so \(f_I(A(I,b,\delta))/\operatorname{OPT}_{I,b}(\delta)\) need not be nonincreasing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: More relaxation need not improve a ratio measured against a simultaneously improving benchmark.
assumptions_latex: The problem is minimization.
The benchmark is allowed to depend on \(\delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Nested feasibility alone does not order moving-benchmark ratios}.
knowledge_statements.title: Moving Benchmarks Destroy Generic Monotonicity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural condition under which additional relaxation cannot worsen the frontier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(X_{I,b}(\delta_1)\subseteq X_{I,b}(\delta_2)\) for every \((I,b)\in\mathcal J\) whenever \(\delta_1\le\delta_2\), while \(\mathcal J\), \(B\), the algorithm class, and runtime convention remain fixed, then \(\alpha^*(\delta_2)\le\alpha^*(\delta_1)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed-benchmark frontier is nonincreasing when larger budgets nest the permitted outputs.
assumptions_latex: \(\delta_1\le\delta_2\).
The permitted output sets are nested.
All comparison and complexity conventions remain fixed.
knowledge_statements.title: Nested-Budget Monotonicity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Corrected lower-envelope formulation with no free resource parameter and an explicit algorithm class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal J\) be a fixed encoded family of pairs \((I,b)\), let \(X_{I,b}(\delta)\) be the outputs allowed at budget \(\delta\), let \(B(I,b)>0\) be a fixed comparison value, and let \(\mathcal A_{\mathrm{poly}}\) contain algorithms polynomial in the declared encoding and runtime convention. Define
\[
\alpha^*(\delta)=\inf_{A\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm{poly}}:\,A(I,b,\delta)\in X_{I,b}(\delta)\ \forall(I,b)\in\mathcal J}\ \sup_{(I,b)\in\mathcal J}\frac{f_I(A(I,b,\delta))}{B(I,b)}.
\]
The attainable upper region is \(\{(\delta,\alpha):\alpha\ge\alpha^*(\delta)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relaxation–quality frontier is a lower envelope over an explicitly fixed instance-resource family, benchmark, admissible algorithm class, and runtime convention.
assumptions_latex: \(B(I,b)>0\) for every \((I,b)\in\mathcal J\).
The encoding, algorithm class, and runtime convention are fixed independently of \(\delta\).
The admissible-algorithm set is interpreted as empty when no algorithm satisfies the required relaxed feasibility condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \alpha^*(\delta)\text{ is a well-defined extended-real worst-case frontier}.

notation.meaning: Fixed encoded family of instance-resource pairs.

knowledge_statements.title: Well-Defined Relaxation–Quality Frontier

assumptions_latex: For every instance \(I\), \(X_I(b)\) is the feasible set under resource vector \(b\ge0\).
The objective is minimization, and the comparison value \(\mathrm{OPT}_I(b)\) is positive and finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The lower envelope records the best worst-case objective factor attainable at each relaxation budget.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case objective frontier parameterized by a uniform feasibility-relaxation budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\delta\ge0\), define the optimal polynomial-time tradeoff by
\[
\alpha^*(\delta)=\inf_{A\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm{poly}}}
\sup_I\frac{f_I(A(I,b,\delta))}{\mathrm{OPT}_I(b)},
\]
where the infimum ranges only over algorithms satisfying \(A(I,b,\delta)\in X_I((1+\delta)b)\) on every instance. The attainable region is \(\{(\delta,\alpha):\alpha\ge\alpha^*(\delta)\}\). Because additional relaxation cannot remove admissible algorithms, \(\alpha^*(\delta)\) is nonincreasing wherever the ratios and feasibility model are defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The tradeoff frontier gives the best worst-case objective factor achievable by polynomial algorithms for each allowed feasibility-relaxation budget.

children.title: Exact Polynomial-Time Solvability
children.top_down_role: Optimization families admitting exact polynomial-time solutions.

assumptions_latex: Instances and candidate solutions have finite binary encodings.
Feasibility and objective values are interpreted in the stated computational model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An exact optimum is produced within polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bit-complexity definition for exact combinatorial optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A combinatorial optimization problem is exactly polynomial-time solvable if there exist an algorithm \(A\) and a polynomial \(p\) such that, for every encoded instance \(I\), the computation terminates within \(p(|I|)\) bit operations and returns \(x^*\in X(I)\) satisfying
\[
f_I(x^*)=\min_{x\in X(I)}f_I(x)
\]
for minimization, with \(\min\) replaced by \(\max\) for maximization. The running-time bound includes the cost of representing and manipulating all numbers produced by the algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact polynomial-time solvability means producing an optimal feasible solution in time polynomial in the binary input length.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Polynomial-Time Solvability

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial-time reduction from linear feasibility to linear programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional algorithmic reduction for rational linear programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose there is a polynomial-time algorithm that, given any \(A\in\mathbb{Q}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{Q}^m\), decides whether \(\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\) is empty. Then there is a polynomial-time algorithm for linear programming that finds an optimal basic solution whenever one exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If emptiness of rational systems of linear inequalities can be decided in polynomial time, then linear programming can be solved in polynomial time, with an optimal basic solution produced whenever one exists.
assumptions_latex: A\in\mathbb{Q}^{m\times n},\quad b\in\mathbb{Q}^m
\text{Emptiness of }\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\text{ is decidable in polynomial time for every rational input }(A,b).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{There is a polynomial-time algorithm for linear programming that returns an optimal basic solution whenever one exists.}

source_evidence.locator: Linear Programming Algorithms / 4.5. Khachiyan's Theorem / Proposition 4.16

assumptions_latex: The problem is a nonnegative minimization problem with finite optimum \(\mathrm{OPT}(I)\).
Approximation is measured multiplicatively.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform multiplicative approximation for nonnegative minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A problem is constant-factor approximable if there exist a constant \(\alpha\ge1\), independent of the instance size, and a polynomial-time algorithm \(A\) such that, for every instance \(I\), \(A(I)\in X(I)\) and
\[
f_I(A(I))\le\alpha\,\mathrm{OPT}(I).
\]
For a nonnegative maximization problem the corresponding condition is \(f_I(A(I))\ge\mathrm{OPT}(I)/\alpha\). The factor may depend on the fixed problem but not on \(I\); allowing \(\alpha\) to grow with \(|I|\) defines a weaker approximability regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A problem is constant-factor approximable when one polynomial algorithm achieves a fixed approximation ratio on every instance.
knowledge_statements.title: Constant-Factor Approximability

children.title: Exactness-to-Approximation Boundary
children.top_down_role: Structural transition from polynomial-time exactness to constant-factor approximation.

assumptions_latex: Complexity is measured in the standard binary encoding model.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Approximation-scheme membership does not generally imply exact polynomial-time solvability.

notation.meaning: class of exactly polynomial-time solvable optimization problems

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard class inclusion and conditional knapsack separation
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional separation between exact optimization and arbitrarily accurate approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Exact polynomial-time solvability implies every standard approximation guarantee, giving
\[
\mathrm{PO}\subseteq\mathrm{FPTAS}\subseteq\mathrm{PTAS}.
\]
The reverse implication fails unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\): binary-encoded zero-one knapsack admits an FPTAS, while computing its exact optimum is NP-hard. Consequently, even a scheme whose running time is polynomial jointly in input size and reciprocal accuracy need not become an exact polynomial-time algorithm, because exact recovery can require accuracy whose reciprocal is exponential in the input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact polynomial solvability implies scheme approximability, but even an FPTAS need not yield an exact polynomial algorithm unless P equals NP.
knowledge_statements.title: Exactness-to-Approximation Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, but the class inclusions, the meaning of PO, and the conditional knapsack separation require authoritative sources with specific locators.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximization counterpart of the seeded minimization convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonnegative maximization problem, a PTAS is a family \(\{A_\varepsilon\}_{0<\varepsilon<1}\) returning feasible solutions satisfying \(f_I(A_\varepsilon(I))\ge(1-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(I)\), such that for every fixed \(\varepsilon\) the running time is polynomial in \(|I|\).

\(0\le f_I(y)\le\operatorname{OPT}(I)<\infty\) for feasible \(y\).
