knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes PTAS runtime from the uniform input-size exponent required by EPTAS.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A PTAS permits a bound \(C_\varepsilon |I|^{c_\varepsilon}\) with \(c_\varepsilon\) unbounded as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\). Consequently, a bound of the form \(|I|^{q(1/\varepsilon)}\), with nonconstant \(q\), certifies polynomial time for every fixed \(\varepsilon\) but does not by itself certify an EPTAS, which requires an alternative bound with one input-size exponent independent of \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A PTAS may place arbitrary accuracy dependence in its input-size exponent, so such an analysis alone need not establish an EPTAS.
assumptions_latex: q:\mathbb R_{>0}\to\mathbb R_{>0}\text{ is nonconstant}.
\varepsilon\text{ is fixed when PTAS polynomiality is evaluated}.

assumptions_latex: The problem is nonnegative minimization with finite optimum \(\mathrm{OPT}(I)\).
The accuracy parameter satisfies \(0<\varepsilon<1\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard minimization PTAS with unrestricted accuracy dependence in the polynomial exponent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A polynomial-time approximation scheme is a family of algorithms \(\{A_\varepsilon:0<\varepsilon<1\}\) such that, for every instance \(I\), the output is feasible and satisfies
\[
f_I(A_\varepsilon(I))\le(1+\varepsilon)\mathrm{OPT}(I).
\]
For every fixed \(\varepsilon\), there exist constants \(c_\varepsilon\) and \(C_\varepsilon\) for which the running time is at most \(C_\varepsilon |I|^{c_\varepsilon}\). Both the multiplicative constant and the exponent may depend arbitrarily on \(\varepsilon\), but neither may depend on \(I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A PTAS gives a factor 1 plus epsilon approximation in polynomial time for every fixed positive epsilon.

\(0\le f_I(y)\le\operatorname{OPT}(I)<\infty\) for feasible \(y\).
\(h\) is computable and \(c\) is independent of \(I,\varepsilon\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates the local EPTAS runtime condition from the stronger FPTAS condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The bound \(h(1/\varepsilon)|I|^c\) permits arbitrary computable dependence \(h\). Thus EPTAS membership alone does not certify polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\). For each fixed \(\varepsilon\), however, \(h(1/\varepsilon)\) is constant, so every EPTAS satisfies the PTAS runtime requirement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every EPTAS is a PTAS, but an EPTAS need not have the reciprocal-accuracy polynomial bound required of an FPTAS.
assumptions_latex: \(h:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R_{>0}\) is computable.
\(c\) is independent of \(I\) and \(\varepsilon\).

assumptions_latex: The problem is nonnegative minimization with finite optimum \(\mathrm{OPT}(I)\).
The accuracy parameter satisfies \(0<\varepsilon<1\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: EPTAS convention with arbitrary computable parameter dependence and constant input-size exponent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An efficient polynomial-time approximation scheme is a family \(\{A_\varepsilon:0<\varepsilon<1\}\) satisfying
\[
f_I(A_\varepsilon(I))\le(1+\varepsilon)\mathrm{OPT}(I)
\]
with running time bounded by
\[
h(1/\varepsilon)|I|^c,
\]
where \(h\) is a computable function and \(c\) is a constant independent of both \(I\) and \(\varepsilon\). Thus the potentially large dependence on accuracy is confined to \(h\), while the exponent of the input length remains uniform across all requested accuracies.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An EPTAS confines arbitrary accuracy dependence to a separate factor while keeping one fixed polynomial exponent in the input size.
knowledge_statements.title: Efficient Polynomial-Time Approximation Schemes

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A fully polynomial-time approximation scheme is a family \(\{A_\varepsilon:0<\varepsilon<1\}\) such that every output is feasible,
\[
f_I(A_\varepsilon(I))\le(1+\varepsilon)\mathrm{OPT}(I),
\]
and there exists a bivariate polynomial \(p\) satisfying
\[
\operatorname{time}(A_\varepsilon,I)\le p(|I|,1/\varepsilon)
\]
for all \(I\) and \(\varepsilon\). Hence both the input-size dependence and the cost of requesting additional accuracy are polynomially bounded; in particular, every FPTAS is an EPTAS and therefore a PTAS.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An FPTAS achieves factor 1 plus epsilon in time polynomial in both input length and reciprocal epsilon.
knowledge_statements.title: Fully Polynomial-Time Approximation Schemes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind correctly characterize an FPTAS, including joint polynomial dependence on input size and reciprocal accuracy, but no authoritative citation is provided.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between an FPTAS for weighted independence-system maximization and polynomial-time solvability of the associated epsilon-dominance problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $\mathcal I$ be a family of independence systems. Let $\mathcal I'$ consist of maximization instances $(E,\mathcal F,c)$ with $(E,\mathcal F)\in\mathcal I$ and $c:E\to\mathbb Z_+$, and let $\mathcal I''$ consist of the corresponding instances $(E,\mathcal F,c,\epsilon,S_1,S_2)$ of the $\epsilon$-dominance problem. The maximization problem restricted to $\mathcal I'$ has a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme if and only if the $\epsilon$-dominance problem restricted to $\mathcal I''$ has an algorithm whose running time is polynomial in the encoded input length and $1/\epsilon$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted maximization over a family of independence systems has an FPTAS exactly when its associated epsilon-dominance problem is solvable in time polynomial in the input length and 1/epsilon.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal I\text{ is a family of independence systems.}
(E,\mathcal F)\in\mathcal I
c:E\to\mathbb Z_+
\epsilon>0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{FPTAS}(\mathcal I')\iff\exists\text{ an algorithm for }\epsilon\text{-DOMINANCE on }\mathcal I''\text{ running in }\operatorname{poly}(|\mathrm{input}|,1/\epsilon).

children.title: Polynomial-Factor Approximability Classes
children.top_down_role: Constant-factor and growing-factor approximability classifications.

children.title: APX
children.top_down_role: Constant-factor polynomial-time approximability as a complexity classification.

knowledge_statements.title: APX
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the symmetric ratio convention for positive-valued minimization and maximization problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An optimization problem \(\Pi\) belongs to \(\mathsf{APX}\) if there are a constant \(c\ge 1\) and a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm \(A\) such that, for every instance \(x\) of \(\Pi\), the algorithm returns a feasible solution \(A(x)\) satisfying \(R(x,A(x))\le c\). The constant \(c\) is independent of \(x\) and its encoding length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: APX consists of optimization problems admitting a polynomial-time approximation algorithm with an instance-independent constant approximation ratio.
assumptions_latex: The feasible solutions and their objective values are recognizable and computable in polynomial time.
All feasible objective values and optimum values are strictly positive.
The input length is \(n=|x|\).

notation.meaning: Symmetric approximation ratio of feasible solution y on instance x.
Class of constant-factor polynomial-time approximable optimization problems.

children.title: Poly-APX
children.top_down_role: Polynomially bounded approximation-factor classifications.

knowledge_statements.title: Poly-APX
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial factor is measured in the binary input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An optimization problem \(\Pi\) belongs to \(\mathsf{Poly\text{-}APX}\) if there are a polynomial \(p\) satisfying \(p(n)\ge 1\) and a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm \(A\) such that, for every instance \(x\), the algorithm returns a feasible solution satisfying \(R(x,A(x))\le p(|x|)\). The same polynomial \(p\) must apply to every instance of \(\Pi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Poly-APX contains problems approximable in polynomial time within a factor bounded by one fixed polynomial in the input length.
assumptions_latex: The feasible solutions and their objective values are recognizable and computable in polynomial time.
All feasible objective values and optimum values are strictly positive.
The input length is \(n=|x|\).

notation.meaning: Class admitting polynomial-factor approximation in polynomial time under the stated convention.

children.title: Intermediate Approximability Classes
children.top_down_role: Classifications positioned between constant-factor and broad polynomial-factor regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Intermediate Approximability Classes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Introduces a factor-indexed convention for discussing guarantees between constant and polynomial factors; it does not assert a universally standardized class name.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed nondecreasing computable function \(g:\mathbb{N}\to[1,\infty)\), let \(\mathsf{A}(g)\) denote the class of optimization problems \(\Pi\) for which a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm \(A\) returns a feasible solution on every instance \(x\) and satisfies \(R(x,A(x))\le g(|x|)\). Under this convention, choices such as an unbounded subpolynomial function satisfying \(g(n)=n^{o(1)}\) describe factor regimes between constant and unrestricted polynomial bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a factor-indexed convention, intermediate regimes use specified growing approximation bounds, such as unbounded subpolynomial factors, between constant and general polynomial factors.
assumptions_latex: The function \(g:\mathbb{N}\to[1,\infty)\) is fixed, nondecreasing, and computable.
All feasible objective values and optimum values are strictly positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathsf{A}(g)=\{\Pi:\exists A\text{ polynomial-time such that }R(x,A(x))\le g(|x|)\text{ for every instance }x\}\).

notation.meaning: Locally defined class of problems approximable within factor g of input length.

children.title: Class-Inclusion Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Containment, separation, and completeness relationships among adjacent approximation classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Class-Inclusion Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States unconditional monotone inclusions; strict boundaries require complexity assumptions and reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(g(n)\le h(n)\) for every input length \(n\), then every \(g\)-approximation is also an \(h\)-approximation, and therefore \(\mathsf{A}(g)\subseteq\mathsf{A}(h)\). In particular, \(\mathsf{APX}\subseteq\mathsf{Poly\text{-}APX}\) under the stated conventions. Equality or strictness does not follow from these definitions. Establishing \(\mathsf{A}(g)\subsetneq\mathsf{A}(h)\) requires membership in the larger class and a hardness result excluding the smaller guarantee under an explicit complexity assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smaller factor bounds induce smaller approximation classes. Strict separation requires a matching algorithm and a complexity-based inapproximability result.
assumptions_latex: The functions \(g,h:\mathbb{N}\to[1,\infty)\) use the same input encoding and approximation-ratio convention.
For every \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), \(g(n)\le h(n)\).

notation.meaning: Polynomial-time approximation class whose factor is bounded by g.

children.title: Extended-Time Approximation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Approximation outside the standard uniform polynomial-time hierarchy.

children.title: Quasipolynomial-Time Approximation
children.top_down_role: Approximation guarantees available within quasipolynomial running time.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accuracy-indexed specialization of quasipolynomial-time approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A quasipolynomial-time approximation scheme is a family \((A_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}\) such that, for every fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1]\), \(A_\varepsilon\) returns a feasible \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximate solution and runs in time \(\exp((\log n)^{c(\varepsilon)})\), where \(c(\varepsilon)\) is finite and independent of the input length \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A QPTAS achieves a 1+epsilon approximation in quasipolynomial time for every fixed accuracy.
assumptions_latex: n\ge2.
\varepsilon\in(0,1].
c(\varepsilon)\text{ is independent of }n.
knowledge_statements.title: Quasipolynomial-Time Approximation Scheme
Quasipolynomial-Time Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses deterministic quasipolynomial time with a fixed exponent and includes polynomial time as the boundary case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A quasipolynomial-time \(\rho\)-approximation is a deterministic algorithm \(A\) for which there is a constant \(c\ge 1\) such that, on every instance \(x\) of length \(n\ge 2\), it returns a feasible solution in time at most \(\exp((\log n)^c)\) and satisfies \(R(x,A(x))\le\rho(n)\). The exponent \(c\) is independent of \(n\). When \(c=1\), this displayed bound is polynomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quasipolynomial-time approximation attains its stated factor within time exponential in a fixed power of the logarithmic input length.
assumptions_latex: The input length is \(n=|x|\ge 2\).
All feasible objective values and optimum values are strictly positive, and approximation uses the symmetric ratio.

notation.meaning: Worst-case running time of algorithm A on length-n inputs.

children.title: Parameterized Approximation
children.top_down_role: Approximation guarantees organized by instance parameters and parameter-dependent running time.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General FPT-time approximation form; the immutable seed supplies the approximation-scheme specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a parameterized optimization problem with instances \((x,k)\), an FPT-time \(\rho\)-approximation returns a feasible solution in time \(f(k)|x|^c\), where \(f\) is computable and \(c\) is independent of \(k\), and has multiplicative ratio at most \(\rho(k)\ge1\). For minimization its value is at most \(\rho(k)\operatorname{OPT}(x,k)\); for maximization it is at least \(\operatorname{OPT}(x,k)/\rho(k)\). A constant \(\rho\) gives the fixed-parameter constant-factor specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An FPT-time parameterized approximation confines nonpolynomial running-time dependence to the parameter and may state either a parameter-dependent or uniform approximation factor.
assumptions_latex: k\in\mathbb N.
f\text{ and }\rho\text{ are computable}.
c\text{ is independent of }x\text{ and }k.
Relevant objective and optimum values are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.title: FPT-Time Parameterized Approximation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates FPT approximation time from XP or merely slice-wise polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bound \(f(k,\varepsilon)|x|^c\) with constant \(c\) is fixed-parameter tractable in \((k,\varepsilon)\). A bound \(|x|^{g(k,\varepsilon)}\) is not thereby fixed-parameter tractable: when \(g\) is unbounded, its parameter-dependent exponent cannot in general be absorbed into a factor depending only on \((k,\varepsilon)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Putting the parameter or accuracy in the input-size exponent gives an XP-style bound, not an FPT approximation bound unless that exponent is uniformly bounded.
assumptions_latex: g(k,\varepsilon)\text{ may be unbounded}.
knowledge_statements.title: FPT Exponent Boundary
Parameterized Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the fixed-parameter approximation-scheme regime, not every form of parameterized approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A fixed-parameter approximation scheme for a parameterized optimization problem is an algorithm \(A\) such that, for every instance \((x,k)\) and accuracy \(\varepsilon\in(0,1]\), it returns a feasible solution in time \(f(k,\varepsilon)|x|^c\), where \(f\) is computable and \(c\) is independent of \(k\) and \(\varepsilon\). For minimization, its value is at most \((1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(x,k)\); for maximization, its value is at least \(\operatorname{OPT}(x,k)/(1+\varepsilon)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed-parameter approximation scheme confines nonpolynomial dependence to the parameter and accuracy and achieves a multiplicative factor of 1+epsilon.
assumptions_latex: Each instance is a pair \((x,k)\) with parameter \(k\in\mathbb{N}\).
The accuracy satisfies \(\varepsilon\in(0,1]\).
Relevant optimum and feasible objective values are strictly positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_A(x,k,\varepsilon)\le f(k,\varepsilon)|x|^c\) with approximation ratio at most \(1+\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Computable parameter- and accuracy-dependent running-time factor.

children.title: Running-Time Regime Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Tradeoffs among polynomial, quasipolynomial, and parameter-dependent approximation.

knowledge_statements.title: Running-Time Regime Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares dependence on input length, parameter, and accuracy without asserting approximation-factor dominance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every polynomial bound \(n^{O(1)}\) is quasipolynomial, and every quasipolynomial bound \(\exp((\log n)^{O(1)})\) is at most exponential in a polynomial in \(n\). A parameterized bound \(f(k,\varepsilon)n^{O(1)}\) is polynomial in \(n\) when \(k\) and \(\varepsilon\) are fixed, but it need not be quasipolynomial when they vary with \(n\). Containment between running-time regimes alone implies no ordering of the approximation factors achieved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial time is contained in quasipolynomial time, while a parameterized bound is polynomial in input length only after fixing its parameters; runtime containment does not order approximation quality.
assumptions_latex: Constants hidden in asymptotic exponents are independent of the input length \(n\).
In a parameterized running-time bound, \(k\) and \(\varepsilon\) are distinguished from \(n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Polynomial-time bounds are quasipolynomial, quasipolynomial bounds are exponential-time bounds, and \(f(k,\varepsilon)n^{O(1)}\) is polynomial in \(n\) for fixed \((k,\varepsilon)\).

notation.meaning: Dependence on the parameter and accuracy independent of n.

source_refs.locator: Section 1.2, Running Time of Algorithms, p. 5

source_witnesses.locator: Section 1.2, Running Time of Algorithms, p. 5

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Condition under which an FPT-form upper bound yields a quasipolynomial upper bound after parameters and accuracy vary with input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T(n)\le f(k(n),\varepsilon(n))n^c\), where \(f\ge1\) and \(c\) is constant. If \[\log f(k(n),\varepsilon(n))=(\log n)^{O(1)},\] then \(T(n)=\exp((\log n)^{O(1)})\). If the displayed logarithm is not bounded by any fixed power of \(\log n\), this FPT-form upper bound alone does not establish quasipolynomial time, although a separate sharper runtime analysis might do so.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An FPT-form bound implies quasipolynomial time along a parameter-growth rule when the logarithm of its parameter factor is polylogarithmic in input size; failure of that condition only makes this bound inconclusive.
assumptions_latex: n\ge2.
f(k,\varepsilon)\ge1.
c\text{ is independent of }n,k,\varepsilon.

notation.meaning: Parameter growth as a function of input length
Accuracy schedule as a function of input length

children.title: Greedy Comparison Algorithm Family
children.top_down_role: Greedy constructions organized by their comparison mechanism.

children.title: Charging-Based Greedy Methods
children.top_down_role: Greedy families analyzed through allocation of cost or benefit.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded-load charging for additive nonnegative minimization objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G be feasible and O optimal, with c(G)=\sum_{g\in G}c_g and c(O)=\sum_{o\in O}c_o. If q(g,o)\ge0, \sum_{o\in O}q(g,o)\ge c_g for every g\in G, and \sum_{g\in G}q(g,o)\le\alpha c_o for every o\in O, then c(G)\le\alpha c(O).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If charges cover every greedy cost while loading each optimal object by at most alpha times its cost, the greedy solution is an alpha-approximation for minimization.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is feasible and }O\text{ is optimal.}
c_g,c_o,q(g,o)\ge0.
\alpha\ge1.

notation.meaning: charge from greedy object g to optimal object o

knowledge_statements.title: Minimization Charging Certificate
Charging-Based Greedy Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract maximization certificate underlying problem-specific charging analyses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(O\) and \(G\) have nonnegative additive contributions satisfying \(\operatorname{val}(O)=\sum_{o\in O}w_o\) and \(\operatorname{val}(G)=\sum_{g\in G}w_g\). Suppose nonnegative charges \(c(o,g)\) satisfy \(\sum_{g\in G}c(o,g)\ge w_o\) for every \(o\in O\) and \(\sum_{o\in O}c(o,g)\le\alpha w_g\) for every \(g\in G\). Then \(\operatorname{val}(O)\le\alpha\operatorname{val}(G)\), so \(G\) is an \(\alpha\)-approximation for the maximization instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A charging certificate covers every optimal contribution while limiting the charge placed on each greedy contribution, thereby proving the greedy approximation ratio.
assumptions_latex: The optimal and greedy solutions have nonnegative additive component contributions \(w_o\) and \(w_g\).
The load parameter satisfies \(\alpha\ge 1\).

notation.meaning: Charge assigned from optimal component o to greedy component g.

children.title: Exchange-Based Greedy Methods
children.top_down_role: Greedy families supported by replacement structure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unbounded Exchange Loss Makes Greedy Arbitrarily Bad
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of descending-weight greedy without bounded replacement structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let V=\{a,b_1,\ldots,b_m\} and let \mathcal I consist of all subsets of \{b_1,\ldots,b_m\} together with \varnothing and \{a\}. Give a weight 1+\varepsilon and every b_i weight 1. Descending-weight greedy selects a and stops, whereas \{b_1,\ldots,b_m\} has weight m.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single slightly heavier choice can block arbitrarily many compatible choices when no bounded exchange property holds.
assumptions_latex: m\ge2.
0<\varepsilon<1.
knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Exchange Loss Makes Greedy Arbitrarily Bad

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded-loss exchange structure supporting greedy approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A hereditary system (V,\mathcal I) is p-extendible if, whenever A\subseteq B\in\mathcal I, A\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I, and e\notin B, there exists Z\subseteq B\setminus A with |Z|\le p such that (B\setminus Z)\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A p-extendible system permits an insertion into a larger feasible set after deleting at most p elements outside a protected subset.
assumptions_latex: (V,\mathcal I)\text{ is finite and hereditary.}
p\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists Z\subseteq B\setminus A:\ |Z|\le p,\ (B\setminus Z)\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I.

notation.meaning: maximum number of displaced elements per insertion

knowledge_statements.title: p-Extendible Exchange System

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Descending-weight greedy for additive maximization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let (V,\mathcal I) be a finite p-extendible system with nonnegative weights. Scan elements in nonincreasing weight order and insert an element exactly when independence is preserved. The resulting G satisfies w(G)\ge p^{-1}\max_{I\in\mathcal I}w(I). For p=1 this specializes to exact matroid greedy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded exchange loss makes descending-weight greedy a p-approximation, with exactness for matroids.
assumptions_latex: (V,\mathcal I)\text{ is p-extendible.}
w_e\ge0\text{ for every }e.
\text{Feasibility is tested exactly.}
knowledge_statements.title: Greedy on p-Extendible Systems
Exchange-Based Greedy Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract additive maximization form of exchange-based greedy analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a greedy solution and \(O\) an optimal solution with nonnegative additive weights. Suppose exchange structure yields a map \(\phi:O\setminus G\to G\setminus O\) such that \(w(o)\le w(\phi(o))\) for every \(o\in O\setminus G\) and \(|\phi^{-1}(g)|\le\alpha\) for every \(g\in G\setminus O\), where \(\alpha\ge1\). Then \(w(O\setminus G)\le\alpha w(G\setminus O)\), and consequently \(w(O)\le\alpha w(G)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exchange-based analysis assigns each nongreedy optimal element to a dominating greedy choice and bounds how many optimal elements each greedy choice supports.
assumptions_latex: Feasible solutions are subsets of a finite ground set with nonnegative additive weights.
The exchange structure supplies the stated dominance map with preimage bound \(\alpha\ge1\).

notation.meaning: Assignment of nongreedy optimal elements to greedy elements justified by exchanges.

children.title: Diminishing-Returns Greedy Methods
children.top_down_role: Greedy families exploiting diminishing marginal improvement.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Priority-queue implementation of monotone submodular cardinality greedy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain for every unchosen e a key u_e that upper-bounds \Delta(e\mid S). Recompute a maximum-key element's true marginal and reset its key; accept it when its recomputed marginal is at least every remaining key. Submodularity preserves stale keys as upper bounds, so every accepted element maximizes the current true marginal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lazy greedy reuses stale marginals as upper bounds and recomputes until a true maximum-marginal element is certified.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is submodular and available through a value oracle.}
\text{Keys are initialized from valid marginal upper bounds and updated after recomputation.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Delta(e\mid S)=\max_{x\notin S}\Delta(x\mid S)\text{ for every accepted }e.

notation.meaning: stored upper bound on the current marginal of e

knowledge_statements.title: Lazy Exact Marginal Greedy

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Value-Oracle Cost of Direct Cardinality Greedy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Straightforward exact marginal-greedy implementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For |V|=n and cardinality bound k, evaluating every available marginal in each round uses at most \sum_{i=0}^{k-1}(n-i)\le kn marginal evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Direct cardinality greedy uses at most kn marginal evaluations.
assumptions_latex: 1\le k\le n.
\text{Each candidate's current marginal is evaluated in every round in which it remains available.}
knowledge_statements.title: Value-Oracle Cost of Direct Cardinality Greedy

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arbitrarily bad marginal greedy without submodularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For M>2, let V=\{a,b,c\}, k=2, f(\varnothing)=0, f(\{a\})=2, f(\{b\})=f(\{c\})=1, f(\{a,b\})=f(\{a,c\})=2, f(\{b,c\})=M, and f(V)=M+2. Then f is monotone, greedy returns value 2, and \operatorname{OPT}=M.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complementarity can make maximum-marginal greedy arbitrarily bad when monotonicity holds but submodularity does not.
assumptions_latex: \text{The cardinality bound is }k=2.
knowledge_statements.title: Monotonicity Without Diminishing Returns

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-set characterization used by marginal-gain greedy methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For f:2^V\to\mathbb R, the following are equivalent: f(A)+f(B)\ge f(A\cup B)+f(A\cap B) for all A,B\subseteq V; and \Delta(e\mid A)\ge\Delta(e\mid B) whenever A\subseteq B\subseteq V and e\notin B.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite set function is submodular exactly when each element's marginal gain cannot increase as the current set grows.
assumptions_latex: V\text{ is finite.}
\Delta(e\mid S)=f(S\cup\{e\})-f(S).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The lattice inequality is equivalent to diminishing marginal returns.}

notation.meaning: marginal gain of e relative to S

knowledge_statements.title: Diminishing-Returns Characterization of Submodularity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simple greedy for monotone submodular maximization over a matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let (V,\mathcal I) be a finite matroid and f:2^V\to\mathbb R_{\ge0} normalized, monotone, and submodular. Repeatedly add a feasible element of maximum marginal gain until a basis is reached. The resulting S satisfies f(S)\ge\tfrac12\max_{T\in\mathcal I}f(T).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximum-marginal feasible greedy is a one-half approximation for monotone submodular maximization under a matroid constraint.
assumptions_latex: (V,\mathcal I)\text{ is a finite matroid.}
f\text{ is normalized, nonnegative, monotone, and submodular.}
\text{Every step chooses a maximum-marginal feasible element.}
knowledge_statements.title: Matroid-Constrained Marginal Greedy Bound
Diminishing-Returns Greedy Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cardinality-constrained monotone submodular maximization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(S_0=\varnothing\). For \(i=0,\ldots,k-1\), choose \(v_i\in V\setminus S_i\) maximizing \(\Delta(v\mid S_i)\), and set \(S_{i+1}=S_i\cup\{v_i\}\). Output \(S_k\). For a normalized, nonnegative, monotone submodular function, \(f(S_k)\ge(1-(1-1/k)^k)\operatorname{OPT}\ge(1-e^{-1})\operatorname{OPT}\), where \(\operatorname{OPT}=\max_{|S|\le k}f(S)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Greedy repeatedly adds an element of largest marginal value and achieves at least a 1-1/e fraction for monotone submodular maximization under a cardinality bound.
assumptions_latex: The finite ground set is \(V\), and \(1\le k\le|V|\).
The function \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\) is normalized, monotone, and submodular.

notation.meaning: Marginal gain from adding v to S.
Optimal value under the cardinality constraint.

children.title: Local-Search Methods
children.top_down_role: Approximation through neighborhood design and structural properties of local optima.

children.title: Bounded-Exchange Local Search
children.top_down_role: Neighborhoods based on bounded-size replacements.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Brute-force inspection of delete-add neighborhoods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the ground set has at most n elements, all moves deleting at most b selected elements and adding at most b unselected elements can be enumerated using at most \left(\sum_{i=0}^b\binom ni\right)^2=O(n^{2b}) candidate checks for fixed b.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A complete scan of a constant-radius delete-add neighborhood uses polynomially many candidate checks, with an exponent depending on the radius.
assumptions_latex: b\text{ is fixed independently of the input size.}
\text{Feasibility and objective change can be checked for each candidate.}
knowledge_statements.title: Enumeration Cost for Constant-Radius Exchanges

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quality measure induced by a fixed exchange radius.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonnegative maximization instances I with optimum O_I and b-exchange local optima \mathcal L_b(I), define \operatorname{gap}_b=\sup_I\sup_{L\in\mathcal L_b(I)}f_I(O_I)/f_I(L), interpreting the ratio as +\infty when f_I(L)=0<f_I(O_I).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The locality gap is the worst ratio between a global optimum and a solution admitting no improving exchange of radius b.
assumptions_latex: f_I\ge0.
\text{Local optimality uses the specified feasible b-exchange neighborhood.}

notation.meaning: b-exchange local optima of instance I

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Exchange Locality Gap

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial Neighborhood Search Does Not Ensure Polynomial Termination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iteration boundary for exact bounded-exchange local search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Strict-improvement local search over a finite family performs at most |\mathcal F|-1 updates, but |\mathcal F| may be exponential in the input length. Without a polynomially bounded progress measure or minimum improvement, polynomial-time neighborhood inspection does not imply polynomial total running time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even if every bounded neighborhood is searchable in polynomial time, exact local search can require exponentially many improving moves.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal F\text{ is finite but may be exponentially large.}
\text{No polynomial progress bound is assumed.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\mathrm{updates}}\le|\mathcal F|-1\text{ need not be polynomial in the input length}.
knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Neighborhood Search Does Not Ensure Polynomial Termination
Bounded-Exchange Local Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic maximization local search with bounded additions and deletions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose an initial solution \(S_0\in\mathcal{F}\). At iteration \(t\), search \(N_b(S_t)\). If some \(S'\in N_b(S_t)\) satisfies \(f(S')>f(S_t)\), set \(S_{t+1}=S'\); otherwise stop and output \(S_t\). Because \(\mathcal{F}\) is finite and every accepted move strictly improves the objective, the process terminates at a solution \(S\) satisfying \(f(S')\le f(S)\) for every \(S'\in N_b(S)\). Polynomial running time and an approximation ratio require additional problem-specific hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded-exchange local search repeatedly replaces at most a fixed number of elements until no improving feasible bounded replacement remains.
assumptions_latex: The feasible family \(\mathcal{F}\subseteq2^V\) is finite.
The objective is \(f:\mathcal{F}\to\mathbb{R}\), and the exchange radius is an integer \(b\ge1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output \(S\) satisfies \(f(S')\le f(S)\) for every \(S'\in N_b(S)\).

notation.meaning: Feasible solutions obtained by deleting and adding at most b elements.

children.title: Geometric Local Search
children.top_down_role: Neighborhood guarantees derived from spatial locality or separators.

knowledge_statements.title: Geometric Local Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional separator-based analysis template, not a universal geometric approximation theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\) be locally optimal for all feasible exchanges of at most \(b\) objects, and let \(O\) be globally optimal for a geometric maximization problem. Suppose a locality or separator decomposition produces region exchanges of size at most \(b\), and the sum of their local nonimprovement inequalities, including all boundary multiplicities, implies \(f(O)\le f(L)+\varepsilon f(O)\). Then \(f(L)\ge(1-\varepsilon)f(O)\). Establishing the aggregate inequality and the required exchange size is problem dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Geometric local search uses bounded regional replacements and a locality or separator decomposition; a global approximation follows when the resulting local inequalities bound all boundary loss.
assumptions_latex: The feasible family is finite, \(L\) is locally optimal for exchanges of size at most \(b\), and \(O\) is globally optimal.
The objective is nonnegative, and \(0<\varepsilon<1\).
A problem-specific locality decomposition yields the stated aggregate inequality \(f(O)\le f(L)+\varepsilon f(O)\).

notation.meaning: Locally optimal and globally optimal geometric solutions.

children.title: Potential-Guided Local Search
children.top_down_role: Local improvement controlled by auxiliary progress measures.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Condition aligning the seed's permitted moves with approximation quality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let L have no neighbor y satisfying both f(y)>f(L) and \Phi(y)>\Phi(L). If, for every feasible benchmark O, f(O)>\alpha f(L) implies the existence of y\in N(L) satisfying both inequalities, then f(L)\ge\alpha^{-1}f(O) for every O.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Termination under the objective-and-potential move rule yields an approximation only when every sufficiently better benchmark forces a permitted improving neighbor.
assumptions_latex: \alpha\ge1.
\text{The benchmark-to-permitted-neighbor implication holds for the chosen }N,f,\Phi.
knowledge_statements.title: Potential-to-Objective Transfer Condition

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity boundary for bounded-integer progress potentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If every accepted move raises an integer potential by at least one and \Phi_{\min}\le\Phi(x)\le\Phi_{\max}, then at most \Phi_{\max}-\Phi_{\min} moves occur. This is polynomial only when that numerical range and the work per move are polynomial in the input length; a binary-encoded potential can have exponentially large range.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded integer potential proves termination, but only a polynomially bounded range and polynomial move search prove polynomial time.
assumptions_latex: \text{Each accepted move increases }\Phi\text{ by at least one.}
\text{Potential values and candidate moves are computable.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\le\Phi_{\max}-\Phi_{\min},\text{ which need not be polynomial in encoding length}.
knowledge_statements.title: Potential Range Versus Encoding Length
Potential-Guided Local Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract finite local search whose auxiliary potential guarantees termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a finite feasible set, \(f:S\to\mathbb{R}\) an objective to maximize, \(N(x)\subseteq S\) a neighborhood, and \(\Phi:S\to\mathbb{Z}\) a potential. Initialize \(x_0\in S\). At iteration \(t\), if some \(y\in N(x_t)\) satisfies \(f(y)>f(x_t)\) and \(\Phi(y)>\Phi(x_t)\), select one such \(y\) and set \(x_{t+1}=y\); otherwise stop and output \(x_t\). If \(\Phi(S)\subseteq\{0,\ldots,M\}\), the algorithm performs at most \(M\) updates and returns a solution having no permitted improving neighbor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly take an objective-improving move that strictly raises a bounded integer potential; termination occurs within the potential range at a locally optimal solution.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is finite and nonempty.
Every permitted update strictly increases both \(f\) and \(\Phi\).
\(\Phi(S)\subseteq\{0,\ldots,M\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method terminates after at most \(M\) updates at \(x\in S\) with no permitted improving neighbor.

The plain statement's “locally optimal” should be understood only relative to moves that improve both the objective and the potential.

children.title: Local-Ratio Methods
children.top_down_role: Weight-decomposition methods with locally preserved guarantees.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of composition when different solutions satisfy different components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \mathcal F=\{\{a\},\{b\}\}, with w^{(1)}_a=0,w^{(1)}_b=1 and w^{(2)}_a=1,w^{(2)}_b=0. Each component has an exact optimum, but no feasible solution is exact for both components; thus guarantees achieved by different solutions cannot be summed into a local-ratio certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local-ratio composition requires one returned solution to satisfy all component guarantees; unrelated component optima do not compose.
knowledge_statements.title: Common-Solution Requirement

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-component extension of the two-component local-ratio principle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \mathcal F\ne\varnothing and w=\sum_{j=1}^r w^{(j)} with nonnegative component weights. If one X\in\mathcal F satisfies w^{(j)}(X)\le\alpha\min_{Y\in\mathcal F}w^{(j)}(Y) for every j, then w(X)\le\alpha\min_{Y\in\mathcal F}w(Y).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A common alpha-approximate solution for every component of a finite weight decomposition is alpha-approximate for the total weight.
assumptions_latex: r\text{ is finite.}
w^{(j)}\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{U}\text{ for every }j.
\text{The same feasible }X\text{ satisfies every component guarantee.}
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Local-Ratio Composition
Local-Ratio Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local-ratio composition principle for minimization over nonnegative weight vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^U\) be a feasible family and let \(w=w^{(1)}+w^{(2)}\) with nonnegative component weights. For \(X\subseteq U\), write \(w(X)=\sum_{e\in X}w_e\). If \(X\in\mathcal F\) satisfies \(w^{(i)}(X)\leq \alpha\min_{Y\in\mathcal F}w^{(i)}(Y)\) for each \(i\in\{1,2\}\), then \(w(X)\leq\alpha\min_{Y\in\mathcal F}w(Y)\). A local-ratio algorithm recursively constructs such decompositions and returns a solution simultaneously satisfying the component guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An α-approximation for each part of an additive nonnegative weight decomposition is also an α-approximation for their sum.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F\) is nonempty.
The same \(X\in\mathcal F\) is an \(\alpha\)-approximation for both component objectives.
review_flags: Standard local-ratio lemma, but no supporting local source locator was supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is the standard local-ratio composition lemma and the principle kind fits the container, but no inspectable source locator is supplied.

children.title: Restriction-Partition Decomposition Family

children.title: Tractable Instance Restrictions
children.top_down_role: Approximation through restriction to tractable instance families.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restriction interface used by approximation decompositions, rather than the deferred generic promise-class definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An algorithmically usable restriction scheme for an optimization problem maps an instance \(I\) and restriction descriptor \(a\) to a subinstance \(I[a]\), and provides polynomial-time procedures that validate \(a\), construct \(I[a]\), solve \(I[a]\) exactly, and lift its solution back to a feasible partial or global solution of \(I\). Polynomial time is measured in the complete binary encoding of \((I,a)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A usable restriction must be constructible, recognizable, exactly solvable, and liftable in polynomial time, not merely easy under an uncheckable promise.
assumptions_latex: Instances and descriptors have finite binary encodings.

notation.meaning: subinstance selected by restriction descriptor a

knowledge_statements.title: Algorithmically Usable Restriction Scheme

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithmic limitations of nominally easy restricted subclasses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Polynomial-time optimization promised on a subclass does not yield a polynomial-time restriction method when membership or a valid restriction descriptor is computationally intractable. Likewise, polynomial-time solution of each restriction does not give an approximation algorithm if exponentially many restrictions must be searched without a selection rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Easy promised instances are unusable for decomposition when recognizing or finding them is hard, and easy individual restrictions do not help if exponentially many must be tried.
knowledge_statements.title: Promise-Recognition and Enumeration Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximation obtained by exactly solving one of a polynomially enumerable family of tractable restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonnegative maximization problem, suppose a polynomially enumerable family \(\mathcal A(I)\) of usable restrictions has the property that some \(a\in\mathcal A(I)\) admits a lifted optimum of value at least \((1-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(I)\). Exactly solving every \(I[a]\) and returning the best lifted solution is a \((1-\varepsilon)\)-approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If one enumerable tractable restriction retains at least a 1−ε share of optimum, solving all restrictions exactly and taking the best gives that approximation.
assumptions_latex: The objective is nonnegative and is being maximized.
\(\mathcal A(I)\) is polynomially enumerable.
Every restricted optimum can be feasibly lifted.
knowledge_statements.title: Restriction-Cover Approximation Principle
Tractable Instance Restrictions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restriction of an optimization problem to instances admitting exact polynomial-time solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an optimization problem \(\Pi\) with instance set \(\mathcal I\), a tractable instance restriction is a recognizable subclass \(\mathcal R\subseteq\mathcal I\) for which there exists an algorithm \(A\) and a polynomial \(p\) such that, for every encoded instance \(I\in\mathcal R\), \(A(I)\) returns an optimal feasible solution of \(I\) within \(p(|I|)\) elementary computation steps. Recognition of membership in \(\mathcal R\) must also take polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tractable restriction is a polynomial-time recognizable instance subclass on which an optimal solution can be computed in polynomial time.
assumptions_latex: Instances have finite encodings and a specified feasibility and objective relation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal R\) is tractable precisely when membership and exact optimization on \(\mathcal R\) are polynomial-time computable.
review_flags: The intended structural restriction family is not specified by the node path.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is coherent, but the taxonomy path suggests a particular restriction-decomposition family while the record gives only a generic complexity-theoretic definition. A source is needed to establish the intended local sense.

children.title: Partition-Based Decomposition
children.top_down_role: Approximation through controlled division into tractable subinstances.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Runtime and certificate size for an explicit finite-interface decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If each layer has at most \(S\) states and every transition value and witness is computed in time \(T\), the layered dynamic program uses at most \(O(kS^2)\) transitions, runs in \(O(kS^2T)\) time up to state-management overhead, and returns a certificate consisting of a state path and one block witness per transition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With at most S interface states per boundary, explicit assembly examines O(kS²) transitions and is polynomial only when the state space and block routines are polynomially bounded.
assumptions_latex: Interface states and transitions are explicitly enumerable.
A transition value and witness require time at most \(T\).

notation.meaning: maximum number of states at one interface

knowledge_statements.title: Interface-State Assembly Complexity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessity of representing all cross-block constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Blockwise feasibility and optimality do not imply global feasibility or optimality when two globally distinct boundary configurations share the same recorded state. In that case the layered program may combine locally feasible witnesses whose union violates an omitted cross-block constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partition method is unsound if its interface merges boundary configurations that have different global compatibility behavior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{nonseparating interface states}\Rightarrow\text{blockwise feasibility need not imply global feasibility}.
knowledge_statements.title: Incomplete-Interface Failure

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact representation of global solutions by block solutions and finite compatibility states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For blocks \(I_1,\ldots,I_k\), let \(\mathcal F_i(\sigma_{i-1},\sigma_i)\) be the feasible solutions of block \(i\) with incoming and outgoing interface states. If global feasibility is equivalent to the existence of states \(\sigma_0,\ldots,\sigma_k\) with \(X_i\in\mathcal F_i(\sigma_{i-1},\sigma_i)\) for every \(i\), and the objective is \(\sum_i f_i(X_i)\), then global optimization is a shortest- or longest-path dynamic program over the layered state graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When interface states exactly capture every cross-block constraint, compatible block solutions form paths in a layered state graph and can be optimized by dynamic programming.
assumptions_latex: The interface-state sets are finite.
The stated compatibility equivalence is exact.
The objective is additive across blocks.

notation.meaning: compatibility state at the boundary after block i
block-i solutions with interface states a and b

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Interface Block Decomposition
Partition-Based Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive decomposition of an instance across blocks plus boundary interactions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an instance have ground set \(U\), partition \(U=U_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}U_k\), and additive atom weights \(w\). For a feasible solution \(X\subseteq U\), put \(X_i=X\cap U_i\). If feasibility is determined by block constraints together with a boundary predicate \(B(X_1,\ldots,X_k)\), then \(X\) is represented by the tuple \((X_1,\ldots,X_k)\), with \(w(X)=\sum_{i=1}^k w(X_i)\). Consequently, global optimization reduces to selecting compatible block solutions and enforcing \(B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partition represents a global solution by block solutions; additive costs sum exactly, while a boundary predicate records cross-block compatibility.
assumptions_latex: \(U_1,\ldots,U_k\) are pairwise disjoint and cover \(U\).
The objective is additive over atoms.
All cross-block feasibility conditions are captured by \(B\).

notation.meaning: restriction of the solution to block i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The block representation is internally consistent under its assumptions, but no source establishes this abstract boundary-predicate formulation as the intended partition-based decomposition in this container.

children.title: Boundary-Loss Control
children.top_down_role: Quality effects caused by excluded structure or interactions across partitions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp limitations of atomwise boundary-loss accounting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A small counted boundary weight implies a small objective loss only when every lost contribution is charged to that boundary measure. With negative weights, nonadditive cross-block bonuses, or uncharged feasibility interactions, \(w(O\cap D)\le\varepsilon w(O)\) alone does not imply any \((1-O(\varepsilon))\) guarantee after deleting or repairing \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Small atomwise boundary weight is not a loss certificate when weights can be negative or valuable cross-block interactions are omitted from the charge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: w(O\cap D)\le\varepsilon w(O)\not\Rightarrow w(X)\ge(1-O(\varepsilon))w(O)\text{ without complete nonnegative charging}.
knowledge_statements.title: Boundary-Charging Failure Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Averaging certificate for choosing a decomposition whose boundary contains only a small share of a fixed reference solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D_1,\ldots,D_t\) be boundary sets and let \(O\) have nonnegative additive weight. If every atom of \(O\) belongs to at most \(b\) of the sets \(D_j\), then \(\sum_{j=1}^t w(O\cap D_j)\le b\,w(O)\). Hence some \(j\) satisfies \(w(O\cap D_j)\le (b/t)w(O)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If each optimal atom is exposed as boundary in at most b of t decompositions, one decomposition has boundary weight at most b/t of the optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(w\) is nonnegative and additive over atoms.
Each atom belongs to at most \(b\) boundary sets.

notation.meaning: maximum boundary multiplicity of an atom

knowledge_statements.title: Averaged Boundary-Share Lemma
Boundary-Loss Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximation loss bound for deleting or separately repairing partition-boundary interactions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(O\) be an optimal solution of nonnegative value \(w(O)\), and let a decomposition designate boundary atoms \(D\subseteq O\). Suppose the block algorithm preserves every atom of \(O\setminus D\), while its assembly or repair step loses at most \(\rho w(D)\), where \(0\leq\rho\leq1\). If \(w(D)\leq\varepsilon w(O)\), the assembled solution \(X\) satisfies \(w(X)\geq w(O)-\rho w(D)\geq(1-\rho\varepsilon)w(O)\). Thus a small boundary share yields a controlled multiplicative loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If boundary interactions contain at most an ε share of optimum and repair loses a ρ fraction of them, the result retains at least 1−ρε.
assumptions_latex: Atom weights are nonnegative and additive.
\(w(D)\leq\varepsilon w(O)\).
Assembly loses at most \(\rho w(D)\) relative to \(O\).

notation.meaning: boundary atoms of the reference solution

review_flags: This is an abstract accounting lemma; the intended decomposition-specific boundary theorem is unspecified.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The accounting inequality is correct once the stated loss assumption is imposed, but an authoritative source is needed to connect this generic property to the intended boundary-loss result.

children.title: Tree-Based Augmentation
children.top_down_role: Augmentation methods built around a connected acyclic backbone.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General weighted approximation obtained from the survivable-network cut formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Treat the tree edges as fixed zero-cost edges and impose residual cut requirement \(f(S)=\max\{0,2-|\delta_T(S)|\}\) on selectable links. This is exactly the tree-edge-cover LP. Standard survivable-network iterative rounding returns, for every feasible nonnegative-cost instance, a link set \(A\) with \[c(A)\leq2\operatorname{OPT}_{LP}\leq2\operatorname{OPT}_{TAP}\] in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Survivable-network iterative rounding gives an LP-relative factor-two approximation for weighted tree augmentation.
assumptions_latex: The weighted tree-augmentation instance is feasible.
Link costs are nonnegative.
The standard skew-supermodular survivable-network iterative-rounding framework is used.

notation.meaning: residual cut requirement after fixing the tree edges
optimum of the fractional tree-edge-cover LP

review_flags: A source should verify the exact LP-relative iterative-rounding specialization.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonintegrality of the Tree-Edge Cut Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit integrality-gap instance for the canonical tree-edge-cover LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be a three-leaf star and give unit cost to the three links joining pairs of leaves. Assigning \(x_\ell=\tfrac12\) to every link covers each spoke to value one and costs \(3/2\). Every integral augmentation needs at least two links, and two suffice. Thus \(\operatorname{OPT}_{LP}=3/2<2=\operatorname{OPT}_{IP}\), giving gap \(4/3\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A three-leaf star with a triangle of leaf links has fractional optimum 3/2 and integral optimum 2.
assumptions_latex: All three leaf-to-leaf links have unit cost.
The relaxation consists of tree-edge covering inequalities and nonnegativity.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonintegrality of the Tree-Edge Cut Relaxation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical covering formulation of minimum-cost two-edge-connectivity augmentation of a tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each link \(\ell=uv\), let \(P_T(\ell)\) be its unique \(u\)-\(v\) path in \(T\). Weighted tree augmentation is \[\min\sum_{\ell\in L}c_\ell x_\ell\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\sum_{\ell:e\in P_T(\ell)}x_\ell\geq1\ (e\in E_T),\qquad x_\ell\in\{0,1\}.\] Its feasible vectors are exactly the link sets making \(T\) two-edge-connected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted tree augmentation covers every tree edge by the unique tree path of a selected link.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is a finite tree.
\(L\) is a finite set of undirected candidate links.
\(c_\ell\geq0\) for every link.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ is feasible}\iff T\cup\{\ell:x_\ell=1\}\text{ is two-edge-connected}.

notation.meaning: unique tree path joining the endpoints of link ell

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Tree Augmentation Formulation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Packing dual of the standard fractional tree-edge-cover relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Replacing integrality by \(x_\ell\geq0\) gives a linear program whose dual is \[\max\sum_{e\in E_T}y_e\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\sum_{e\in P_T(\ell)}y_e\leq c_\ell\ (\ell\in L),\qquad y_e\geq0.\] Equal primal and dual values certify LP optimality; if the primal cover is integral, they also certify integer optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cut LP is dual to packing weights on tree edges subject to each link path's cost.
assumptions_latex: The fractional tree-edge-cover LP is feasible and bounded.
Link costs are nonnegative.

notation.meaning: dual weight on tree edge e

knowledge_statements.title: Cut-LP Dual for Tree Augmentation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Augmentation on a Path Backbone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact restricted tree-augmentation family whose link paths are intervals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the backbone \(T\) is a path, each link covers a consecutive interval of tree edges. The edge-by-link incidence matrix consequently has the consecutive-ones property and is totally unimodular. Thus the standard covering relaxation has an integral optimum, and minimum-cost augmentation of a path can be solved exactly in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a path backbone, link paths are intervals and the covering LP is integral, giving an exact polynomial-time algorithm.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is a finite path.
Candidate links and nonnegative rational costs are explicitly encoded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{OPT}_{LP}=\operatorname{OPT}_{TAP}\text{, and an optimum is computable in polynomial time.}
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Augmentation on a Path Backbone

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Star Augmentation as Minimum-Cost Edge Cover
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact restricted-family representation when selectable links join leaves of a star.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be a star with leaf set \(R\), and suppose every candidate link joins two distinct leaves. Each link covers exactly the two spokes incident with its endpoints. Hence a link set augments \(T\) to two-edge-connectivity exactly when it is an edge cover of the candidate graph \((R,L)\). Minimum-cost star augmentation is therefore minimum-cost edge cover, including detection of infeasibility, and is polynomial-time solvable by weighted-matching methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Leaf-to-leaf augmentation of a star is exactly minimum-cost edge cover on its leaves.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is a finite star.
Every candidate link joins two distinct leaves.
Link costs are nonnegative rational numbers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\text{ augments }T\iff A\text{ is an edge cover of }(R,L).
knowledge_statements.title: Star Augmentation as Minimum-Cost Edge Cover

knowledge_statements.statement_title: NP-Hardness Boundary for General Tree Augmentation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity boundary separating general tree backbones from the accepted path and star cases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Minimum-cardinality Tree Augmentation is NP-hard on general tree backbones. Therefore, unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\), the exact polynomial-time algorithms for path backbones and leaf-link star instances do not extend to arbitrary trees and link sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: General unweighted tree augmentation is NP-hard, despite polynomially solvable path and leaf-link star restrictions.
assumptions_latex: Candidate links are explicitly listed.
The objective is the number of selected links.
knowledge_statements.title: NP-Hardness Boundary for General Tree Augmentation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial feasibility recognition for explicitly listed tree-augmentation links.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A tree-augmentation instance \((T,L)\) is feasible if and only if every tree edge belongs to \(P_T(\ell)\) for at least one candidate link \(\ell\in L\). Computing the union of all candidate-link paths therefore either certifies feasibility or returns an uncovered tree edge; deleting that edge gives a cut crossed by no candidate link and certifies infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tree augmentation is feasible exactly when the listed link paths cover every tree edge; an uncovered edge certifies infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is a finite tree.
The candidate links \(L\) are explicitly listed.

notation.meaning: Unique tree path between the endpoints of link ell.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility Test and Uncovered-Edge Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary lower certificate for unweighted tree augmentation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r\) be the number of leaves of a nontrivial tree \(T\). Every feasible augmentation must cover all \(r\) leaf-incident tree edges, while a link path contains at most two such edges. Hence every feasible link set \(A\) satisfies \(|A|\ge\lceil r/2\rceil\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Covering all leaf edges requires at least half as many links as the tree has leaves.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is a finite tree with at least two vertices.
Links join distinct vertices.
The objective is link cardinality.

notation.meaning: Number of leaves of the tree.

knowledge_statements.title: Leaf-Edge Cardinality Lower Bound

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical preprocessing closure for tree-augmentation link sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A link \(\ell'\) is a shadow of \(\ell\) when \(P_T(\ell')\subseteq P_T(\ell)\). Add every shadow \(\ell'\) with cost \[c'(\ell')=\min\{c(\ell):P_T(\ell')\subseteq P_T(\ell)\}.\] The completed instance has the same optimum as the original: original solutions remain available, and each selected shadow can be replaced by an original minimum-cost containing link whose path covers a superset at the same cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding every subpath shadow at the cheapest containing-link cost preserves the tree-augmentation optimum.
assumptions_latex: The backbone is a finite tree.
Candidate links and nonnegative costs are explicitly represented.
Parallel links may be retained or consolidated by minimum cost.

notation.meaning: Unique tree path covered by link ell.
Cost assigned to a shadow link.

knowledge_statements.title: Cost-Preserving Shadow Completion
Tree-Based Augmentation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cut-cover formulation of two-edge-connectivity augmentation of a tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T=(V,E_T)\) be a tree and let \(L\subseteq\binom{V}{2}\setminus E_T\) be candidate links. For \(e\in E_T\), deleting \(e\) induces a cut \(\delta_T(e)\). A link \(\ell=uv\) covers \(e\) when \(u\) and \(v\) lie on opposite sides of this cut. For \(A\subseteq L\), the graph \((V,E_T\cup A)\) is two-edge-connected if and only if every tree edge is covered by at least one link in \(A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Links augment a tree to two-edge-connectivity exactly when every tree edge lies on the tree path of at least one chosen link.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is a finite tree.
Links are undirected edges joining distinct vertices of \(T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((V,E_T\cup A)\) is two-edge-connected if and only if \(\sum_{\ell\text{ covers }e}\mathbf 1[\ell\in A]\geq1\) for every \(e\in E_T\).

notation.meaning: cut induced by deleting tree edge e

review_flags: Standard tree-augmentation characterization, but no matching source locator was supplied.

children.title: Forest-Based Augmentation
children.top_down_role: Augmentation methods built around multiple acyclic components.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact optimization of nonnegative-cost links for ordinary connectivity of a spanning forest.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Contract each of the \(q\) components of \(F\), discard links internal to a component, and form the weighted component multigraph \(H\). A connectivity augmentation exists exactly when \(H\) is connected. If all link costs are nonnegative, lifting any minimum spanning tree of \(H\) gives a minimum-cost augmentation. After the components are known, a comparison-based implementation runs in \(O(|L|\log q)\) time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With nonnegative link costs, connecting a forest reduces exactly to a minimum spanning tree in its contracted component graph.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a finite spanning forest with \(q\) components.
Candidate links are undirected and have nonnegative costs.
The target is ordinary connectivity.

notation.meaning: weighted multigraph obtained by contracting the forest components

review_flags: Nonnegativity is essential: with negative-cost links, an optimum may include additional links beyond an MST.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Cost Forest Connectivity by Contraction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cardinality and certificate structure of inclusion-minimal forest-connectivity augmentations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) have \(q\geq1\) components and let \(A\) connect them. Then \(A\) contains a feasible subset of exactly \(q-1\) intercomponent links. Moreover, \(A\) is inclusion-minimal feasible if and only if it contains no link internal to a component of \(F\) and its contracted component multigraph \(H_A\) is a tree. Consequently every inclusion-minimal augmentation has \(q-1\) links.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every feasible augmentation contains a component-spanning tree, and the inclusion-minimal augmentations are exactly those trees with no irrelevant intracomponent links.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a finite spanning forest with \(q\) components.
\(A\) is a set of candidate links.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\text{ is inclusion-minimal feasible}\iff A\text{ has no intracomponent link and }H_A\text{ is a tree}.

notation.meaning: component multigraph induced by the intercomponent links of A

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal Forest-Connectivity Augmentations
Forest-Based Augmentation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cut characterization for augmenting a spanning forest to a connected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=(V,E_F)\) be a finite spanning forest with components \(C_1,\ldots,C_q\), and let \(L\subseteq\binom{V}{2}\setminus E_F\) be candidate links. Contract every \(C_i\) to one vertex and let \(H_A\) be the resulting multigraph formed by links \(A\subseteq L\) whose endpoints lie in different components. Then \((V,E_F\cup A)\) is connected if and only if \(H_A\) is connected, equivalently if every nonempty proper union of components is crossed by a selected link.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A forest becomes connected exactly when selected links connect its contracted component graph, or equivalently cross every nontrivial component cut.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a finite spanning forest.
Only links with endpoints in distinct forest components affect component connectivity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((V,E_F\cup A)\) is connected if and only if \(H_A\) is connected.

notation.meaning: component multigraph induced by selected links

review_flags: The title may instead intend higher-connectivity forest augmentation.

children.title: Connectivity-Restoration Regimes
children.top_down_role: Connectivity requirements imposed on augmented tree or forest structures.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimum-Cost Connectivity Restoration by Component Contraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact target-connectivity-one regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(k=1\), contract every connected component of \(G_0\) to one vertex and retain candidate links as weighted multiedges. Restoration is feasible exactly when the quotient is connected; with nonnegative costs, a minimum spanning tree of the quotient gives a minimum-cost augmentation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ordinary connectivity restoration is exactly an MST problem after contracting existing components.
assumptions_latex: Candidate-link costs are nonnegative.
The graph and link set are finite and undirected.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Cost Connectivity Restoration by Component Contraction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact existence obstruction and verifier for target edge connectivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A feasible augmentation exists exactly when \(|\delta_{E_0}(S)|+|\delta_L(S)|\ge k\) for every nontrivial \(S\subset V\), since selecting all candidate links then meets every cut. For a proposed augmentation \(A\), a global minimum cut of value at least \(k\) certifies feasibility; a smaller cut certifies its failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Candidate insufficiency across a cut exactly certifies impossibility, while a minimum-cut computation verifies a proposed augmentation.
assumptions_latex: Edges are undirected and counted with multiplicity.
Each candidate link may be selected at most once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists A\subseteq L:\lambda(V,E_0\cup A)\ge k\iff \lambda(V,E_0\cup L)\ge k.
knowledge_statements.title: Cut Certificates for Connectivity Restoration

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Edge-Cut Restoration Does Not Characterize Vertex Connectivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit boundary between edge- and vertex-connectivity augmentation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Two triangles sharing exactly one vertex have no bridge and hence are \(2\)-edge-connected, but deleting their common vertex disconnects the graph, so they are not \(2\)-vertex-connected. Therefore residual edge-cut inequalities do not characterize vertex-connectivity restoration, which requires separator, set-pair, or biset deficiencies.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two triangles sharing an articulation vertex satisfy the two-edge-connectivity cut condition but fail two-vertex-connectivity.
assumptions_latex: The graph is finite, simple, and undirected.
knowledge_statements.title: Edge-Cut Restoration Does Not Characterize Vertex Connectivity
Connectivity-Restoration Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cut-demand condition for restoring a prescribed edge-connectivity level.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G_0=(V,E_0)\) be a finite undirected graph, let \(L\subseteq\binom{V}{2}\setminus E_0\) be a finite set of candidate links, and fix an integer \(k\geq1\). For every \(\varnothing\neq S\neqq V\), define \(r(S)=\max\{0,k-|\delta_{E_0}(S)|\}\). A selected set \(A\subseteq L\) restores \(k\)-edge-connectivity exactly when \(|A\cap\delta_L(S)|\geq r(S)\) for every such \(S\). The regime \(k=1\) restores connectivity, while \(k=2\) also eliminates bridges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restoring k-edge-connectivity requires and suffices to add enough links across every nontrivial cut to meet its residual demand.
assumptions_latex: \(G_0\) and all candidate links are finite and undirected.
Parallel edges, when present, are counted with multiplicity.
\(k\) is a positive integer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((V,E_0\cup A)\) is \(k\)-edge-connected if and only if \(|A\cap\delta_L(S)|\geq r(S)\) for every \(\varnothing\neq S\neqq V\).

notation.meaning: edges of E with exactly one endpoint in S
residual connectivity demand of cut S
