Hyperplane Rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Random-hyperplane rounding of unit vectors to binary signs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given unit vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\mathbb R^d\), sample \(g\sim N(0,I_d)\) and output \(x_i=1\) when \(\langle g,v_i\rangle\ge0\), and \(x_i=-1\) otherwise. Independent repetitions may be evaluated and the best rounded solution retained. For every pair \(i,j\), rotational invariance gives \[\Pr[x_i\ne x_j]=\frac{\arccos(\langle v_i,v_j\rangle)}{\pi}.\] Thus the expected value of any weighted cut objective is obtained by replacing each relaxed inner product with its angular separation probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A random origin-centered hyperplane assigns signs by vector side; two vectors are separated with probability equal to their angle divided by pi.

notation.meaning: Gaussian normal defining the random hyperplane.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Gaussian-hyperplane algorithm and angular separation identity are mathematically standard and fit the algorithm container, but the record supplies no source or locator. An authoritative rounding reference is required.

children.title: Gaussian Rounding
children.top_down_role: Rounding based on Gaussian directions, thresholds, or projections.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multi-coordinate extension of one-direction Gaussian projection rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_{ij}=\langle v_i,v_j\rangle\), and independently sample \(g^{(1)},\ldots,g^{(k)}\sim N(0,I_d)\). Define \(Y_{i\ell}=\langle g^{(\ell)},v_i\rangle\). Then \[\operatorname{Cov}(Y_{i\ell},Y_{jm})=X_{ij}\mathbf1_{\{\ell=m\}},\] so the columns of \(Y\) are independent copies of \(N(0,X)\). A specified measurable vector quantizer \(Q_i:\mathbb R^k\to\mathcal L_i\) yields \(x_i=Q_i(Y_{i1},\ldots,Y_{ik})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent Gaussian directions produce independent projection columns with covariance X, permitting vector-valued finite-label quantizers.
assumptions_latex: \(g^{(1)},\ldots,g^{(k)}\) are independent standard Gaussian vectors.
Each \(Q_i\) is measurable with finite range \(\mathcal L_i\).
knowledge_statements.title: Independent Multi-Projection Gaussian Rounding
Gaussian Rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gaussian projection followed by scalar quantization or thresholding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\mathbb R^d\), sample \(g\sim N(0,I_d)\), form correlated projections \(y_i=\langle g,v_i\rangle\), and output \(x_i=Q_i(y_i)\), where each measurable quantizer \(Q_i:\mathbb R\to\mathcal L_i\) maps to the required finite label set. The algorithm returns the resulting labeled solution, optionally choosing the best of finitely many independent samples. The projection vector \(y\) is jointly Gaussian with \[\mathbb E[y_i]=0,\qquad \mathbb E[y_i y_j]=\langle v_i,v_j\rangle,\] so the SDP Gram matrix determines every joint projection distribution used by the rounding rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gaussian rounding projects SDP vectors onto one Gaussian direction and quantizes the correlated scalar projections into feasible labels.
assumptions_latex: Each \(Q_i\) is measurable and has range \(\mathcal L_i\).

notation.meaning: Scalar label quantizer for variable i.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The covariance identity is correct for Gaussian projections, and the construction is an algorithm, but the unrestricted family of variable-specific measurable quantizers is broader than many named Gaussian-rounding schemes. With no citation, the intended variant and scope cannot be verified.

children.title: Projection-Based Regimes
children.top_down_role: Geometric rounding classified by the role of vector projections.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection-Based Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unified representation of one-dimensional projection rounding regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v_i\in\mathbb R^d\), sample a random direction \(g\), and set \(y_i=\langle g,v_i\rangle\). A projection-based rounding regime is specified by a measurable partition \(\{R_{i,a}:a\in\mathcal L_i\}\) of \(\mathbb R\), with output \(x_i=a\) exactly when \(y_i\in R_{i,a}\). Binary hyperplane rounding is the special case \(R_{i,+}=[0,\infty)\) and \(R_{i,-}=(-\infty,0)\). Multi-threshold and asymmetric regimes arise from interval partitions, while randomized thresholds are represented by enlarging the sampled randomness. Feasibility requires that the resulting label vector belong to the combinatorial feasible set almost surely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection rounding is determined by a random direction and measurable scalar regions that convert each projection into a label, subject to almost-sure feasibility.
assumptions_latex: The regions \(R_{i,a}\) measurably partition \(\mathbb R\).
The sampled output is feasible almost surely.

notation.meaning: Projection region producing label a for variable i.
Finite label set of variable i.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation covers coordinatewise one-dimensional projection rules, but it does not by itself cover all projection-based rounding regimes. The treatment of randomized thresholds also requires a formally parameterized random partition. A source defining the intended regime is needed before the statement can be fixed reliably.

children.title: Moment-Correlation Rounding Interface
children.top_down_role: Semidefinite rounding for quadratic and correlation objectives.

children.title: Quadratic-Objective Rounding
children.top_down_role: Semidefinite rounding organized around quadratic objective structure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-over-Pi Guarantee for Positive-Semidefinite Quadratic Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gaussian-sign approximation for PSD binary quadratic maximization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\succeq0\), and let \(X\) satisfy \(X\succeq0\) and \(X_{ii}=1\). Gaussian-sign rounding gives \[\mathbb E[x^{\mathsf T}Qx]=\left\langle Q,\frac{2}{\pi}\arcsin[X]\right\rangle\ge\frac{2}{\pi}\langle Q,X\rangle.\] Consequently, if \(X\) is optimal for \(\max\{\langle Q,X\rangle:X\succeq0,\ X_{ii}=1\}\), then \[\mathbb E[x^{\mathsf T}Qx]\ge(2/\pi)\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{SDP}}\ge(2/\pi)\operatorname{OPT}_{\pm1}.\] The PSD assumption on \(Q\) is essential to this universal comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gaussian-sign rounding gives a two-over-pi approximation for maximizing a positive-semidefinite quadratic form over binary signs.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\succeq0\).
\(X\succeq0\) and \(X_{ii}=1\).
knowledge_statements.title: Two-over-Pi Guarantee for Positive-Semidefinite Quadratic Forms
Quadratic-Objective Rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gaussian-sign rounding for binary quadratic objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be symmetric and let \(X\succeq0\) satisfy \(X_{ii}=1\). Factor \(X=V^{\mathsf T}V\), sample \(g\sim N(0,I)\), and output \(x_i=\operatorname{sgn}(\langle g,v_i\rangle)\), using either sign at zero. The rounded vector lies in \(\{-1,1\}^n\), and its quadratic objective has expectation \[\mathbb E[x^{\mathsf T}Qx]=\sum_{i,j}Q_{ij}\frac{2}{\pi}\arcsin(X_{ij}).\] Repeated independent samples followed by objective evaluation may be used to return the best observed feasible vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Factor the SDP correlation matrix, apply Gaussian-sign rounding, and evaluate samples; the expected quadratic value follows the entrywise arcsine transform.
assumptions_latex: \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\).
\(X\succeq0\) and \(X_{ii}=1\) for every \(i\).

notation.meaning: Gram factor whose columns are the vectors v_i.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Gaussian-sign rounding algorithm and entrywise arcsine expectation formula are mathematically consistent and fit an algorithm leaf. No cited source or inspectable locator supports the identity.

children.title: Correlation-Structure Rounding
children.top_down_role: Semidefinite rounding organized around pairwise or higher-order correlation information.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Higher-order correlations induced by centered Gaussian-sign rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z\sim N(0,X)\), where \(X\succeq0\) has unit diagonal, and set \(x_i=\operatorname{sgn}(Z_i)\). For every \(S\subseteq[n]\), \[\mathbb E\!\left[\prod_{i\in S}x_i\right]=\sum_{\varepsilon\in\{-1,1\}^{S}}\left(\prod_{i\in S}\varepsilon_i\right)\Pr[\varepsilon_iZ_i>0\ \forall i\in S].\] Central symmetry gives \(\mathbb E[\prod_{i\in S}x_i]=0\) whenever \(|S|\) is odd. Even higher-order moments are determined by Gaussian orthant probabilities for the corresponding principal submatrix of \(X\), not by independently applying the pairwise arcsine formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Odd Gaussian-sign moments vanish, while even higher-order moments are signed sums of Gaussian orthant probabilities.
assumptions_latex: \(X\succeq0\) and \(X_{ii}=1\).

notation.meaning: Centered Gaussian vector with covariance X.
Index set of a sign moment.

knowledge_statements.title: Higher-Order Sign Correlations
Correlation-Structure Rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correlation map induced by Gaussian-sign rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\in\mathbb S^n_+\) have unit diagonal, choose vectors satisfying \(X_{ij}=\langle v_i,v_j\rangle\), sample \(g\sim N(0,I)\), and set \(x_i=\operatorname{sgn}(\langle g,v_i\rangle)\). Then the rounded correlation matrix \(C=\mathbb E[xx^{\mathsf T}]\) is given entrywise by \[C_{ij}=\frac{2}{\pi}\arcsin(X_{ij}).\] Consequently \(C\) belongs to the convex hull of binary rank-one matrices \(xx^{\mathsf T}\), even though the relaxed matrix \(X\) need not belong to that hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gaussian-sign rounding converts an SDP correlation matrix through the entrywise arcsine map into realizable binary correlations.
assumptions_latex: \(X\succeq0\) and \(X_{ii}=1\).
\(g\) is a standard Gaussian vector.

notation.meaning: Correlation matrix of the rounded signs.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The arcsine correlation map and convex-hull conclusion are mathematically consistent and fit a representation container, but the record has no citation or locator.

children.title: Moment-Consistency Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on translating relaxed moment information into discrete solutions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit dimension-three separation between PSD and binary moment consistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[X=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1/2&-1/2\\-1/2&1&-1/2\\-1/2&-1/2&1\end{pmatrix}.\] Its eigenvalues are \(0,3/2,3/2\), so \(X\in\mathcal E_3\). Binary realizability would require \(1+X_{12}+X_{13}+X_{23}\ge0\), but the left side equals \(-1/2\). Hence \(X\notin\operatorname{COR}_{\pm}(3)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The three-dimensional equicorrelation matrix with off-diagonal entries minus one-half is positive semidefinite but is not a binary correlation matrix.
knowledge_statements.title: Smallest Elliptope Consistency Counterexample

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact consistency test for three binary pair moments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A triple \((r_{12},r_{13},r_{23})\in[-1,1]^3\) is realizable as \(r_{ij}=\mathbb E[x_ix_j]\) for random \(x\in\{-1,1\}^3\) if and only if \[1+a r_{12}+b r_{13}+c r_{23}\ge0\] for every \((a,b,c)\in\{-1,1\}^3\) satisfying \(abc=1\). Equivalently, \(p_{abc}=(1+a r_{12}+b r_{13}+c r_{23})/4\), indexed by \(abc=1\), is a probability distribution for \((x_1x_2,x_1x_3,x_2x_3)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Three pair correlations are jointly realizable by binary signs exactly when four tetrahedral inequalities hold.

notation.meaning: Probability of the indicated triple of pair products.

knowledge_statements.title: Three-Variable Binary-Correlation Characterization

assumptions_latex: \(n\) is an integer with \(n\ge 3\).
Only moments through degree two are specified.

notation.meaning: Convex set of realizable binary correlation matrices.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between semidefinite second moments and realizable binary moments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an integer \(n\ge 3\), define \[\operatorname{COR}_{\pm}(n)=\operatorname{conv}\{xx^{\mathsf T}:x\in\{-1,1\}^n\}\] and \[\mathcal E_n=\{X\in\mathbb S^n:X\succeq0,\ X_{ii}=1\text{ for every }i\}.\] Every realizable binary second-moment matrix belongs to \(\mathcal E_n\), but the converse fails: \[\operatorname{COR}_{\pm}(n)\subsetneq\mathcal E_n.\] Thus positive semidefiniteness and unit diagonal guarantee a Gram representation but do not guarantee a joint binary distribution having the specified pairwise moments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every dimension n at least three, realizable binary correlation matrices form a strict subset of the unit-diagonal positive semidefinite matrices; valid SDP second moments therefore need not be exact moments of any joint binary distribution.
knowledge_statements.title: Moment-Consistency Boundaries

children.title: Semidefinite CSP Rounding
children.top_down_role: Semidefinite architectures for constraint-satisfaction objectives.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basic Local-Distribution SDP for Finite-Domain CSPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical SDP architecture coupling label vectors to constraint-local distributions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite-domain weighted maximization CSP, introduce a unit vector \(v_0\), vectors \(v_{i,a}\) for variable-label pairs, and for each constraint \(C\) a distribution \(\lambda_C\) on assignments to its scope. Impose \[\sum_a v_{i,a}=v_0,\qquad \langle v_{i,a},v_{i,b}\rangle=0\quad(a\ne b),\] and require the one- and two-variable marginals of every \(\lambda_C\) to equal the corresponding squared norms and inner products. The objective is \(\sum_C w_C\mathbb E_{\sigma\sim\lambda_C}[P_C(\sigma)]\). Every integral assignment embeds in this relaxation, so its optimum upper-bounds the integral optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The basic finite-domain CSP SDP couples orthogonal label vectors to consistent constraint-local distributions and upper-bounds maximization CSPs.
assumptions_latex: Variable domains and constraint scopes are finite.
Constraint weights are nonnegative.
The displayed marginal constraints are imposed for labels and variable pairs occurring in each constraint scope.

notation.meaning: Vector representing label a for variable i.

knowledge_statements.title: Basic Local-Distribution SDP for Finite-Domain CSPs

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst integral value compatible with a specified basic-SDP value for a fixed normalized CSP language.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a finite-domain maximization CSP language \(\Gamma\), normalize each instance to total constraint weight one, and let \(c\in[0,1]\) be such that the defining class below is nonempty. Define \[g_\Gamma(c)=\inf\{\operatorname{OPT}(I): I\text{ is a }\Gamma\text{-instance and }\operatorname{SDP}(I)\ge c\}.\] Any uniform lower guarantee depending only on \(\operatorname{SDP}(I)\ge c\) is at most \(g_\Gamma(c)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The basic-SDP gap curve is the worst integral optimum among normalized instances whose SDP value is at least a given level.
assumptions_latex: \(\Gamma\) is a fixed finite-domain CSP language.
Constraint weights are nonnegative and sum to one.
The class of instances with \(\operatorname{SDP}(I)\ge c\) is nonempty.

notation.meaning: Basic-SDP integrality-gap curve for language Gamma.

knowledge_statements.title: Basic-SDP Integrality-Gap Curve

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Universally defined rounding of the basic finite-domain CSP SDP that ignores cross-variable correlations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each variable \(i\), independently output label \(a\) with probability \(p_{i,a}=\|v_{i,a}\|^2\). Under the basic-SDP normalization, \(p_{i,a}\ge0\) and \(\sum_a p_{i,a}=1\), so this produces a feasible assignment. For a constraint \(C\), \[\mathbb E[P_C(x)]=\sum_{\sigma:P_C(\sigma)=1}\prod_{i\in\operatorname{scope}(C)}p_{i,\sigma_i}.\] This rule alone provides no language-independent comparison with the correlated SDP objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sampling variables independently from their SDP label marginals is feasible but discards the SDP's cross-variable correlations.
assumptions_latex: The basic SDP label vectors satisfy orthogonality and normalization with \(\|v_0\|=1\).
Variable domains are finite.

notation.meaning: Marginal probability assigned to label a of variable i.

knowledge_statements.title: Independent Marginal Rounding Baseline

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Independent Rounding Loses Perfect Equality Correlation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit witness that correct SDP marginals do not preserve constraint-local correlations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider two Boolean variables with one equality constraint. A basic-SDP local distribution may satisfy \(\lambda(0,0)=\lambda(1,1)=1/2\), giving SDP value one and uniform marginals for both variables. Independent marginal rounding satisfies equality with probability \(1/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A perfectly satisfied SDP equality constraint can fall to satisfaction probability one half under independent marginal rounding.
assumptions_latex: The CSP domain is \(\{0,1\}\).
The sole predicate accepts exactly equal labels.
knowledge_statements.title: Independent Rounding Loses Perfect Equality Correlation
Semidefinite CSP Rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic local-vector rounding architecture for finite-domain CSPs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite-domain CSP, solve an SDP assigning vectors \(v_{i,a}\) to variable-label pairs, with orthogonality, normalization, and constraint-local consistency conditions. Sample shared randomness \(\omega\), and for each variable output a label according to a measurable rule \(x_i=R_i(\{v_{i,a}\}_{a},\omega)\). The rules must produce exactly one label per variable and hence a feasible assignment to the CSP variables. Their joint law is chosen so that, for every constraint \(C\), the satisfaction probability \(\Pr[C(x)=1]\) is bounded below as a function of the corresponding SDP local moments. The algorithm returns the sampled assignment, or the best of repeated samples.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve a vector SDP, use shared randomness to round each variable to one label, and relate every constraint’s satisfaction probability to its SDP moments.
assumptions_latex: The CSP has finite variable domains.
The SDP vectors satisfy the selected relaxation's local consistency constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_i\) is a single valid label for every variable, with constraint values analyzed from SDP local moments.

notation.meaning: SDP vector for assigning label a to variable i.
Randomized rounding rule for variable i.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a broad architecture rather than a fully specified CSP rounding algorithm: the SDP constraints, rounding law, and lower-bound function are left unspecified. Different CSP relaxations require materially different hypotheses and analyses, so an authoritative source identifying a concrete variant is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: UGC Optimality of the Basic SDP Integrality-Gap Curve
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proposed conditional approximation frontier for fixed finite-domain CSP languages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed finite-domain CSP language, the proposed statement asserts that, assuming the Unique Games Conjecture, the approximation curve achievable from the basic SDP coincides up to arbitrary additive error with the hardness curve generated by its integrality-gap instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proposed frontier theorem says that under UGC the basic SDP's gap curve determines the optimal approximation threshold for every fixed finite-domain CSP language.
assumptions_latex: The CSP language is fixed and finite-domain.
The Unique Games Conjecture holds.
Completeness, soundness, weighting, and normalization conventions must be fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{UGC}\Longrightarrow\text{basic-SDP gap curve equals the polynomial-time approximation frontier}.
knowledge_statements.title: UGC Optimality of the Basic SDP Integrality-Gap Curve

children.title: Cut-Spreading Metric Pair
children.top_down_role: Metric encodings for cut, partition, and arrangement objectives.

children.title: Cut Metrics
children.top_down_role: Metric representations tailored to cuts and discrete separations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-cone certificate of failure to admit a nonnegative cut decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A coefficient vector \(a=(a_{uv})\) satisfying \(\sum_{u<v}a_{uv}\delta_S(u,v)\ge0\) for every cut \(S\) belongs to \(\operatorname{CUT}(V)^*\). If \(\sum_{u<v}a_{uv}d(u,v)<0\), then \(d\notin\operatorname{CUT}(V)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inequality valid for every cut semimetric but violated by a candidate certifies nonmembership in the cut cone.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite.

notation.meaning: dual cone of linear functionals nonnegative on every cut semimetric

knowledge_statements.title: Separating-Inequality Certificate for Non-Cut Metrics

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic structural properties of the finite cut cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(S\subseteq V\), \(\delta_S=\delta_{V\setminus S}\), while \(\delta_\varnothing=\delta_V=0\). Hence \(\operatorname{CUT}(V)\) is a finitely generated polyhedral cone, with one generator selectable from each nontrivial complementary pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complementary cuts define the same semimetric, so the cut cone has one generator per nontrivial cut up to complementation.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.title: Complement Symmetry and Finite Generation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate realization equivalent to a nonnegative cut decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(d=\sum_S\lambda_S\delta_S\) with \(\lambda_S\ge0\), map \(v\) to \(\phi(v)=(\lambda_S\mathbf1[v\in S])_S\). Then \(d(u,v)=\|\phi(u)-\phi(v)\|_1\). Conversely, restricting a finite \(\ell_1\) embedding to the finitely many coordinate thresholds determined by the embedded points yields a nonnegative cut decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cut decompositions and finite weighted-Hamming embeddings are equivalent.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite.
Only coordinate thresholds determined by the finite embedded set are retained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d\in\operatorname{CUT}(V)\iff d\text{ admits a finite weighted-Hamming representation}.
knowledge_statements.title: Weighted-Hamming Representation of Cut-Cone Metrics
Cut Metrics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semimetrics generated by nonnegative combinations of cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite set \(V\) and a subset \(S\subseteq V\), define the cut semimetric \(\delta_S:V\times V\to\{0,1\}\) by \(\delta_S(u,v)=1\) exactly when one of \(u,v\) lies in \(S\) and the other lies in \(V\setminus S\), and set it to zero otherwise. A cut-cone metric is any semimetric of the form \[d(u,v)=\sum_{S\subseteq V}\lambda_S\delta_S(u,v),\qquad \lambda_S\ge0.\] On finite sets these are precisely the semimetrics admitting an isometric embedding into an \(\ell_1\) space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cut metric separates pairs across one cut; nonnegative sums of cut metrics are exactly finite l1 semimetrics.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite.
\(\lambda_S\ge0\) for all \(S\subseteq V\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cut-semimetric definition, nonnegative cut-cone representation, and finite l1 characterization are standard and consistent with a definition leaf. The record nevertheless has no citation or locator supporting the characterization.

children.title: Spreading Metrics
children.top_down_role: Metric representations enforcing dispersion across selected subsets.

knowledge_statements.title: Spreading Metrics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subset-spreading inequalities used in balanced partition relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be a finite set of size \(n\), let \(d\) be a semimetric on \(V\), and let \(b\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) be a prescribed cluster-size bound. The metric satisfies the \(b\)-spreading condition when, for every \(u\in V\) and every nonempty \(S\subseteq V\), \[\sum_{v\in S}d(u,v)\ge |S|-b.\] In particular, no set of more than \(b\) points can lie at zero distance from the same center. Together with nonnegativity, symmetry, zero diagonal, and triangle inequalities, these constraints define a standard spreading-metric relaxation for bounded-size decomposition problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A b-spreading semimetric forces every set larger than b to have positive aggregate distance from each chosen center.
assumptions_latex: \(|V|=n<\infty\).
\(1\le b\le n\).
\(d\) is a semimetric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{v\in S}d(u,v)\ge |S|-b\) for all \(u\in V\) and nonempty \(S\subseteq V\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Spreading inequalities occur with problem-dependent scaling and right-hand sides. The stated b-spreading condition is plausible for a bounded-cluster formulation, but no source identifies that normalization or the exact decomposition problem, so the mathematical variant cannot be verified.

children.title: Metric-Feasibility Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Compatibility of metric encodings with partition, arrangement, or cut requirements.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hypermetric Inequalities as Necessary Cut-Cone Conditions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A standard family of compatibility conditions stronger than triangle inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(d\in\operatorname{CUT}(V)\), then for every \(b\in\mathbb Z^V\) with \(\sum_{v\in V}b_v=1\), \[\sum_{u<v}b_ub_vd(u,v)\le0.\] Violation of one such inequality certifies that a metric-feasible \(d\) is not cut representable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every cut-cone metric satisfies all hypermetric inequalities; a violation certifies incompatibility with a cut decomposition.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite.
\(b\) is integral with coordinate sum one.

notation.meaning: integer hypermetric coefficient vector with coordinate sum one

knowledge_statements.title: Hypermetric Inequalities as Necessary Cut-Cone Conditions

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Five-Point Bipartite Metric Outside the Cut Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit smallest-cardinality witness to metric feasibility without cut representability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition five points into \(A\) and \(B\), with \(|A|=3\) and \(|B|=2\), and set \(d(u,v)=1\) across the partition and \(d(u,v)=2\) for distinct points within one part. This is the shortest-path metric of \(K_{3,2}\). Setting \(b_v=1\) on \(A\) and \(b_v=-1\) on \(B\) gives \(\sum_vb_v=1\) and \[\sum_{u<v}b_ub_vd(u,v)=3\cdot2+1\cdot2-6\cdot1=2>0.\] Thus the metric violates a hypermetric inequality and is outside \(\operatorname{CUT}(V)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The shortest-path metric of K3,2 satisfies the metric axioms but violates a hypermetric inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Five-Point Bipartite Metric Outside the Cut Cone

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hypermetric Tests Are Only Necessary in General
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits the certificate interpretation of the displayed hypermetric family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A violated hypermetric inequality certifies nonmembership in the cut cone, but absence of a violation from this family does not by itself provide a nonnegative cut decomposition. Cut-cone membership requires an explicit decomposition or separation over the complete dual cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Passing hypermetric tests alone is not a generic certificate of cut representability.
assumptions_latex: The candidate is a finite semimetric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(\forall b\in\mathbb Z^V,\ \sum b_v=1:\ \sum_{u<v}b_ub_vd(u,v)\le0\bigr)\centernot\Longrightarrow\text{an exhibited cut decomposition}.
review_flags: A strict hypermetric-cone versus cut-cone locator is recommended if this boundary is strengthened to a cardinality-specific separation.
knowledge_statements.title: Hypermetric Tests Are Only Necessary in General

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp cardinality threshold for equality of the metric and cut cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(|V|\le4\), every semimetric on \(V\) is a nonnegative combination of cut semimetrics, so \(\operatorname{MET}(V)=\operatorname{CUT}(V)\). Together with strict containment for \(|V|\ge5\), five points are the smallest cardinality at which metric feasibility can fail to imply cut representability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The metric and cut cones coincide through four points and first differ on five points.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Small-Cardinality Boundary

assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite and \(|V|\ge 5\).
Metric feasibility means nonnegativity, symmetry, zero diagonal, and all triangle inequalities.

notation.meaning: Cone generated by cut semimetrics on V.
Cone of semimetrics on V defined by nonnegativity, symmetry, zero diagonal, and triangle inequalities.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation between metric feasibility and cut representability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be a finite set with \(|V|\ge 5\). Every nonnegative combination of cut semimetrics satisfies nonnegativity, symmetry, zero diagonal, and all triangle inequalities, so \[\operatorname{CUT}(V)\subseteq\operatorname{MET}(V).\] This containment is strict: \[\operatorname{CUT}(V)\subsetneq\operatorname{MET}(V).\] Hence triangle-inequality feasibility alone does not imply a representation \(d=\sum_{S\subseteq V}\lambda_S\delta_S\) with \(\lambda_S\ge0\), and a cut-based rounding analysis requires additional structure or an embedding that may incur distortion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On every finite set of at least five points, the cut cone is a strict subset of the semimetric cone, so triangle inequalities alone do not guarantee a nonnegative cut decomposition.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Feasibility Boundaries

children.title: Tree-Metric Approximation
children.top_down_role: Approximation of general metrics by tree-structured representations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructive FRT-style sampling of a hierarchically separated tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite metric \((V,d)\), choose a random permutation of \(V\) and a random shift of geometrically decreasing radius scales. At each scale, process potential centers in permutation order and assign points to the first eligible center, refining the preceding partition. Connecting every cluster to its parent produces a random \(2\)-HST. With the standard radius normalization, the resulting leaf metric dominates \(d\) and realizes the probabilistic tree guarantee of the FRT theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Random shifted scales and a random center order construct the nested hierarchy used by the FRT embedding.
assumptions_latex: \((V,d)\) is a finite metric space.
The pairwise distance matrix is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{A random dominating }2\text{-HST is constructible in randomized polynomial time}.
knowledge_statements.title: Random-Permutation Hierarchical Decomposition

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structured tree targets used by probabilistic metric decompositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A \(k\)-hierarchically separated tree, \(k>1\), is a rooted tree whose leaves include \(V\), with labels \(\Delta(v)\ge0\) such that leaves have label zero and every child \(w\) of \(v\) satisfies \(\Delta(w)\le\Delta(v)/k\). For distinct leaves define \[d_T(x,y)=\Delta(\operatorname{lca}(x,y)),\] and set \(d_T(x,x)=0\). Then \(d_T\) is an ultrametric; equivalent conventions differ by constant rescaling or use the associated weighted-tree path metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An HST is a rooted hierarchy with geometrically decreasing scales and leaf distances determined by least common ancestors.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite.

notation.meaning: Scale label of a hierarchy node.
Least common ancestor of two leaves.

knowledge_statements.title: Hierarchically Separated Tree Metrics

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimality of Logarithmic Probabilistic Tree Distortion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case lower bound for distributions over dominating tree metrics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There is a universal constant \(c>0\) and, for infinitely many \(n\), an \(n\)-point metric \((V,d)\) such that every distribution \(\mathcal D\) over tree metrics satisfying \(d_T\ge d\) pointwise has a pair \(u,v\in V\) for which \[\mathbb E_{T\sim\mathcal D}[d_T(u,v)]\ge c\log n\,d(u,v).\] Hence the universal expected stretch cannot be \(o(\log n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Some finite metrics require logarithmic expected stretch under every distribution of dominating tree metrics.
assumptions_latex: Every sampled tree metric dominates the source metric pointwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{\mathcal D}\max_{u\ne v}\frac{\mathbb E_{T\sim\mathcal D}[d_T(u,v)]}{d(u,v)}=\Omega(\log n)\text{ for some }n\text{-point metrics}.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimality of Logarithmic Probabilistic Tree Distortion
Tree-Metric Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Probabilistic dominating-tree approximation of finite metrics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((V,d)\) be an \(n\)-point metric space. There exists a probability distribution over weighted tree metrics \(d_T\), possibly using a tree whose leaves contain \(V\), such that every sampled metric dominates the original metric, \[d_T(u,v)\ge d(u,v)\qquad\text{for all }u,v\in V,\] and there is a universal constant \(C>0\) for which \[\mathbb E[d_T(u,v)]\le C\log n\,d(u,v)\qquad\text{for all }u,v\in V.\] Consequently every nonnegative weighted sum of pairwise distances increases by at most an expected \(O(\log n)\) factor under the same random embedding.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite metric admits a random dominating tree representation whose expected pairwise stretch, and hence weighted aggregate stretch, is logarithmic in its size.
assumptions_latex: \((V,d)\) is a finite metric space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_T\ge d\) pointwise and \(\mathbb E[d_T(u,v)]\le C\log n\,d(u,v)\).

notation.meaning: Random weighted tree metric on the embedded points.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement is the standard probabilistic dominating-tree approximation theorem and the weighted-sum consequence follows for nonnegative weights. It fits a theorem container, but no FRT or equivalent authoritative theorem citation and locator is present.

children.title: Low-Distortion Embeddings
children.top_down_role: Embedding interfaces supporting cut and routing approximation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case lower boundary for universal embeddings into L1 and Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There is a universal constant \(c>0\) and an infinite family of \(n\)-point shortest-path metrics of bounded-degree expander graphs such that every embedding into \(\ell_1\), and every embedding into \(\ell_2\), has distortion at least \(c\log n\). Thus constant-distortion embeddings of all finite metrics into either target are impossible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expander metrics require logarithmic distortion in both L1 and Euclidean space.
assumptions_latex: The source metric is the shortest-path metric of a suitable bounded-degree expander.

notation.meaning: Least distortion of an embedding of X into Y.

knowledge_statements.title: Logarithmic Worst-Case Distortion Is Unavoidable

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary invariances and composition law for bi-Lipschitz distortion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Distortion is invariant under positive rescaling of either metric. If \(f:X\to Y\) is injective, then the inverse map on \(f(X)\) has the same distortion. If \(f:X\to Y\) and \(g:Y\to Z\) are embeddings, then \[\operatorname{dist}(g\circ f)\le \operatorname{dist}(g)\operatorname{dist}(f).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distortion is scale invariant, unchanged under inversion onto the image, and submultiplicative under composition.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y,Z\) are metric spaces.
The displayed maps are injective.
knowledge_statements.title: Distortion Calculus

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Universal low-distortion embedding of finite metrics into classical normed spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every fixed \(1\le p<\infty\), there is a universal constant \(C_p\) such that every \(n\)-point metric space \((X,d)\), \(n\ge2\), admits an embedding \(f:X\to\ell_p^{m}\), where \(m=O(\!\log^2 n)\), with distortion at most \(C_p\log n\). A randomized polynomial-time construction uses coordinates formed from distances to sampled subsets at logarithmically many sampling scales.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite metric embeds algorithmically into finite-dimensional Lp with logarithmic distortion.
assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is an \(n\)-point metric space with \(n\ge2\).
\(1\le p<\infty\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.title: Bourgain Embedding Theorem

assumptions_latex: \((X,d_X)\) and \((Y,d_Y)\) are metric spaces.
\(f:X\to Y\) is injective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The distortion of \(f\) is at most \(D\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard bi-Lipschitz definition of metric distortion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the bi-Lipschitz metric notion relevant to cut and routing approximations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An injective map \(f:X\to Y\) is a distortion-\(D\) embedding if there exists a scale \(s>0\) such that, for every \(u,v\in X\), \[s\,d_X(u,v)\le d_Y(f(u),f(v))\le D s\,d_X(u,v).\] Equivalently, when \(X\) is finite, its distortion is \[\operatorname{dist}(f)=\left(\max_{u\ne v}\frac{d_Y(f(u),f(v))}{d_X(u,v)}\right)\left(\max_{u\ne v}\frac{d_X(u,v)}{d_Y(f(u),f(v))}\right),\] and \(f\) has distortion at most \(D\) precisely when \(\operatorname{dist}(f)\le D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A low-distortion embedding preserves every pairwise distance up to one common scaling factor and a multiplicative factor D.
knowledge_statements.title: Low-Distortion Embeddings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically standard, internally consistent, and appropriate for the container, but no inspectable citation or locator is supplied.

children.title: Relaxation Hierarchies
children.top_down_role: Systematic strengthenings interpolating between basic relaxations and discrete solution spaces.

children.title: Linear Lifting-Projection Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Progressively stronger linear hierarchy families.

children.title: Linear Lifting Hierarchies
children.top_down_role: Linear hierarchy views organized around higher-dimensional lifted representations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation dependence under redundant auxiliary coordinates and constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A projected relaxation \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) generally has many linear lifts. If \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+m}\) satisfies \(\pi_x(Q)=P\), then \[Q'=\{(x,y,z):(x,y)\in Q,\ z=0\}\] also satisfies \(\pi_x(Q')=P\). Adding inequalities already valid for \(Q\), or applying an invertible affine change of auxiliary coordinates, likewise preserves the projected set. Thus the displayed auxiliary dimension and row count are properties of a chosen representation, not invariants of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The same projected relaxation can have many different lifts, so raw lift dimension and row count are representation-dependent.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is a polyhedral lift of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.title: Nonuniqueness of Linear Lifts

assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is the discrete feasible set.
Each \(Q_t\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+m_t}\) is a polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each \(Q_t\) is a linear extended formulation of the relaxation \(P_t=\pi_x(Q_t)\supseteq\operatorname{conv}(S)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard extended-formulation description of linear lift-and-project levels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes linear hierarchy levels through auxiliary-variable extended formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A linear lifting hierarchy for \(S\) is a sequence of polyhedra \[Q_t=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^{n+m_t}:A_t x+B_t y\le b_t\},\qquad t=0,1,\ldots,T,\] whose projection onto the original coordinates, \(P_t=\pi_x(Q_t)\), contains \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\). The auxiliary coordinates encode level-dependent products, local assignments, or valid linear consequences. If the hierarchy is nested, then \(P_{t+1}\subseteq P_t\); if it is exact at level \(T\), then \(P_T=\operatorname{conv}(S)\). Thus optimization over \(Q_t\) supplies a linear extended formulation of the level-\(t\) relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each hierarchy level lifts the original variables into a larger linear system whose projection is a valid relaxation of the discrete hull.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear Lifting Hierarchies

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The extended-formulation representation fits linear lifting hierarchies, but the generic hierarchy characterization and exactness conditions lack a supporting source.

children.title: Linear Projection Hierarchies
children.top_down_role: Linear hierarchy views organized around projected strengthened formulations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between a compact lifted system and an explicit original-space inequality description.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Eliminating auxiliary variables from a linear system by Fourier--Motzkin elimination can generate exponentially many intermediate inequalities. Moreover, there exist polynomial-size polyhedral lifts \(Q\) whose projections \(P=\pi_x(Q)\) have exponentially many facets in the original space. Thus a compact explicit description of \(Q\) need not yield a compact explicit inequality description of \(P\), although optimizing an objective depending only on \(x\) over \(P\) is equivalent to optimizing it over \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compact lift can project to a polyhedron with a much larger explicit original-space description.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is a polyhedron given by finitely many linear inequalities.
Projection removes auxiliary coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Compactness of a displayed lift does not imply a polynomial-size explicit inequality description of its projection.
review_flags: explicit lower-bound families would benefit from an extension-complexity source
knowledge_statements.title: Projection Description Blowup

assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is the discrete feasible set.
\(Q_t\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+m_t}\) is a valid lifted relaxation at every level.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The projected sets form valid relaxations, and under nestedness satisfy \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\subseteq P_{t+1}\subseteq P_t\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard projection property of nested lift-and-project hierarchies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers projection back to the original-variable space after linear lifting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every level \(t\), define the projected relaxation by \[P_t=\pi_x(Q_t)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists y\in\mathbb R^{m_t}\text{ with }(x,y)\in Q_t\}.\] Validity of the lifted formulation implies \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\subseteq P_t\). If every feasible point of \(Q_{t+1}\) projects to a point in \(P_t\), then \[\operatorname{conv}(S)\subseteq P_{t+1}\subseteq P_t.\] Consequently, for a minimization objective \(c\), the lower bounds \(\min\{c^\top x:x\in P_t\}\) are nondecreasing with \(t\); for maximization they are nonincreasing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projecting each lifted level yields a valid original-space relaxation; nested levels give monotonically stronger optimization bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear Projection Hierarchies

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The projection and bound-monotonicity statements are correct under the stated validity and nestedness assumptions, but no citation supports them.

children.title: Hierarchy-Strength Regimes
children.top_down_role: Relaxation strength across successive levels of linear hierarchies.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Objective-Wise Exactness Characterizes the Integer Hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective class under which value exactness is equivalent to geometric exactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(H=\operatorname{conv}(S)\subseteq P\) be nonempty compact convex sets. Then \[P=H\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \max_{x\in P}c^\top x=\max_{x\in H}c^\top x\quad\text{for every }c\in\mathbb R^n.\] Agreement only on a restricted objective class need not imply \(P=H\); it suffices precisely when that class separates every point of \(P\setminus H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equality for every linear objective is equivalent to equality with the integer hull; a restricted objective class may be insufficient.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(H\) are nonempty compact convex sets.
\(H\subseteq P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=H\) if and only if their support functions agree for every \(c\in\mathbb R^n\).

notation.meaning: convex hull of the discrete feasible set

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Wise Exactness Characterizes the Integer Hull

assumptions_latex: \(P_0\supseteq P_1\supseteq\cdots\supseteq P_T\supseteq\operatorname{conv}(S)\).
\(c^\top x\) is a nonnegative maximization objective with positive integral optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactness and approximation strength are classified by the least level attaining \(P_t=\operatorname{conv}(S)\) or a prescribed gap bound.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard exactness-rank and integrality-gap regimes for nested hierarchies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates exact, approximate, and ineffective ranges of hierarchy levels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the exactness rank by \[r(S)=\min\{t:P_t=\operatorname{conv}(S)\},\] with \(r(S)=\infty\) if no such level exists. For objective \(c\), define \[g_t(c)=\frac{\max\{c^\top x:x\in P_t\}}{\max\{c^\top x:x\in S\}}.\] Level \(t\) is exact when \(g_t(c)=1\) for every admissible \(c\), is an \(\alpha\)-strength regime when \(g_t(c)\le\alpha\) for the specified objective class, and remains ineffective for that class when a family has \(g_t(c)\ge\beta>1\). Nestedness gives \(g_{t+1}(c)\le g_t(c)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hierarchy strength is measured by the first exact level or by the worst integrality gap attained at each earlier level.
knowledge_statements.title: Hierarchy-Strength Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The gap regimes are plausible, but the admissible objective class must be sourced and specified before objective-wise gap one can be related to geometric exactness.

children.title: Sum-of-Squares Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Semidefinite hierarchy and certificate interfaces.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monomial-basis dimensions and the conditional fixed-order SDP complexity regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\) variables, there are \(\binom{n+t}{t}\) monomials of degree at most \(t\), so the order-\(t\) moment matrix has that dimension, while the moment vector through degree \(2t\) has \(\binom{n+2t}{2t}\) entries. With \(m\) explicitly listed constraints of bounded degree, the resulting SDP has size polynomial in \(m\) and \(n^{O(t)}\). Consequently, fixed \(t\) gives polynomial explicit size. Approximate polynomial-time optimization additionally requires the usual rational encoding, boundedness, and regularity or oracle hypotheses of the chosen SDP model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Order-t SoS has n-to-the-order-t explicit size; fixed order is polynomial-size, subject to the usual assumptions for approximate SDP optimization.
assumptions_latex: Constraint degrees are bounded independently of \(n\).
The \(m\) polynomial constraints are explicitly represented.
Any optimization-time claim uses an SDP model with suitable rational encoding, boundedness, and regularity or oracle data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim M_t=\binom{n+t}{t}\) and the explicit order-\(t\) formulation has size \(\operatorname{poly}(m)\,n^{O(t)}\).

notation.meaning: number of monomials of degree at most t
number of explicitly listed polynomial constraints

review_flags: exact SDP bit complexity requires model-specific regularity and encoding assumptions
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Order SoS Size

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Asymptotic Convergence Requires a Positivstellensatz Hypothesis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary for convergence of the quadratic-module SoS hierarchy on a general semialgebraic description.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Finite-level validity of the quadratic-module SoS hierarchy is unconditional, but convergence to the polynomial optimum is not automatic for an arbitrary description. A standard sufficient condition is that the quadratic module generated by \(g_1,\ldots,g_m\) is Archimedean, for example that it contains \(R-\|x\|_2^2\) for some \(R>0\). Under this condition, every polynomial strictly positive on the feasible set has a finite-degree quadratic-module certificate, and the SoS bounds converge to the optimum. Compactness of the feasible set alone does not necessarily make the displayed quadratic module Archimedean.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: SoS levels are valid without compactness, but generic convergence requires an Archimedean quadratic module or another suitable Positivstellensatz condition.
assumptions_latex: The convergence conclusion uses an Archimedean quadratic module.
The feasible set is described by the stated polynomial constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under the Archimedean hypothesis, \(\operatorname{val}_t\to\operatorname{OPT}\); arbitrary polynomial descriptions carry no universal convergence guarantee.
review_flags: an authoritative Positivstellensatz source is desirable
knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Convergence Requires a Positivstellensatz Hypothesis

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strength relation between successive compatible SoS levels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Restricting a feasible degree-\(2(t+1)\) pseudoexpectation to polynomials of degree at most \(2t\) gives a feasible order-\(t\) pseudoexpectation. Therefore, for minimization, the SoS lower bounds are nondecreasing in \(t\); for maximization, the SoS upper bounds are nonincreasing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every higher-order SoS solution restricts to a lower-order one, so the relaxation bounds improve monotonically.
assumptions_latex: Successive levels use the same polynomial constraints and compatible truncations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{val}^{\min}_t\le\operatorname{val}^{\min}_{t+1}\le\operatorname{OPT}\), with the bound orientation reversed for maximization.
knowledge_statements.title: Nestedness and Bound Monotonicity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semidefinite representation equivalent to truncated pseudoexpectation positivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a degree-\(2t\) pseudoexpectation with moments \(y_\alpha=\widetilde{\mathbb E}[x^\alpha]\), define \(M_t(y)_{\alpha,\beta}=y_{\alpha+\beta}\) for \(|\alpha|,|\beta|\le t\). Then \(\widetilde{\mathbb E}[q^2]\ge0\) for every \(\deg q\le t\) if and only if \(M_t(y)\succeq0\). For \(g_j\ge0\), with \(s_j=t-\lceil\deg(g_j)/2\rceil\ge0\), the conditions \(\widetilde{\mathbb E}[q^2g_j]\ge0\) for \(\deg q\le s_j\) are equivalent to \(M_{s_j}(g_jy)\succeq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pseudoexpectation positivity is exactly encoded by positive-semidefinite moment and localizing matrices.
assumptions_latex: All referenced moments have degree at most \(2t\).
For each included inequality, \(t\ge\lceil\deg(g_j)/2\rceil\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_t(y)\succeq0\) and \(M_{s_j}(g_jy)\succeq0\) encode the order-\(t\) positivity constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: Moment and Localizing Matrix Form

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Treatment of polynomial equalities in the pseudoexpectation and dual-certificate interfaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For polynomial equalities \(h_k(x)=0\), the order-\(t\) pseudoexpectation imposes \[\widetilde{\mathbb E}[p(x)h_k(x)]=0\qquad\text{whenever }\deg(ph_k)\le2t.\] Equivalently, moments are considered modulo the degree-truncated ideal generated by the \(h_k\). In the dual certificate, equality constraints contribute unrestricted polynomial multiples \(r_kh_k\), alongside sums of squares and the terms \(\sigma_jg_j\), with every summand truncated to total degree at most \(2t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial equalities are enforced through vanishing ideal multiples, and their dual certificate multipliers need not be sums of squares.
assumptions_latex: The equality and inequality descriptions refer to the same polynomial feasible set.
All imposed products and certificate terms have degree at most \(2t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equality constraints are represented by truncated ideal relations in the primal and unrestricted ideal multiples in the dual certificate.
knowledge_statements.title: Equality Constraints and Quotient Form

assumptions_latex: \(K=\{x:g_j(x)\ge0,\ j=1,\ldots,m\}\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a polynomial feasible set.
The relaxation order \(t\) is at least half the largest relevant polynomial degree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible degree-\(2t\) pseudoexpectations define the order-\(t\) semidefinite relaxation and its dual polynomial certificates.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard pseudoexpectation formulation of the sum-of-squares hierarchy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the pseudoexpectation formulation for polynomial optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The order-\(t\) sum-of-squares relaxation replaces evaluation at a feasible point by a linear functional \(\widetilde{\mathbb E}\) on polynomials of degree at most \(2t\), subject to \(\widetilde{\mathbb E}[1]=1\), \(\widetilde{\mathbb E}[q(x)^2]\ge0\) whenever \(\deg q\le t\), and \(\widetilde{\mathbb E}[q(x)^2g_j(x)]\ge0\) whenever \(\deg(q^2g_j)\le2t\). Optimizing \(\widetilde{\mathbb E}[f(x)]\) under these constraints is a semidefinite program. Its dual expresses a certified polynomial bound using sums of squares and constraint multiples of total degree at most \(2t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The order-t sum-of-squares level optimizes over positive degree-limited pseudoexpectations and has dual bounded-degree polynomial certificates.
knowledge_statements.title: Sum-of-Squares Hierarchy

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pseudoexpectation formulation is a standard basic quadratic-module version of the SoS hierarchy and fits the container, but its degree conditions and dual-certificate statement require an authoritative citation.

children.title: Hierarchy Utility-Limitation Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Algorithmic uses and limitations of strengthened relaxations.

children.title: Hierarchy Rounding
children.top_down_role: Rounding interfaces that exploit strengthened hierarchy solutions.

assumptions_latex: \(z_t\) is a feasible level-\(t\) hierarchy solution for instance \(I\).
\(R_t\) is a specified polynomial-time randomized or deterministic rounding map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output \(X=R_t(I,z_t)\) is integral and satisfies the stated feasibility and approximation guarantee.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: generic formal interface shared by hierarchy-rounding algorithms
specific rounding theorem depends on the optimization problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the abstract interface; problem-specific conditioning and rounding rules require child results.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an instance \(I\), a relaxation level \(t\), and an optimal or near-optimal hierarchy solution \(z_t\), apply the prescribed map \[X=R_t(I,z_t).\] The map may query marginals encoded by \(z_t\), condition on selected variables, and sample or deterministically choose assignments, but it must terminate with \(X\) in the integral feasible family \(\mathcal F(I)\). For a maximization problem, an \(\alpha_t\)-rounding guarantee requires \[\mathbb E[\operatorname{val}_I(X)]\ge \frac{\operatorname{relax}_t(I)}{\alpha_t};\] for minimization, it requires \(\mathbb E[\operatorname{val}_I(X)]\le\alpha_t\operatorname{relax}_t(I)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hierarchy rounding converts a level-t pseudo-solution into an integral feasible solution while controlling expected objective loss.
knowledge_statements.title: Hierarchy Rounding

children.title: Integrality-Gap Families
children.top_down_role: Limitation patterns exhibited across hierarchy levels or instance families.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nested Levels Need Not Strictly Improve the Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary on interpreting increasing hierarchy depth as automatic approximation progress.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Validity and nestedness alone do not imply strict improvement of a worst-case integrality gap. In particular, a hierarchy may repeat the same relaxation at successive levels, so \(P_{t+1}(I)=P_t(I)\) for all \(I\) and consequently \(G_{t+1}=G_t\). More generally, equality persists whenever the additional constraints do not improve the instances approaching the supremal gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deeper valid hierarchy level may leave the worst-case integrality gap unchanged.
assumptions_latex: Only validity and nestedness of the hierarchy levels are assumed.
knowledge_statements.title: Nested Levels Need Not Strictly Improve the Gap

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal I\) is a family of maximization instances.
Every instance has positive integral optimum and a valid level-\(t\) relaxation bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The family has level-\(t\) gap at least \(\gamma\) when \(\sup_{I\in\mathcal I}\operatorname{REL}_t(I)/\operatorname{OPT}(I)\ge\gamma\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard maximization integrality-gap definition for relaxation families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the maximization convention; minimization reverses the ratio.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A family \(\mathcal I\) is a level-\(t\) integrality-gap family with gap at least \(\gamma\ge1\) if \[\sup_{I\in\mathcal I}\frac{\operatorname{REL}_t(I)}{\operatorname{OPT}(I)}\ge\gamma.\] An asymptotic gap \(\gamma\) is witnessed by instances \((I_n)\) of growing size satisfying \[\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{\operatorname{REL}_t(I_n)}{\operatorname{OPT}(I_n)}\ge\gamma.\] Such a family rules out every rounding procedure whose guarantee would imply a strictly smaller worst-case ratio from all feasible level-\(t\) solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integrality-gap family contains instances whose level-t relaxation value remains a specified factor above the integral optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Integrality-Gap Families

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The maximization integrality-gap definition is precise and appropriate, but the asserted implication for all rounding procedures is nontrivial and uncited.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-wise monotonicity of hierarchy strength rather than the construction of gap families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nested valid maximization relaxations \(S(I)\subseteq P_{t+1}(I)\subseteq P_t(I)\) with finite positive optima, the properly oriented instance gaps and their suprema satisfy \(1\le g_{t+1}(I)\le g_t(I)\) and \(1\le G_{t+1}\le G_t\). The analogous statement holds for minimization with the ratio reversed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nested strengthening cannot worsen a properly oriented integrality gap.
assumptions_latex: The relaxations are valid and nested.
The relevant optima are finite and positive.

children.title: Round-Limit Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Relationships among hierarchy depth, computational cost, and approximation quality.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Explicit-Size Upper Bounds Do Not Establish Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary on interpreting round-dependent formulation-size estimates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An explicit level-size and solution-time upper bound \(n^{O(t)}\) yields the corresponding polynomial, quasipolynomial, or exponential upper-time regime, but it supplies no matching lower bound. A level may admit a smaller equivalent formulation, an oracle implementation, or a problem-specific simplification. Hence an displayed size bound \(n^{O(n)}\) at \(t=\Theta(n)\) does not by itself prove that optimizing the level requires exponential time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A large explicit hierarchy formulation gives an implementation upper bound, not a computational lower bound.
assumptions_latex: Only an explicit formulation-size upper bound is known.
No complexity or extension-complexity lower bound is supplied.
knowledge_statements.title: Explicit-Size Upper Bounds Do Not Establish Hardness
Round-Limit Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional complexity regimes for hierarchies whose explicit level size grows as a power of the instance dimension with exponent proportional to the round count.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If an \(n\)-variable hierarchy has level-\(t\) encoding size \(n^{O(t)}\) and can be optimized in time polynomial in its explicit size, then its level-\(t\) running time is \(n^{O(t)}\). Consequently, fixed \(t=O(1)\) gives polynomial time, while \(t=O(\log n)\) gives the quasipolynomial upper bound \(n^{O(\log n)}=\exp(O((\log n)^2))\), and \(t=\Theta(n)\) gives the upper bound \(n^{O(n)}\). When relaxation strength is monotone in \(t\), increasing the round count trades potentially stronger bounds and rounding guarantees against the growth in formulation size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under an n-to-the-order-t size bound, constant rounds are polynomial, logarithmically many rounds have a quasipolynomial upper bound, and linearly many rounds have an n to the order n upper bound.
assumptions_latex: Level \(t\) has an encoding of size \(n^{O(t)}\).
The level can be optimized in time polynomial in its explicit encoding size.
Any claimed strength tradeoff assumes relaxation strength is monotone in \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resulting running-time upper bound is \(n^{O(t)}\), with polynomial, quasipolynomial, and \(n^{O(n)}\) regimes for constant, logarithmic, and linear \(t\), respectively.

notation.meaning: explicit encoding-size and running-time upper bound

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: conditional asymptotic calculation from an assumed n^{O(t)} encoding size
hierarchy-specific encoding and optimization bounds require sources

children.title: Approximation Scheme Architectures
