children.title: Numerical Compression Scheme Family
children.top_down_role: Schemes compressing numerical ranges or item types.

children.title: Objective-Value Scaling Family
children.top_down_role: State-space reduction through objective discretization.

children.title: Value Scaling
children.top_down_role: State-space compression through discretization of value quantities.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation of exact scaling from lossy rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(K>0\), \(\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in\mathcal F}c^Tx=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in\mathcal F}(c/K)^Tx\). Thus positive rescaling preserves all objective comparisons; approximation loss arises only from subsequent rounding or truncation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive rescaling does not change optimizers; discretization causes the loss.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal F is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.title: Positive Rescaling Invariance

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer range produced by common-quantum floor scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(0\le c_i\le C\), \(K>0\), and \(\widehat c_i=\lfloor c_i/K\rfloor\), then \(0\le\widehat c_i\le\lfloor C/K\rfloor\) and every binary solution satisfies \(\widehat c^Tx\le n\lfloor C/K\rfloor\). A dynamic program indexed only by total scaled value therefore has at most \(n\lfloor C/K\rfloor+1\) value indices, provided its other state coordinates and transitions are polynomially bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Floor scaling converts a bounded objective range into a bounded integer state range, but does not by itself bound the rest of a dynamic program.
assumptions_latex: 0\le c_i\le C for every \(i\).
Solutions are binary vectors.
knowledge_statements.title: Integer State-Range Compression
Value Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic floor scaling for nonnegative additive maximization objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(K>0\), set \(\widehat c_i=\lfloor c_i/K\rfloor\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n\), maximize \(\sum_{i=1}^n\widehat c_i x_i\) over \(x\in\mathcal F\), and return an optimizer \(\widehat x\). If \(x^*\) maximizes \(\sum_{i=1}^n c_i x_i\) over \(\mathcal F\), then \[\sum_{i=1}^n c_i\widehat x_i>\sum_{i=1}^n c_i x_i^*-nK.\] If a bound \(0<L\le\sum_{i=1}^n c_i x_i^*\) is known and \(K\le\varepsilon L/n\) for \(0<\varepsilon<1\), then \[\sum_{i=1}^n c_i\widehat x_i>(1-\varepsilon)\sum_{i=1}^n c_i x_i^*.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Floor the nonnegative objective coefficients by a common positive quantum and optimize the resulting integer objective. The returned solution loses less than n times the quantum, and an appropriately chosen quantum gives a one-minus-epsilon guarantee.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\) is nonempty.
\(c_i\ge0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An optimizer of the scaled objective has additive loss less than \(nK\), with the stated relative guarantee when \(K\le\varepsilon L/n\).

notation.meaning: positive lower bound on the original optimum

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard floor-scaling lemma for nonnegative additive objectives

children.title: Profit Scaling
children.top_down_role: State-space compression through discretization of profit quantities.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Range induced by standard profit normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(K=\varepsilon P/n\) and \(q_i=\lfloor p_i/K\rfloor\), if \(0\le p_i\le P\), then \(0\le q_i\le\lfloor n/\varepsilon\rfloor\) and \(\sum_iq_i\le n\lfloor n/\varepsilon\rfloor=O(n^2/\varepsilon)\). Therefore an exact routine polynomial in \(n\) and \(\sum_iq_i\) runs in time polynomial in \(n\) and \(1/\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Standard normalization bounds each scaled profit and the total scaled-profit range polynomially in n and one over epsilon.
assumptions_latex: 0\le p_i\le P and P>0.
K=\varepsilon P/n with \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Scaled-Profit Range Bound

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions supporting both relative loss and bounded scaled range.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The normalization \(P\) must satisfy \(P\le\operatorname{OPT}\) to convert \(\operatorname{OPT}-\varepsilon P\) into a \((1-\varepsilon)\)-bound, and \(p_i\le P\) for retained items to bound their scaled values. In a downward-closed family, after deleting items occurring in no feasible solution, the largest feasible singleton profit supplies both conditions. If \(P=0\), then \(\operatorname{OPT}=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The largest relevant singleton profit is both a lower bound on optimum and an upper bound on retained item profits.
assumptions_latex: The feasible family is downward closed and nonempty.
Items occurring in no feasible solution have been removed.
Profits are nonnegative.

notation.meaning: Largest profit of a relevant feasible singleton.

knowledge_statements.title: Valid Profit Normalization Conditions
Profit Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Profit-scaling template for downward-closed packing problems with exact scaled-objective optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P>0\) be the largest profit of an item feasible by itself, let \(0<\varepsilon<1\), and set \(K=\varepsilon P/n\) and \(\widehat p_i=\lfloor p_i/K\rfloor\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n\). Find a feasible set \(\widehat S\) maximizing \(\sum_{i\in S}\widehat p_i\), and return \(\widehat S\) evaluated using the original profits. If \(\operatorname{OPT}\) is the maximum original profit, then \[\sum_{i\in\widehat S}p_i>\operatorname{OPT}-\varepsilon P\ge(1-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scale profits into nonnegative integers, optimize the scaled objective exactly, and evaluate the returned set using the original profits; the resulting profit is greater than one minus epsilon times optimum.
assumptions_latex: There are \(n\ge1\) items with profits \(p_i\ge0\).
The feasible family is nonempty and downward closed.
The largest profit \(P\) of an individually feasible item satisfies \(P>0\).
An exact optimizer for the scaled objective is available.
\(0<\varepsilon<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned feasible set has original profit greater than \((1-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}\).

notation.meaning: largest profit of an individually feasible item

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard profit-scaling template for downward-closed packing problems
runtime depends on the exact scaled-objective optimizer

children.title: Discretization-Loss Regimes
children.top_down_role: Approximation effects associated with numerical rounding granularity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit failure of multiplicative accuracy without an optimum-comparable scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\Delta>0\) and let \(\mathcal F=\{0,e_1\}\) with \(c_1=\eta\in(0,\Delta)\). Downward rounding to width \(\Delta\) gives \(\widetilde c_1=0\), so the rounded problem may return \(0\), whose original value is zero although \(\operatorname{OPT}=\eta>0\). Thus an additive loss below \(\Delta\) does not imply any positive multiplicative ratio.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tiny positive optimum can be rounded to zero, showing that additive control alone gives no relative guarantee.
assumptions_latex: \Delta>0.
0<\eta<\Delta.

notation.meaning: A positive objective value smaller than one rounding quantum.

knowledge_statements.title: Additive Error Without Relative Control

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic loss when coefficient errors are not one-sided.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(|c_i-\widetilde c_i|\le\delta\) and every feasible solution has support at most \(r\), then an optimizer \(\widehat x\) of \(\widetilde c^Tx\) satisfies \(c^Tx^*-c^T\widehat x\le2r\delta\). The sharper \(r\Delta\) estimate requires one-sided downward error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two-sided coefficient error can perturb both compared solutions and doubles the generic support-sensitive bound.
assumptions_latex: |c_i-\widetilde c_i|\le\delta for every \(i\).
\|x\|_0\le r for every feasible \(x\).
knowledge_statements.title: Two-Sided Rounding-Loss Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Refinement of additive discretization loss by feasible support size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If every \(x\in\mathcal F\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\) has \(\|x\|_0\le r\), \(0\le c_i-\widetilde c_i<\Delta\), \(x^*\) maximizes \(c^Tx\), and \(\widehat x\) maximizes \(\widetilde c^Tx\), then \(c^Tx^*-c^T\widehat x<r\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When feasible solutions use at most r items, downward rounding loses less than r quanta rather than n.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal F\subseteq\{0,1\}^n is nonempty.
\|x\|_0\le r for every \(x\in\mathcal F\).
0\le c_i-\widetilde c_i<\Delta for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.title: Support-Sensitive Downward-Rounding Loss

assumptions_latex: \(x\in\mathcal F\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\) and \(c_i\ge0\).
Approximations satisfy \(0\le c_i-\widetilde c_i<\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The discretization loss is below \(n\Delta\), becoming relative error \(\varepsilon\) when \(n\Delta\le\varepsilon\operatorname{OPT}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes additive-loss and relative-loss scaling regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\widehat x\) maximize \(\sum_i\widetilde c_i x_i\) and let \(x^*\) maximize \(\sum_i c_i x_i\). Coordinatewise downward discretization yields \[\sum_i c_i x_i^*-\sum_i c_i\widehat x_i<n\Delta.\] Therefore \(n\Delta\) is the additive-loss regime. If a certified lower bound \(L\le\operatorname{OPT}\) is available and \(n\Delta\le\varepsilon L\), then \[\sum_i c_i\widehat x_i>(1-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT},\] giving a relative-loss regime. Without a positive lower bound comparable to \(\operatorname{OPT}\), the additive estimate alone does not imply a multiplicative approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A discretization width gives additive loss below n times the width; it gives relative error only when that quantity is small compared with optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Discretization-Loss Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The additive-to-relative loss distinction is mathematically correct and well matched to the container, but no inspectable source supports the stated bound.

children.title: Size-Class Grouping
children.top_down_role: Compression through representative item classes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Class-count bound over a finite positive range.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(0<s_{\min}\le s_i\le s_{\max}\), the geometric classes with ratio \(1+\varepsilon\) have at most \(1+\lceil\log_{1+\varepsilon}(s_{\max}/s_{\min})\rceil\) nonempty indices. For \(0<\varepsilon\le1\), this is \(O(1+\varepsilon^{-1}\log(s_{\max}/s_{\min}))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Geometric grouping uses logarithmically many classes across a bounded positive size range.
assumptions_latex: 0<s_{\min}\le s_i\le s_{\max}.
\varepsilon>0.
knowledge_statements.title: Number of Geometric Size Classes

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Why lower representatives do not preserve packing feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For capacity \(1\), two items of size \(0.51\) are infeasible together. If both are represented from below by \(0.50\), their rounded total is \(1\), so the rounded instance declares the pair feasible. Thus lower rounding does not ensure that rounded-feasible selections are feasible under original sizes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rounding sizes downward can create false packing feasibility.
assumptions_latex: Packing capacity is \(1\).
Representative sizes may be smaller than original sizes.
knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Rounding Feasibility Failure

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compressed size representation after class rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: After all items in class \(C_k\) receive representative size \(r_k\), the rounded size multiset is represented by pairs \((r_k,m_k)\), where \(m_k=|C_k|\). A size-level selection uses integers \(0\le y_k\le m_k\) and has rounded load \(\sum_kr_ky_k\). Attributes not constant within a class must remain separately represented.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A grouped size multiset uses one representative and multiplicity per class; unrelated attributes are not automatically interchangeable.
assumptions_latex: All items in \(C_k\) receive the same rounded size \(r_k\).
Multiplicities are integral.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiplicity Representation of Grouped Instances
Size-Class Grouping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric size classes with conservative upper representatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\varepsilon>0\) and every integer \(k\), define \[C_k=\{i:(1+\varepsilon)^k\le s_i<(1+\varepsilon)^{k+1}\}.\] For each \(i\in C_k\), replace \(s_i\) by the upper representative \(r_k=(1+\varepsilon)^{k+1}\), retaining item multiplicities and other attributes. Every grouped item satisfies \[s_i\le r_k\le(1+\varepsilon)s_i.\] Thus rounding is conservative for packing constraints: any selected set feasible under the rounded sizes is feasible under the original sizes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Geometric grouping replaces nearby positive item sizes by a common upper representative. Each rounded size lies between the original size and one plus epsilon times that size, so rounded feasibility implies original feasibility.
assumptions_latex: There are finitely many items indexed by \(i\), with \(s_i>0\).
The grouping parameter satisfies \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each rounded size satisfies \(s_i\le r_k\le(1+\varepsilon)s_i\), and feasibility under rounded packing sizes implies feasibility under the original sizes.

notation.meaning: geometric size class indexed by integer k

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard geometric upper-rounding construction for packing approximation schemes

children.title: Large–Small Item Decomposition
children.top_down_role: Separate treatment of structurally significant and residual items.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Candidate count implied by unit-capacity thresholding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With \(L_\tau=\{i:a_i>\tau\}\), every unit-capacity feasible set contains at most \(k=\lceil1/\tau\rceil-1\) large items. Hence all possible large-item parts occur among at most \(\sum_{j=0}^{k}\binom{|L_\tau|}{j}=O(n^k)\) subsets for fixed \(\tau\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed threshold, every feasible large-item choice occurs among polynomially many bounded-cardinality subsets.
assumptions_latex: 0<\tau\le1.
a_i>0 and \(\sum_{i\in F}a_i\le1\) for every feasible \(F\).
knowledge_statements.title: Enumeration Bound for Large Items

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary on what thresholding alone establishes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(m\ge1/\tau\), a unit-capacity instance with \(m\) items of size \(1/m\le\tau\) admits all \(m\) items. Thus small individual size does not bound selected cardinality, and a per-item error \(\delta\) may accumulate to \(m\delta\). An approximation guarantee therefore requires an aggregate-error, cardinality, or objective argument beyond thresholding.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Small items can have unbounded multiplicity, so thresholding alone is not an approximation guarantee.
assumptions_latex: 0<\tau\le1.
The item count is unrestricted.
knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Small-Item Multiplicity
Large–Small Item Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacity-threshold decomposition for one-dimensional packing instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the packing capacity be normalized to \(1\), let \(a_i\in(0,1]\) be item sizes, and fix \(\tau\in(0,1]\). Define \(L_\tau=\{i:a_i>\tau\}\) and \(S_\tau=\{i:a_i\leq\tau\}\). Every feasible set \(F\), satisfying \(\sum_{i\in F}a_i\leq1\), obeys \[|F\cap L_\tau|<\frac1\tau.\] Thus the large items have bounded cardinality for fixed \(\tau\), while every residual item contributes at most \(\tau\) to the capacity. An approximation scheme may therefore enumerate or otherwise represent the large-item choices and handle the small items through aggregation, rounding, or greedy completion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Thresholding leaves only constantly many large items in any feasible packing, while every remaining item has individually small capacity impact.
assumptions_latex: \(a_i\in(0,1]\) and \(\sum_{i\in F}a_i\leq1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|F\cap L_\tau|<1/\tau\) and \(a_i\leq\tau\) for every \(i\in F\cap S_\tau\).

notation.meaning: Items no larger than the threshold.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cardinality bound is correct, but the final approximation-scheme claim does not follow from thresholding alone and requires an authoritative source with a specific locator and applicable problem assumptions.

children.title: Pseudopolynomial-to-Scheme Transfer
children.top_down_role: Connections between numerical dynamic programming and fully polynomial schemes.

children.title: Knapsack Scaling Family
children.top_down_role: Canonical numerical dynamic-programming transfer.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Time and storage for the profit-indexed scaled dynamic program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With \(K=\varepsilon P/n\), \(q_i=\lfloor p_i/K\rfloor\), and \(Q=\sum_iq_i\), preprocessing ensures \(Q=O(n^2/\varepsilon)\). The layered recurrence takes \(O(nQ)=O(n^3/\varepsilon)\) transitions and \(O(Q)=O(n^2/\varepsilon)\) working entries with rolling layers. Predecessors may be stored, or layers recomputed, to recover a subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The standard scaled knapsack DP has cubic-over-epsilon time and quadratic-over-epsilon rolling-table space.
assumptions_latex: Every retained item satisfies \(0\le w_i\le C\) and \(p_i>0\).
0<\varepsilon<1.
Table arithmetic and comparisons have polynomial bit cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Knapsack Scaled-DP Complexity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Edge cases before defining the canonical scaling quantum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Items with \(w_i>C\) occur in no feasible solution and may be deleted; zero-profit items may be deleted without reducing the optimum. If no positive-profit feasible item remains, \(\operatorname{OPT}=0\) and the empty set is optimal. Otherwise \(P=\max\{p_i:w_i\le C\}>0\) satisfies \(p_i\le P\le\operatorname{OPT}\) for every retained item.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Preprocessing removes infeasible and irrelevant items and separates the zero-optimum case.
assumptions_latex: Weights and capacity are nonnegative.
Profits are nonnegative.

notation.meaning: Largest profit of an individually feasible item.

knowledge_statements.title: Knapsack Scaling Preprocessing Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: State domain and out-of-range convention for the scaled knapsack recurrence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q_i=\sum_{j=1}^iq_j\). For \(q\in\{0,\ldots,Q_i\}\), let \(D_i(q)\) be the minimum weight of a subset of the first \(i\) items having scaled profit exactly \(q\). Set \(D_0(0)=0\), \(D_0(q)=+\infty\) for \(q>0\), and interpret \(D_{i-1}(t)=+\infty\) when \(t<0\) or \(t>Q_{i-1}\). Then \(D_i(q)=\min\{D_{i-1}(q),D_{i-1}(q-q_i)+w_i\}\), and the largest \(q\) with \(D_n(q)\le C\) is the optimal scaled feasible profit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The recurrence ranges over attainable total-profit indices and treats negative or otherwise out-of-range predecessor indices as infinity.
assumptions_latex: q_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}.
Each item may be selected at most once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max\{q:D_n(q)\le C\}\text{ is the optimal scaled knapsack value}.

notation.meaning: Total scaled profit of the first \(i\) items.
Minimum weight attaining exact scaled profit \(q\).

knowledge_statements.title: Complete Profit-Indexed Recurrence Domain
Knapsack Scaling Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Profit-scaling FPTAS for zero-one knapsack.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\) individually feasible items with weights \(w_i\), profits \(p_i\geq0\), capacity \(C\), and \(P=\max_i p_i>0\), choose \(K=\varepsilon P/n\) and set \(q_i=\lfloor p_i/K\rfloor\). Initialize \(D_0(0)=0\) and \(D_0(q)=+\infty\) for \(q>0\), then update \[D_i(q)=\min\{D_{i-1}(q),D_{i-1}(q-q_i)+w_i\}.\] Return a set attaining the largest \(q\) with \(D_n(q)\leq C\). For \(0<\varepsilon<1\), its true profit is at least \((1-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}\), and the table has \(O(n^2/\varepsilon)\) profit states.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Round profits downward, solve the resulting profit-indexed dynamic program, and obtain a knapsack solution worth at least one minus epsilon times optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(w_i\leq C\), \(p_i\geq0\), and \(P=\max_i p_i>0\).
\(0<\varepsilon<1\).

notation.meaning: Scaled integral profit of item i.
Minimum weight achieving scaled profit q using the first i items.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The standard profit-scaling FPTAS is recognizable, but no source is supplied. The state domain and the treatment of q-q_i<0 also require specification before the recurrence and state bound can be accepted.

children.title: Weak–Strong Hardness Boundary
children.top_down_role: The numerical-encoding boundary governing fully polynomial schemes.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak–Strong Hardness Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: FPTAS-to-pseudopolynomial implication for integer-valued maximization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Pi\) be an optimization problem whose feasible objective values are nonnegative integers bounded by an instance parameter \(U\). If \(\Pi\) has an FPTAS running in time polynomial in the binary input length and \(1/\varepsilon\), then running it with \(\varepsilon=1/(2U)\) returns an exact optimum: its integral value is greater than \(\operatorname{OPT}-1/2\). Hence \(\Pi\) has a pseudopolynomial exact algorithm. If \(\Pi\) remains NP-hard on instances for which \(U\) is polynomially bounded by the input length, such an FPTAS would imply \(P=NP\); this is the strong-hardness obstruction to scaling-based FPTASs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An FPTAS for a bounded integer objective yields a pseudopolynomial exact algorithm; strong NP-hardness therefore excludes such an FPTAS unless P equals NP.
assumptions_latex: All feasible objective values lie in \(\{0,1,\ldots,U\}\).
The approximation algorithm guarantees at least \((1-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}\) in time polynomial in the input length and \(1/\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{FPTAS}\Rightarrow\text{pseudopolynomial exact algorithm}\), and strong NP-hardness implies no FPTAS unless \(P=NP\).

notation.meaning: Numerical upper bound on feasible objective values.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limit of the FPTAS-to-exact argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Exact recovery requires a known positive separation between distinct attainable objective values. For arbitrary rational or real values with no encoding-controlled gap, an error below \(1/2\) need not identify the optimum, and choosing \(\varepsilon\) solely from an objective upper bound need not yield an exact algorithm. A minimization problem with possible optimum zero also requires a guarantee that separately detects or excludes zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The strong-hardness transfer depends on a controlled objective gap and careful treatment of zero optimum.
assumptions_latex: No known positive encoding-controlled gap separates distinct feasible objective values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{FPTAS}\not\Rightarrow\text{exact recovery by rounding alone without a controlled objective gap}.
knowledge_statements.title: Discrete-Gap Requirement for Exact Recovery

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimization Form of the FPTAS Exactness Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-integer minimization counterpart of the accepted maximization boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a minimization problem have positive integral feasible objective values and \(1\le\operatorname{OPT}\le U\). If an FPTAS returns value at most \((1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}\), choosing \(\varepsilon<1/U\) returns a value strictly below \(\operatorname{OPT}+1\), hence exactly \(\operatorname{OPT}\). The resulting runtime is polynomial in the input length and \(U\), so it is pseudopolynomial. Strong NP-hardness on polynomially bounded-\(U\) instances therefore excludes such an FPTAS unless \(P=NP\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For positive integer minimization objectives, sufficiently small relative error recovers the exact optimum and yields the same strong-hardness obstruction.
assumptions_latex: All feasible objective values are positive integers.
1\le\operatorname{OPT}\le U.
The approximation runtime is polynomial in input length and \(1/\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Numerical upper bound on the optimum.

children.title: Shifting Strategies

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Runtime of deterministic best-shift selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If each of \(k\) shifts is constructed in time \(P(n,k)\) and its residual subinstances are solved in total time \(T(n,k)\), evaluating every shift and selecting the best takes \(O(k(P(n,k)+T(n,k)))\) time. This is polynomial in \(n\) for fixed accuracy when \(k=k(\varepsilon)\) is independent of \(n\) and both component bounds are polynomial for fixed \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enumerating all accuracy-dependent shifts remains polynomial when their number is independent of input size.
assumptions_latex: k=k(\varepsilon)
P(n,k),T(n,k)\in n^{O_k(1)}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure without bounded aggregate exposure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete one-dimensional exclusion-pattern realization of shifting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose solution contributions have integer layers \(\ell(e)\), and deleting one residue class modulo \(k\) decomposes the residual instance into independently solvable blocks of at most \(k-1\) consecutive layers. For every \(r\in\{0,\ldots,k-1\}\), delete \(D_r=\{e:\ell(e)\equiv r\pmod k\}\), solve all residual blocks exactly, and return the best shift. Because the \(D_r\) partition every feasible solution's contributions, the returned nonnegative additive maximization value is at least \((1-1/k)\operatorname{OPT}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Delete each layer residue in turn; one shift loses at most one kth of the optimum and leaves bounded-width independent blocks.
assumptions_latex: The objective is nonnegative and additive over contributions.
Each contribution has exactly one integer layer.
Deleting one residue class separates the residual instance into independently solvable blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Periodic Layer-Deletion Shifting

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete multidimensional grid shifting for contributions with bounded layer spans.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let each contribution \(e\) occupy, in coordinate \(j\in[d]\), an integer interval \(I_j(e)\) containing at most \(b_j\) consecutive layers. For \(k>\max_j b_j\) and \(r\in\{0,\ldots,k-1\}^d\), delete \(e\) if some \(I_j(e)\) contains a layer congruent to \(r_j\pmod k\). Enumerate all \(k^d\) shifts, solve the resulting independent cells exactly, and return the best solution. Then every nonnegative additive optimum \(O\) loses, on average, at most the fraction \(1-\prod_{j=1}^d(1-b_j/k)\), and hence \[\operatorname{ALG}\ge\prod_{j=1}^d\left(1-\frac{b_j}{k}\right)\operatorname{OPT}\ge\left(1-\frac{\sum_{j=1}^d b_j}{k}\right)\operatorname{OPT}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enumerating translated multidimensional grids loses only the fraction of shifts in which a bounded-span contribution meets a deleted layer.
assumptions_latex: \(d\) and \(b_1,\ldots,b_d\) are fixed positive integers.
The objective is nonnegative and additive over solution contributions.
Deleting boundary-intersecting contributions leaves independently solvable cells.
Every contribution occupies at most \(b_j\) consecutive integer layers in coordinate \(j\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Randomly Translated Grid Shifting for Bounded-Diameter Objects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous Euclidean realization of bounded-exposure shifting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let every geometric contribution \(e\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) have nonnegative additive weight and coordinate width at most \(\Delta\). Choose \(\tau\) uniformly from \([0,L)^d\), where \(L=k\Delta\), translate the axis-parallel grid of cell side \(L\) by \(\tau\), and delete every contribution meeting a grid hyperplane. In each coordinate, translations causing \(e\) to meet a grid hyperplane have measure at most \(\Delta\), so \[\Pr[e\text{ is deleted}]\le\frac{d}{k}.\] Therefore, for every feasible solution \(O\), \[\mathbb E_\tau[w(O\cap D_\tau)]\le\frac{d}{k}w(O).\] If the surviving cells are independently solvable exactly, the resulting randomized shifting algorithm has expected value at least \((1-d/k)\operatorname{OPT}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A random translated grid deletes each bounded-width object with probability at most d over k, giving the continuous geometric form of shifting.
assumptions_latex: Every contribution has coordinate width at most \(\Delta\) in each of \(d\) dimensions.
The objective is nonnegative and additive.
After boundary-intersecting contributions are deleted, grid cells are independently solvable exactly.
\(k>d\) is an integer.

notation.meaning: Contributions meeting a grid boundary under translation tau.
A fixed feasible solution, particularly an optimum.

Shifting Strategies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Averaging principle for periodically shifted geometric decompositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(k\geq1\) shifts and let \(D_r\) be the objects discarded or cut under shift \(r\). Suppose an optimal solution \(O\) has nonnegative additive weight and each contribution of \(O\) belongs to at most \(c\) of the sets \(D_0,\ldots,D_{k-1}\). Then \[\sum_{r=0}^{k-1}w(O\cap D_r)\leq c\,w(O),\] so some shift \(r^*\) loses at most \(c\,w(O)/k\). If deletion under each shift produces independent subinstances and each subinstance is solved exactly, selecting the best shift returns value at least \((1-c/k)\operatorname{OPT}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Among k periodic shifts, one loses at most a c-over-k fraction when each optimal contribution is exposed to only c shifts.
assumptions_latex: The objective is nonnegative and additive over solution contributions.
Each optimal contribution is discarded under at most \(c\) shifts.
Deleting \(D_r\) separates the remaining instance into independently solvable components.

notation.meaning: Maximum number of shifts charging one contribution.

children.title: Partition Strategies
children.top_down_role: Geometric decompositions organized by spatial subdivision.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural condition for independent regional optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let deleting a buffer \(B\) leave regions \(R_1,\ldots,R_m\). If every inclusion-minimal infeasible set among retained objects is contained in one region and the objective is additive, then a retained set is feasible exactly when all of its regional restrictions are feasible, and \(\operatorname{OPT}(\bigcup_jR_j)=\sum_j\operatorname{OPT}(R_j)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regional optimization separates exactly when no minimal retained obstruction crosses two regions.
assumptions_latex: \text{Feasibility is hereditary}
\text{Every inclusion-minimal infeasible retained set lies in one }R_j
w(S)=\sum_jw(S\cap R_j)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of independent optimization when an obstruction crosses regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(u\in R_1\) and \(v\in R_2\) are individually feasible but \(\{u,v\}\) is infeasible, independently optimal regional solutions can have an infeasible union. Cross-region interactions must therefore be deleted, encoded by interface states, or reconciled globally.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Spatial subdivision alone does not justify combining independently optimized regions.
assumptions_latex: u\in R_1
v\in R_2
\{u,v\}\text{ is infeasible}

Partition Strategies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient conditions for loss-bounded regional decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R_1,\ldots,R_m\) partition the retained domain after deleting a boundary set \(B\). A valid approximation partition satisfies: feasible regional solutions have a feasible union; the restriction of an optimum \(O\) to the regions has total value at least \((1-\delta)w(O)\); and each regional algorithm returns at least an \(\alpha\)-fraction of its regional optimum. Under these conditions, combining the regional outputs gives \[w\!\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^m A_j\right)\geq \alpha(1-\delta)\operatorname{OPT}.\] For a scheme, \(\delta\) must be made arbitrarily small while the regional subproblems remain polynomially solvable for every fixed accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partition supports approximation when regional solutions combine feasibly, boundary deletion loses little optimum value, and every region can be approximated uniformly.
assumptions_latex: Regional feasible solutions have a feasible union.
Boundary deletion removes at most \(\delta\operatorname{OPT}\).
Each regional solution is an \(\alpha\)-approximation.

notation.meaning: A retained region of the partition.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated sufficient-condition template fits Partition Strategies, but it needs a source and an explicit additive decomposition linking regional values, the restricted optimum, and the value of the union.

L\geq1

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Depth-independent aggregate loss control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If every deleted contribution is charged to nonnegative contributions of an optimum and the total charge assigned to each optimal contribution \(e\) is at most \(\varepsilon w_e\), then all boundary deletions together have weight at most \(\varepsilon\operatorname{OPT}\), independently of recursion depth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A global per-contribution charging bound prevents recursive boundary losses from accumulating.
assumptions_latex: w_e\geq0
\text{Every deleted contribution is fully charged}
\operatorname{charge}(e)\leq\varepsilon w_e
knowledge_statements.title: Global Charging Bound for Boundary Loss
Boundary-Loss Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic criterion for boundary-deletion approximation schemes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a decomposition parameter \(k\), let \(\beta(k)\) be the worst-case fraction of optimal value charged to deleted boundaries after choosing the best permitted shift or partition. Pure boundary deletion yields a PTAS architecture only if \(\beta(k)\to0\) and the residual subinstances are solvable in polynomial time for every fixed \(k\). Choosing \(k\) with \(\beta(k)\leq\varepsilon\) then gives value at least \((1-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}\). Conversely, if \(\inf_k\beta(k)\geq\delta>0\), every algorithm restricted to this deletion architecture has approximation ratio at most \(1-\delta\) on some instance and cannot form a PTAS.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Boundary deletion supports a PTAS exactly when its worst-case fractional loss can vanish while fixed-parameter residual instances remain tractable.
assumptions_latex: Boundary losses are measured against a nonnegative maximization optimum.
Residual instances are solved exactly after deletion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\beta(k)\to0\) enables ratios \(1-\varepsilon\); \(\inf_k\beta(k)>0\) blocks a PTAS within the deletion architecture.

notation.meaning: Worst-case fractional boundary loss at parameter k.
A positive lower bound on unavoidable boundary loss.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sufficiency direction is plausible, but the claimed exact boundary and converse depend on a formally defined deletion-only algorithm class and worst-case loss function. No source supports that formulation.

children.title: Portal Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Portal Usage and Connectivity State Count
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combinatorial bound under limited crossings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With \(m\) portals and at most \(b\) crossing occurrences, there are at most \(\binom{m+b}{b}\) portal multisets. Recording an arbitrary partition of the occurrences into connectivity classes gives at most \(\binom{m+b}{b}B_b\) states, up to harmless overcounting for fewer than \(b\) occurrences.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded portal count and crossing multiplicity give finitely many usage-and-connectivity states.
assumptions_latex: m=m(\varepsilon)
b=b(\varepsilon)
knowledge_statements.title: Portal Usage and Connectivity State Count

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Crossing-multiplicity boundary for portal dynamic programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(b\) distinguishable boundary crossings each carry one of two externally relevant labels, there are \(2^b\) interface patterns. Portal discretization alone therefore does not ensure polynomial state complexity when \(b=\Omega(n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite portal set does not prevent exponential state complexity when crossing multiplicity is unbounded.
assumptions_latex: b=\Omega(n)
\text{Each crossing has two externally distinguishable labels}
knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded-Crossing State Explosion

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric cost of moving crossings to portals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a path crossing a boundary at \(x\) is rerouted through portal \(p\), the added metric length is at most \(2d(x,p)\). Snapping crossings \(x_1,\ldots,x_q\) to portals \(p_1,\ldots,p_q\) therefore adds at most \(2\sum_i d(x_i,p_i)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Snapping crossings to nearby portals costs at most twice their total snapping distance.
assumptions_latex: d\text{ is a metric}
knowledge_statements.title: Portal-Snapping Detour Bound

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract portal restriction independent of the underlying problem's internal feasibility semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal D\) be a recursive dissection and let each region \(Q\in\mathcal D\) have a finite portal set \(P_Q\subseteq\partial Q\). A geometric solution \(T\) is \((P,b)\)-portal-respecting if every crossing of \(\partial Q\) by \(T\) occurs at a portal in \(P_Q\), with total crossing multiplicity at most \(b\), for every \(Q\in\mathcal D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A portal-respecting solution crosses every region boundary only at designated portals and with bounded multiplicity.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal D\text{ is a recursive dissection}
P_Q\subseteq\partial Q\text{ is finite for every }Q
b\in\mathbb N
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\text{ is }(P,b)\text{-portal-respecting}\iff \forall Q\in\mathcal D:\ T\text{ crosses }\partial Q\text{ only in }P_Q\text{ and at most }b\text{ times}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic runtime composition from region, state, and transition bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a dissection has \(N\) regions, every region has at most \(S\) states, and all candidate transitions for one region can be generated and checked in time at most \(C\), then a bottom-up portal dynamic program runs in \(O(NC)\) time and stores \(O(NS)\) table entries. If every region has at most \(a\) children and transitions enumerate all child-state tuples, one may take \(C=O(S^ap)\), where \(p\) bounds the time to check and score one tuple.

p\text{ bounds one compatibility-and-scoring operation}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exactness of a Sufficient Portal Interface Dynamic Program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional correctness theorem for a portal-restricted interface state system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal D\) be a finite rooted recursive dissection. Suppose each region state is a sufficient interface equivalence class: partial solutions with the same state have the same feasible exterior completions and exterior interaction. If leaf tables enumerate all feasible partial solutions, internal transitions enumerate exactly the compatible child-state tuples, and root acceptance is equivalent to global feasibility, then bottom-up minimization returns the minimum-cost represented portal-respecting feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A portal dynamic program is exact for its restricted class when states preserve exterior interactions, transitions are exhaustive, and root acceptance exactly characterizes feasibility.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal D\text{ is a finite rooted recursive dissection}
\text{States are sufficient for exterior completion}
\text{Leaf and internal transitions are sound and complete}
\text{Root acceptance is equivalent to global feasibility}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c(\operatorname{DP})=\min\{c(T):T\text{ is represented, portal-respecting, and globally feasible}\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Exactness of a Sufficient Portal Interface Dynamic Program
Portal Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dynamic programming over discretized dissection-boundary crossings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a recursive dissection \(\mathcal D\), assign each region \(Q\) a finite portal set \(P_Q\subseteq\partial Q\). Enumerate states recording the used portals, their bounded crossing multiplicities, and the connectivity required inside \(Q\). Solve leaf states directly and combine compatible child states bottom-up; output the minimum-cost feasible root state. If every feasible solution \(T\) can be transformed into a portal-respecting solution \(T'\) with at most \(b(\varepsilon)\) crossings per region and \(c(T')\leq(1+\varepsilon)c(T)\), then the dynamic program returns a \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximation whenever its state encoding represents all such restricted solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restrict boundary crossings to finitely many portals, encode their connectivity, and optimize compatible states through the dissection hierarchy.
assumptions_latex: Each region \(Q\) has a finite portal set \(P_Q\subseteq\partial Q\).
A portal-respecting near-optimum with bounded crossings exists.
The state system exactly represents every permitted boundary connectivity pattern.

notation.meaning: Portals on the boundary of region Q.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic role fits Portal Methods, but the generic statement does not identify the geometric problem, feasible objects, connectivity semantics, or a polynomial state bound. A problem-specific portal theorem and locator are required.

children.title: Recursive Dissection Methods
children.top_down_role: Hierarchical spatial decomposition into recursively nested regions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Runtime and storage requirements for bottom-up dissection dynamic programming.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a dissection tree has \(T\) regions, branching at most \(b\), at most \(S\) states per region, and at most \(H\) work per child-state tuple, direct bottom-up enumeration takes \(O(TS^bH)\) time and stores \(O(TS)\) table entries. For fixed \(\varepsilon\), polynomial time requires \(T\), \(S^b\), and \(H\) to be polynomially bounded in the encoded input size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finitely many states do not imply polynomial time; the region count, state tuples, and transition work must be polynomially bounded.
assumptions_latex: The dissection tree has at most \(T\) nodes and branching at most \(b\).
Each region has at most \(S\) states.
Each child-state tuple is processed in time at most \(H\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactness condition for recursive-dissection state compression.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a region \(Q\), let \(X\sim_QY\) mean that \(X\) and \(Y\) admit exactly the same compatible exterior extensions with the same interface-dependent objective contribution. If \(s_Q(X)=s_Q(Y)\Rightarrow X\sim_QY\), the objective decomposes through the recorded interfaces, and every compatible child-state tuple is enumerated, retaining the best partial solution for each state preserves the optimum over all representable solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A state is sufficient when it never merges partial solutions having different exterior completions or interface costs.
assumptions_latex: The objective decomposes into region contributions and contributions recorded by interface states.
Every representable parent solution restricts to an enumerated compatible tuple of child states.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Statewise bottom-up compression preserves the representable optimum.}

notation.meaning: Extension equivalence at the boundary of \(Q\).

knowledge_statements.title: Extension-Sufficient Interface States

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of pruning under an interface description that is not extension-sufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(s_Q(X)=s_Q(Y)\) but some exterior partial solution is compatible with exactly one of \(X,Y\), or gives them different unrecorded interface contributions, retaining only the locally better representative can discard every globally optimal completion. Statewise dominance is sound only when it is preserved under every exterior completion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Merging partial solutions with different exterior behavior can destroy the global optimum.
assumptions_latex: The state map aliases partial solutions distinguishable by an exterior completion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: s_Q(X)=s_Q(Y)\not\Rightarrow X\sim_QY\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\text{statewise pruning is not generally sound}.

Recursive Dissection Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bottom-up optimization over a hierarchical spatial partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Construct a rooted dissection tree whose leaves contain base subinstances and whose internal region \(Q\) is the union of its children. For each region and each finite interface state \(\sigma\), store the best partial solution realizing \(\sigma\). Initialize leaf tables by direct optimization; at an internal node, enumerate compatible child states and retain the best combined value for every parent state. Return the best feasible root state. If a solution of value at least \((1-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}\) for maximization, or cost at most \((1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}\) for minimization, is representable by these states, the dynamic program inherits the corresponding guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recursively partition space and combine optimal compatible interface states from leaves to the root.
assumptions_latex: The dissection has bounded branching.
Each region has finitely many interface states for fixed \(\varepsilon\).
Compatible child solutions combine without unrecorded interactions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The root table optimizes over all representable dissection-respecting solutions.

notation.meaning: A region in the dissection tree.
An interface state for a region.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic binary-dissection DP complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a binary dissection tree with \(N\) regions, at most \(S\) states per region, and transition cost \(C\) per parent-state and child-state pair, exhaustive bottom-up evaluation uses \(O(NS)\) table space and \(O(NS^3C)\) time.

|\Sigma_Q|\leq S

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If two partial solutions share one state although some exterior completion is feasible with exactly one of them, discarding either representative can remove the only globally feasible optimum. Polynomial state count is therefore insufficient without completion-equivalence preservation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic sufficiency condition for an interface encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Two partial solutions in a region are completion-equivalent when every admissible exterior completion is compatible with both or with neither and induces the same exterior interaction data. An exact dynamic program over a restricted solution class may retain only the best interior objective value in each state when its states refine these equivalence classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An interface state must preserve every boundary distinction visible to an exterior completion.
assumptions_latex: \text{The objective decomposes into recorded interior and exterior contributions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Keeping the best representative in each completion class preserves the restricted optimum}

Interface-Restriction Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: State-space criterion for dissection-based approximation schemes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A dissection interface restriction is scheme-admissible at accuracy \(\varepsilon\) if every instance has a structured solution within factor \(1\pm\varepsilon\) of optimum, every region admits at most \(n^{g(\varepsilon)}\) interface states, and compatibility and transition costs are computable in \(n^{g(\varepsilon)}\) time. These conditions yield polynomial running time for every fixed \(\varepsilon\). The architecture fails to give a PTAS if, for some fixed \(\varepsilon_0>0\), every restriction with polynomially many states either excludes all \((1\pm\varepsilon_0)\)-optimal solutions or requires superpolynomial transition computation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Separator Recursion Depth by Balanced Measure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Depth bound in the measure actually balanced.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If every child \(J\) satisfies \(\mu(J)\leq\rho\mu(I)\) for fixed \(0<\rho<1\), and recursion stops below \(\mu_{\min}>0\), every root-to-leaf path has length at most \(\lceil\log_{1/\rho}(\mu(I_0)/\mu_{\min})\rceil\). This is \(O(\log n)\) only when the measure ratio is polynomially bounded in \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separator depth is logarithmic in the balanced-measure ratio, not automatically in item count.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Balanced Circle Separator for Bounded-Ply Disks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Planar geometric separator theorem for a specified regularity class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal D\) be a family of \(n\) disks in the plane with ply at most \(p\), meaning that no point lies in the interiors of more than \(p\) disks. There exists a circle for which the disks wholly inside and wholly outside each number at most \(\alpha n\), for an absolute constant \(\alpha<1\), and which intersects \(O(\sqrt{pn})\) disks. Handling the intersected disks therefore separates the remaining family into two balanced noninteracting subfamilies.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded-ply planar disk family has a balanced circle intersecting O(square root of p n) disks.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal D\) is a finite family of planar disks.
The ply is at most \(p\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Why balanced separator depth alone does not imply polynomial runtime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If every separator generates \(b(s)\) interface states that must all be explored, branching factors can multiply along a root-to-leaf path. A scheme therefore requires separate bounds on interface states and compatibility testing.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a weighted geometric subinstance \(I\), choose a separator whose two open sides each contain at most \(\rho w(I)\) relevant weight for a fixed \(\rho<1\). Discard or enumerate the objects interacting with the separator, recurse on both sides, and combine the compatible outputs. Stop on constant-size subinstances and solve them directly. If the recursion admits a charging rule under which all discarded optimal contributions total at most \(\varepsilon\operatorname{OPT}\), and enumerated interactions include those of a corresponding near-optimum, then the returned maximization solution has value at least \((1-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}\). Balance gives logarithmic recursion depth.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete Baker-style scheme for maximum-weight independent set on planar graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a finite plane graph with nonnegative vertex weights, and let \(L_0,L_1,\ldots\) be its iterative outer-face layers. Set \(k=\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil\). For each residue \(r\in\{0,\ldots,k-1\}\), delete \(R_r=\bigcup_{j\equiv r\pmod k}L_j\), compute a maximum-weight independent set in every component of \(G-R_r\) by bounded-treewidth dynamic programming, and return the best union. Each remaining component is at most \((k-1)\)-outerplanar and has treewidth at most \(3k-4\). For some residue, the deleted vertices contain at most \(\operatorname{OPT}/k\) weight of an optimum independent set. Hence the returned set has weight at least \((1-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}\), with running time \(2^{O(1/\varepsilon)}n^{O(1)}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be planar, assign nonnegative weights to vertices, and form BFS layers \(L_0,L_1,\ldots\). knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic dynamic-programming interface for exact bounded-treewidth subroutines inside approximation schemes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each leaf bag, initialize the feasible states and their exact local values. At an introduce, forget, or join bag, compute every state value by the prescribed compatibility transition and retain the best value among compatible child states. Because feasibility and objective contributions are compositional, the table at each bag records the exact optimum conditional on its boundary state. Reading the accepting state at the root therefore returns \(\operatorname{OPT}(G)\). If each transition is evaluable in \(\operatorname{poly}(|\Sigma_k|)\) time, the total running time is \(O(|V|\,\operatorname{poly}(|\Sigma_k|))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-state dynamic programming over a width-k decomposition exactly solves any locally compositional problem, with running time linear in graph size times a polynomial in the state count.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Treewidth Interfaces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The generic finite-state interface is plausible and the algorithm kind fits, but no cited source certifies the required compositional conditions, transition cost, or stated space bound. The statement also contains proof-style justification.

children.title: Dense-Instance Schemes
children.top_down_role: Schemes enabled by density, sampling, or regularity.

children.title: Dense-Graph Sampling
children.top_down_role: Sampled summaries for dense graph objectives.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointwise Accuracy Does Not Imply Uniform Optimization Accuracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifier boundary for optimizing sampled objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Bounds \(\Pr(|F(x)-\widehat F(x)|>\varepsilon M)\leq\delta\) for each fixed \(x\in X\) do not imply a uniform bound with failure probability \(\delta\). For \(|X|=N\), the error events can have union probability \(\min\{1,N\delta\}\), and overestimation on an erroneous candidate can cause the sampled optimizer to select it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pointwise concentration cannot replace simultaneous accuracy over the optimization class.
assumptions_latex: |X|=N
\Pr(|F(x)-\widehat F(x)|>\varepsilon M)\leq\delta\text{ for every fixed }x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pr(\exists x\in X:|F(x)-\widehat F(x)|>\varepsilon M)\text{ may be }\min\{1,N\delta\}
knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise Accuracy Does Not Imply Uniform Optimization Accuracy

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cut-Norm Summary for Dense Cut Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform representation of ordered cut objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For matrices \(A,\widehat A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), let \(\|A-\widehat A\|_\square=\max_{S,T\subseteq[n]}|\sum_{i\in S,j\in T}(A_{ij}-\widehat A_{ij})|\). If this norm is at most \(\eta n^2\), every ordered cut objective \(F_{S,T}(A)=\sum_{i\in S,j\in T}A_{ij}\) is represented within \(\eta n^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Small cut-norm error simultaneously controls every ordered cut objective.
assumptions_latex: \|A-\widehat A\|_\square\leq\eta n^2
knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Norm Summary for Dense Cut Objectives

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Constant-Size Sampling of Dense Maximum-Cut Value
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Induced-sample estimation of the normalized optimum value; it does not construct a cut of the full graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\varepsilon,\delta>0\) there is an integer \(q=q(\varepsilon,\delta)\), independent of \(n\), such that if \(G\) is a simple graph on \(n\ge q\) vertices and \(S\) is a uniformly random \(q\)-vertex subset, then \[\Pr\!\left[\left|\frac{\operatorname{MaxCut}(G[S])}{q^2}-\frac{\operatorname{MaxCut}(G)}{n^2}\right|\leq\varepsilon\right]\geq1-\delta.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant-size induced vertex sample estimates a graph's normalized maximum-cut value to fixed additive accuracy.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is a finite simple undirected graph}
n\geq q(\varepsilon,\delta)
S\text{ is uniform among the }q\text{-vertex subsets}

notation.meaning: Subgraph induced by the sampled vertices.
Maximum number of edges crossing a cut of G.

knowledge_statements.title: Constant-Size Sampling of Dense Maximum-Cut Value

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constant-complexity cut-norm summary for bounded dense matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(A\in[-1,1]^{n\times n}\) and \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist \(m=O(\varepsilon^{-2})\) weighted cut matrices \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\), each supported on a rectangle \(S_i\times T_i\), such that \[\left\|A-\sum_{i=1}^m C_i\right\|_\square\le\varepsilon n^2.\] Consequently their rectangle memberships and coefficients form a low-complexity summary simultaneously approximating all ordered cut objectives to additive error \(\varepsilon n^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every bounded dense matrix has an O(1/epsilon squared)-term cut decomposition uniformly approximating all ordered cuts.
assumptions_latex: \(\varepsilon>0\).

notation.meaning: Weighted cut matrix supported on a vertex rectangle.

knowledge_statements.title: Frieze–Kannan Weak Cut Decomposition

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Greedy Cut Decomposition with a Cut-Norm Oracle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructive weak decomposition conditional on exact rectangle-correlation optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R_0=A\in[-1,1]^{n\times n}\). While \(\|R_j\|_\square>\varepsilon n^2\), obtain \(S_j,T_j\) maximizing the absolute rectangle sum \(c_j\), set \(\alpha_j=c_j/(|S_j||T_j|)\), \(C_j=\alpha_j\mathbf1_{S_j}\mathbf1_{T_j}^{\mathsf T}\), and \(R_{j+1}=R_j-C_j\). Each iteration decreases squared Frobenius norm by more than \(\varepsilon^2n^2\); hence at most \(\lceil\varepsilon^{-2}\rceil\) matrices are produced and the final residual has cut norm at most \(\varepsilon n^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact cut-norm oracle constructs a weak cut decomposition in O(1/epsilon squared) iterations.
assumptions_latex: An exact maximizing rectangle oracle is available.
\(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Greedy Cut Decomposition with a Cut-Norm Oracle

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Computational qualification for greedy cut decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The energy decrement bounds only the number of iterations. It does not yield a polynomial-time implementation because maximizing \(|\sum_{i\in S,j\in T}R_{ij}|\) is a separate combinatorial optimization problem. A constructive runtime must specify an exact or approximate oracle and propagate any approximation loss into the threshold and term count.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Few decomposition iterations do not imply efficient construction without an implementable cut-norm oracle.
assumptions_latex: The method uses rectangle-correlation optimization on each residual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Iteration complexity alone does not establish polynomial total running time}.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Cut-Norm Oracle Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructive weak cut decomposition with approximation loss propagated from a multiplicative rectangle-sum oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R_0=A\in[-1,1]^{n\times n}\). Suppose an oracle, on every residual \(R\), returns \(S,T\subseteq[n]\) and the signed rectangle sum \(c=\sum_{i\in S,j\in T}R_{ij}\) satisfying \(|c|\ge\gamma\|R\|_\square\), where \(0<\gamma\le1\). While \(|c|>\gamma\varepsilon n^2\), set \(C=(c/(|S||T|))\mathbf1_S\mathbf1_T^{\mathsf T}\) and replace \(R\) by \(R-C\). The procedure performs at most \(\lceil(\gamma^2\varepsilon^2)^{-1}\rceil\) subtractions; upon termination, \(\|R\|_\square\le\varepsilon n^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multiplicative approximate rectangle oracle constructs an epsilon cut-norm summary in at most O(1/(gamma squared epsilon squared)) iterations.
assumptions_latex: \(0<\gamma\le1\) and \(\varepsilon>0\).
On every residual, the oracle returns a nonempty rectangle with signed sum \(c\) satisfying \(|c|\ge\gamma\|R\|_\square\).

notation.meaning: Multiplicative quality of the rectangle oracle.
Signed sum of the selected residual rectangle.
Signed weighted rectangle matrix subtracted at iteration j.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximate-Oracle Weak Cut Decomposition

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Constant-Factor Rectangle Oracle via Semidefinite Rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial-time oracle interface sufficient for constructive weak cut decomposition of rational matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There are universal constants \(\gamma,c>0\) and a randomized polynomial-time algorithm which, given a rational matrix \(R\), returns subsets \(S,T\) satisfying \[\Pr\!\left[\left|\sum_{i\in S,j\in T}R_{ij}\right|\ge\gamma\|R\|_\square\right]\ge c.\] A Grothendieck-type semidefinite relaxation with randomized sign rounding supplies such an oracle; independent repetition amplifies its success probability. Combined with approximate-oracle weak cut decomposition, constant \(\gamma\) yields \(O(\varepsilon^{-2})\) oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Semidefinite sign rounding gives a universal constant-factor approximation to the maximum absolute rectangle sum.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) has rational entries of finite encoding length.
The SDP is weakly optimized to sufficient inverse-polynomial accuracy.
knowledge_statements.title: Constant-Factor Rectangle Oracle via Semidefinite Rounding

assumptions_latex: \(F:X\to\mathbb R\) is the full dense-graph objective and \(\widehat F:X\to\mathbb R\) is the objective reconstructed from a sampled summary.
For some scale \(M>0\), \(\sup_{x\in X}|F(x)-\widehat F(x)|\leq \varepsilon M\).
\(\widehat x\in\arg\max_{x\in X}\widehat F(x)\).

notation.meaning: Natural dense-instance objective scale, commonly n squared.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic uniform-approximation interface underlying sampled dense-graph summaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x^*\in\arg\max_{x\in X}F(x)\). Uniform approximation by the sampled summary implies that optimizing the summary loses at most twice its uniform error: \[F(\widehat x)\geq \widehat F(\widehat x)-\varepsilon M\geq \widehat F(x^*)-\varepsilon M\geq F(x^*)-2\varepsilon M.\] Thus any sampling procedure establishing the stated uniform bound supplies a \(2\varepsilon M\)-additive approximation interface; its probability of success is exactly the probability with which that uniform bound holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sampled objective uniformly accurate within epsilon times the dense scale yields a solution within twice that additive error of the full optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Dense-Graph Sampling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The deterministic uniform-error implication is correct and locally relevant, but it does not itself establish a dense-graph sampling theorem or sample complexity. No source is cited, and the statement includes a derivation.

children.title: Dense Constraint-Satisfaction Schemes
children.top_down_role: Scheme families for dense constraint systems.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constraint-mass convention for bounded-weight fixed-arity CSPs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An \(r\)-ary CSP on \(n\) variables over a fixed finite domain is dense when its total bounded constraint weight satisfies \(W=\Omega(n^r)\); in the unweighted case this is equivalent to having \(\Omega(n^r)\) constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed-arity CSP is dense when it has a constant fraction of the possible constraint mass.
assumptions_latex: r\text{ and }|D|\text{ are fixed}
0\leq w_C\leq1
W=\sum_Cw_C
knowledge_statements.title: Dense Fixed-Arity CSP Regime

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limit of dense-scale additive guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\operatorname{OPT}\leq\varepsilon n^r\), even an assignment of value zero satisfies \(\operatorname{val}(A)\geq\operatorname{OPT}-\varepsilon n^r\); consequently that additive guarantee alone implies no positive multiplicative ratio.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dense-scale additive guarantees can be vacuous when optimum density vanishes.
assumptions_latex: \operatorname{OPT}\leq\varepsilon n^r
knowledge_statements.title: Vanishing-Optimum-Density Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion using a lower bound on optimum density.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\operatorname{OPT}\geq\gamma n^r\) and \(\operatorname{val}(A)\geq\operatorname{OPT}-\eta n^r\), then \(\operatorname{val}(A)\geq(1-\eta/\gamma)\operatorname{OPT}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive lower bound on optimum density converts dense-scale additive error into relative error.
assumptions_latex: \operatorname{OPT}\geq\gamma n^r
\operatorname{val}(A)\geq\operatorname{OPT}-\eta n^r
\gamma>0
knowledge_statements.title: Additive-to-Multiplicative Conversion in Dense CSPs

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Multiplicative PTAS for Dense Nontrivial Max-r-CSP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dense fixed-arity unweighted maximization CSPs with nonempty predicates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(r,q\in\mathbb N\), \(\gamma>0\), and \(\varepsilon>0\). Consider an unweighted Max-\(r\)-CSP on \(n\) variables over a \(q\)-element domain with at least \(\gamma n^r\) constraints, each predicate accepting at least one local assignment. A randomized dense-CSP approximation scheme returns an assignment \(A\) with \(\operatorname{val}(A)\ge(1-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}\) with probability at least \(2/3\), in polynomial time in \(n\) for fixed \(r,q,\gamma,\varepsilon\). Independent repetition and selection of the best evaluated assignment raises success to \(1-\delta\) with \(O(\log(1/\delta))\) runs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dense nontrivial fixed-arity Max-CSPs admit a randomized multiplicative PTAS for fixed domain, density, and accuracy.
assumptions_latex: \(r,q,\gamma,\varepsilon\) are fixed.
The instance has at least \(\gamma n^r\) unweighted constraints.
Every predicate accepts at least one local assignment.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiplicative PTAS for Dense Nontrivial Max-r-CSP

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower bound supporting multiplicative conversion in dense unweighted Max-r-CSPs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an unweighted CSP with \(m\) constraints of arity at most \(r\) over a \(q\)-element domain, if every predicate accepts at least one local assignment, then a uniform random assignment satisfies each constraint with probability at least \(q^{-r}\). Therefore \[\operatorname{OPT}\ge m q^{-r}.\] If \(m\ge\gamma n^r\), then \(\operatorname{OPT}\ge\gamma q^{-r}n^r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonempty predicates give a dense Max-CSP a constant optimum-density lower bound.
assumptions_latex: The domain size is \(q\).
Constraint arity is at most \(r\).
Every predicate accepts at least one tuple.
knowledge_statements.title: Nontrivial-Predicate Optimum-Density Lower Bound

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exhaustive Derandomization of Constant-Sample Dense-CSP Schemes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic conversion when every random choice is encoded by a constant-size sample and completed assignments are exactly evaluable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a randomized dense-CSP scheme draws an ordered sample of at most \(s\) variables, enumerates its \(q^s\) labelings, and deterministically constructs a full assignment from the sample and labels. Enumerate every ordered sample and every sample labeling, construct every resulting assignment, evaluate it on the full instance, and return the best. If any sampled outcome has value at least \(B\), the exhaustive algorithm returns value at least \(B\). Its running time is \(n^{O(s)}q^sP(n)\), where \(P(n)\) is the extension-and-evaluation time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant-sample dense-CSP scheme can be derandomized by enumerating all samples and sampled labelings when extension is deterministic.
assumptions_latex: All random choices are encoded by an ordered sample of at most \(s\) variables.
The extension rule is deterministic after fixing the sample and labels.
A completed assignment is exactly evaluable in time \(P(n)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Exhaustive Derandomization of Constant-Sample Dense-CSP Schemes

assumptions_latex: The instance is a dense \(r\)-ary maximization CSP on \(n\) variables over a fixed finite domain \(D\), with \(\Theta(n^r)\) constraints of value in \([0,1]\).
The arity \(r\), domain \(D\), and accuracy \(\varepsilon>0\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr[\operatorname{val}(A)\geq \operatorname{OPT}-\varepsilon n^r]\geq 2/3\), with running time polynomial in \(n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive randomized scheme for fixed-arity dense maximization CSPs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exists a randomized approximation scheme which samples a number of variables depending only on \(r\), \(|D|\), and \(\varepsilon\), enumerates assignments on the sample, estimates each remaining variable's contribution, and extends the best sampled assignment. For every dense instance satisfying the assumptions, the returned assignment \(A\) obeys \[\Pr\!\left[\operatorname{val}(A)\geq \operatorname{OPT}-\varepsilon n^r\right]\geq \frac23.\] For fixed \(r\), \(|D|\), and \(\varepsilon\), its running time is polynomial in \(n\); independent repetition raises the success probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed-arity dense maximization CSPs admit randomized polynomial-time additive approximation schemes for every fixed domain and accuracy.
knowledge_statements.title: Dense Constraint-Satisfaction Schemes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind fits the scheme-family leaf, but the density definition, sampling scheme, additive normalization, success probability, and polynomial runtime require an authoritative dense-CSP source.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic conditional-expectation CSP baseline; it is not a dense-instance scheme.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Sequentially choose each variable's label to maximize the conditional expected number of satisfied constraints when remaining variables are uniform. For predicates of arity at most \(r\) over a \(q\)-element domain, each accepting at least one tuple, the final assignment satisfies at least \(m/q^r\) constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conditional expectations deterministically realize the uniform-random CSP baseline.
assumptions_latex: Predicates are explicitly evaluable and have arity at most fixed \(r\).
The domain has fixed size \(q\).
Every predicate accepts at least one assignment.
knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Uniform-Baseline Assignment

intermediate_metadata.reason: This leaf owns approximation schemes for dense fixed-arity constraint systems, including density conventions, additive and multiplicative guarantees, and the optimum-density condition. Generic conditional-expectation rounding was deferred to CSP rounding; generic dense summaries remain in the sibling leaf.
