knowledge_statements.statement_title: Frequency approximation guarantee for the Bar-Yehuda–Even algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximation factor determined by maximum element frequency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every minimum-weight set-cover instance $(U,\mathcal S,c)$, define $p:=\max_{e\in U}|\{S\in\mathcal S:e\in S\}|$. The Bar-Yehuda–Even algorithm returns a set cover $\mathcal R$ satisfying $\sum_{R\in\mathcal R}c(R)\le p\operatorname{OPT}(U,\mathcal S,c)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Bar-Yehuda–Even algorithm is a p-approximation for minimum-weight set cover, where p is the maximum number of input sets containing any one universe element.
assumptions_latex: \bigcup_{S\in\mathcal S}S=U
c:\mathcal S\to\mathbb R_+
p=\max_{e\in U}|\{S\in\mathcal S:e\in S\}|

source_evidence.locator: Approximation Algorithms / 16.1. Set Covering / Theorem 16.5

knowledge_statements.title: Frequency approximation guarantee for the Bar-Yehuda–Even algorithm

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-cost and element-dual construction for weighted set cover.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given $(U,\mathcal S)$ with $\bigcup_{S\in\mathcal S}S=U$ and $c:\mathcal S\to\mathbb R_+$, initialize $\mathcal R:=\varnothing$, $W:=\varnothing$, $y(e):=0$ for every $e\in U$, and $c'(S):=c(S)$ for every $S\in\mathcal S$. While $W\ne U$, choose any $e\in U\setminus W$, choose $R\in\mathcal S$ with $e\in R$ minimizing $c'(R)$, set $y(e):=c'(R)$, replace $c'(S)$ by $c'(S)-y(e)$ for every $S\ni e$, and set $\mathcal R\leftarrow\mathcal R\cup\{R\}$ and $W\leftarrow W\cup R$. Upon termination, $\mathcal R$ is a set cover.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain residual set costs and initially zero element variables. Choose an uncovered element, select a containing set of minimum residual cost, assign that cost to the element, subtract it from every set containing the element, and add the selected set to the cover. Continue until the universe is covered.
assumptions_latex: \bigcup_{S\in\mathcal S}S=U
c:\mathcal S\to\mathbb R_+

source_evidence.locator: Approximation Algorithms / 16.1. Set Covering / Algorithm 16.1-extra-4

knowledge_statements.title: Bar-Yehuda–Even set-cover algorithm

children.title: Greedy Set-Cover Regimes
children.top_down_role: Set-cover approximation organized around greedy selection.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical weighted and unweighted greedy regimes for Set Cover.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Starting with uncovered set \(R=U\), repeatedly choose a set \(S\) minimizing \(c_S/|S\cap R|\) among sets meeting \(R\), add it to the cover, and delete \(S\cap R\) from \(R\). If \(D=\max_{S\in\mathcal S}|S|\), the resulting cover \(C\) satisfies \(c(C)\leq H_D\operatorname{OPT}\leq(1+\ln D)\operatorname{OPT}\). For unit costs the rule is maximum-new-coverage greedy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Greedy chooses minimum cost per newly covered element and achieves the harmonic H_D approximation guarantee.
assumptions_latex: (U,\mathcal S,c)\text{ is finite and coverable}.
c_S>0\text{ for every candidate set}.
D=\max_{S\in\mathcal S}|S|.
knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Cost-Effectiveness Greedy

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Worst-Case Tightness of Greedy Set Cover
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic worst-case boundary for maximum-new-coverage greedy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There are unweighted Set Cover families with \(n\to\infty\) on which maximum-new-coverage greedy, with an adverse permissible tie-breaking rule, returns a cover of size \((1-o(1))\ln n\) times optimum. Thus this greedy rule has no constant approximation guarantee on unrestricted instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The logarithmic worst-case guarantee of set-cover greedy is asymptotically tight on unrestricted instances.
assumptions_latex: n=|U|\to\infty.
Ties may be resolved adversarially.
knowledge_statements.title: Worst-Case Tightness of Greedy Set Cover

assumptions_latex: \((U,\mathcal S,c)\) is a weighted set-cover instance with \(c_S>0\) and every element covered by some set.
\(D=\max_{S\in\mathcal S}|S|\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted greedy set cover with the harmonic guarantee parameterized by maximum set size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(C=\varnothing\) and let \(R=U\) be the uncovered elements. While \(R\neq\varnothing\), choose a set \(S\in\mathcal S\) minimizing \(c_S/|S\cap R|\) among sets meeting \(R\), add \(S\) to \(C\), and replace \(R\) by \(R\setminus S\). Output \(C\). The resulting cover satisfies \[c(C)=\sum_{S\in C}c_S\leq H_D\operatorname{OPT}\leq (1+\ln D)\operatorname{OPT}.\] In particular, since \(D\leq |U|\), greedy is also an \(H_{|U|}\)-approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted greedy repeatedly minimizes cost per newly covered element and returns an H_D-approximate cover, where D is the largest set size.
knowledge_statements.title: Greedy Set-Cover Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm and harmonic guarantee are standard and fit the greedy-regime leaf, but no inspectable citation supports the weighted H_D guarantee.

children.title: Rounding-Based Set-Cover Regimes
children.top_down_role: Set-cover approximation organized around relaxation rounding.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logarithmic randomized rounding of the standard weighted set-cover LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be a feasible weighted set-cover LP solution, let \(n=|U|\), choose \(0<\delta<1\), and set \(\alpha=\ln(n/\delta)\). Independently select each set \(S\) with probability \(p_S=\min\{1,\alpha x_S\}\). The resulting family has expected cost at most \(\alpha\sum_Sc_Sx_S\) and covers all elements with probability at least \(1-\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling and independently rounding a feasible cover LP gives logarithmic expected cost and high-probability coverage.
assumptions_latex: x_S\geq0\text{ and }\sum_{S\ni e}x_S\geq1\text{ for every }e.
n=|U|\geq1.
0<\delta<1.
c_S\geq0\text{ for all }S.
knowledge_statements.title: Independent Randomized Set-Cover Rounding

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic rounding on bounded-frequency Set Cover instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If every element belongs to at most \(f\) candidate sets and \(x\) is a feasible fractional cover, selecting every set with \(x_S\geq1/f\) produces a cover \(C\) satisfying \(c(C)\leq f\sum_Sc_Sx_S\leq f\operatorname{OPT}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On frequency-f instances, the 1/f threshold deterministically rounds the cover LP to an f-approximate cover.
assumptions_latex: x_S\geq0\text{ and }\sum_{S\ni e}x_S\geq1\text{ for every }e.
|\{S:e\in S\}|\leq f\text{ for every }e.
c_S\geq0\text{ for all }S.
knowledge_statements.title: Frequency-Threshold LP Rounding

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Difference between high-probability coverage and an always-feasible output.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Independent rounding can leave an element uncovered with positive probability whenever all its incident sets are selected with probabilities strictly below one. Therefore an algorithm required always to return a cover needs conditioning, repetition with feasibility testing, alteration, or deterministic rounding; an expected-cost bound alone is not a feasible-solution guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent rounding is not automatically feasible and needs a repair, conditioning, or repetition mechanism for an always-returned cover.
assumptions_latex: Set selections are independent.
Some element has every incident selection probability strictly below one.
knowledge_statements.title: Independent-Rounding Feasibility Boundary

assumptions_latex: \(x\) is feasible for the weighted set-cover LP: \(x_S\geq0\) and \(\sum_{S\ni e}x_S\geq1\) for every \(e\in U\).
\(n=|U|\), \(0<\delta<1\), and \(\alpha=\ln(n/\delta)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent randomized rounding of the standard weighted set-cover relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Independently include each \(S\in\mathcal S\) in \(C\) with probability \(p_S=\min\{1,\alpha x_S\}\). For an element \(e\), LP feasibility gives \[\Pr[e\text{ is uncovered}]=\prod_{S\ni e}(1-p_S)\leq \exp\!\left(-\alpha\sum_{S\ni e}x_S\right)\leq e^{-\alpha}=\frac{\delta}{n}.\] Hence the union bound yields \(\Pr[C\text{ covers }U]\geq1-\delta\). Moreover, \(\mathbb E[c(C)]=\sum_Sc_Sp_S\leq\alpha\sum_Sc_Sx_S\). Conditional repetition or alteration may be used when a cover must always be returned.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling and independently rounding a feasible cover LP produces a cover with high probability and expected cost at most ln(n/delta) times the LP value.
knowledge_statements.title: Rounding-Based Set-Cover Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rounding claim is mathematically plausible and the algorithm kind fits, but it lacks an authoritative citation and contains a probability derivation rather than only a knowledge statement.

children.title: Dual-Fitting Set-Cover Regimes
children.top_down_role: Set-cover approximation organized around fitted dual certificates.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-cover specialization of scaled-dual approximation certification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In weighted cost-per-new-element greedy, assign each element \(e\) the price \(y_e\) charged when it is first covered. If \(D=\max_{S\in\mathcal S}|S|\), then the selected cover \(C\) satisfies \(c(C)=\sum_e y_e\), and \(y/H_D\) is feasible for the dual of the standard weighted set-cover LP. Consequently \(c(C)\leq H_D\operatorname{OPT}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Greedy element prices become dual feasible after division by H_D and certify the weighted greedy approximation ratio.
assumptions_latex: (U,\mathcal S,c)\text{ is a finite coverable weighted Set Cover instance with }c_S>0.
C\text{ is returned by cost-per-new-element greedy}.
D=\max_{S\in\mathcal S}|S|.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y/H_D\text{ is dual feasible and }c(C)\leq H_D\operatorname{OPT}.

notation.meaning: Greedy price charged to element e when first covered.

knowledge_statements.title: Greedy Dual-Fitting Certificate

assumptions_latex: \((U,\mathcal S,c)\) is a weighted set-cover instance and \(C\) is the cover returned by cost-per-new-element greedy.
\(D=\max_{S\in\mathcal S}|S|\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-fitting certificate for the weighted greedy set-cover guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: When greedy selects \(S\), assign each newly covered element \(e\in S\) the price \(y_e=c_S/|S\cap R|\), where \(R\) is the uncovered set immediately before selection. These prices satisfy \(c(C)=\sum_{e\in U}y_e\). knowledge_statements.scope_note: Frequency-sensitive primal-dual algorithm for weighted set cover.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(y_e=0\) and \(C=\varnothing\). While an uncovered element \(e\) remains, increase \(y_e\) until some set \(S\ni e\) becomes tight, meaning \(\sum_{u\in S}y_u=c_S\), and add one such tight set to \(C\). Stop when all elements are covered and output \(C\). Dual feasibility is maintained. Since every selected set is tight, \[c(C)=\sum_{S\in C}\sum_{e\in S}y_e=\sum_{e\in U}y_e|\{S\in C:e\in S\}|\leq f\sum_{e\in U}y_e\leq f\operatorname{OPT}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Raising dual variables until incident sets become tight gives a frequency-f approximation for weighted set cover.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed \(f\ge2\), let the available sets correspond to the vertices of an \(n\)-element ground set for an \(f\)-uniform hitting-set instance whose obstructions are all \(f\)-subsets. In the equivalent Set Cover instance, every universe element has frequency \(f\). The integral optimum is \(n-f+1\), while the fractional optimum is \(n/f\); hence the gap is \(f(n-f+1)/n\), which approaches \(f\) as \(n\to\infty\).

After selecting forced vertices and deleting covered elements, minimum-weight Set Cover is exactly minimum-weight Vertex Cover in the resulting graph.

Every element occurs in at most two sets.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite set-cover instances represented by points and geometric ranges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite point set \(P\) and a finite effectively represented family of geometric ranges \(\mathcal R\), the induced set-cover instance is \((P,\{P\cap R:R\in\mathcal R\})\). A subfamily \(\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal R\) is a cover exactly when \(P\subseteq\bigcup_{R\in\mathcal C}R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Geometric set cover selects represented geometric ranges whose union contains every input point.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Computational limitation of epsilon-net-based approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An existential epsilon-net bound yields an existential integral-cover bound, but it yields a polynomial-time approximation algorithm only when the required net can be constructed or sampled and the resulting coverage can be verified in polynomial time under the chosen range representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Small epsilon-nets do not by themselves give an efficient covering algorithm; an effective construction and feasibility test are also required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epsilon-Net Conversion for Geometric Set Cover
knowledge_statements.scope_note: LP-relative cover bound obtained from the dual incidence range space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be a feasible fractional cover, let \(\tau=\sum_{S\in\mathcal S}x_S\geq1\), and put \(p(S)=x_S/\tau\). If the dual incidence range space \((\mathcal S,\{\{S:e\in S\}:e\in U\})\), with probability measure \(p\), has an \(\eta\)-net of size at most \(g(1/\eta)\), then an integral cover of size at most \(g(\tau)\) exists. In particular, dual VC dimension at most \(d\) gives a cover of size \(O(d\tau\log(1+\tau))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An epsilon-net for the dual incidence space converts a fractional geometric cover into an integral cover; bounded dual VC dimension gives an O(d tau log(1+tau)) bound.
assumptions_latex: U\neq\varnothing.
x_S\geq0\text{ and }\sum_{S\ni e}x_S\geq1\text{ for every }e\in U.
The stated epsilon-net bound applies to the probability measure induced by x.

For \(p(S)=x_S/\tau\), every induced range space on \(\mathcal S\) has an \(\eta\)-net of size at most \(g(1/\eta)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epsilon-net interface for approximation guarantees in geometric set systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each element \(e\in U\), define the range \(R_e=\{S\in\mathcal S:e\in S\}\). Fractional feasibility gives \[p(R_e)=\sum_{S\ni e}\frac{x_S}{\tau}\geq\frac1\tau.\] Therefore any \((1/\tau)\)-net \(N\subseteq\mathcal S\) for the range space \((\mathcal S,\{R_e:e\in U\})\) intersects every \(R_e\), so \(N\) is a set cover. Under the assumed net bound, \(|N|\leq g(\tau)\). A polynomial-time approximation additionally requires a polynomial-time construction or sampling theorem for such nets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An epsilon-net bound for the dual incidence range space converts a fractional geometric cover of value tau into an integral cover of size at most g(tau).

children.title: Restriction-Sensitive Frontiers
children.top_down_role: Changes in approximation guarantees across structured set-system restrictions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical transfer rules for algorithms and hardness when the instance class is restricted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal I'\subseteq\mathcal I\) be classes of the same minimization problem using the same approximation convention. Every polynomial-time \(\rho\)-approximation on \(\mathcal I\) is a \(\rho\)-approximation on \(\mathcal I'\). An inapproximability bound for \(\mathcal I\) transfers to \(\mathcal I'\) only when the underlying gap reduction has image in \(\mathcal I'\) and preserves the asserted gap and encoding conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: General algorithms remain valid after restriction, whereas hardness transfers only through reductions that preserve the restriction and approximation gap.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal I'\subseteq\mathcal I.
Both classes use the same objective, encoding model, and approximation-ratio convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho_{\mathrm{alg}}(\mathcal I')\leq\rho_{\mathrm{alg}}(\mathcal I),\text{ while general-class hardness alone implies no lower bound on }\mathcal I'.

notation.meaning: Best polynomial-time approximation factor under the fixed convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximation-Frontier Transfer under Restrictions

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal I'\subseteq\mathcal I\) is a restricted class of set-cover instances.

notation.meaning: Best achievable polynomial-time approximation factor on a class.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical transfer rules governing approximation frontiers under restrictions of set systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Any polynomial-time \(\rho\)-approximation valid on \(\mathcal I\) remains valid after restriction to \(\mathcal I'\), hence \(\rho_{\mathrm{alg}}(\mathcal I')\leq\rho_{\mathrm{alg}}(\mathcal I)\). The converse need not hold because restrictions may enable stronger algorithms. Likewise, an inapproximability result for \(\mathcal I\) establishes the same lower bound on \(\mathcal I'\) only if its reduction always produces instances in \(\mathcal I'\) and preserves the claimed gap. Thus frequency, set size, geometry, or other structural promises must be checked on both the algorithmic and hardness sides of a frontier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricting instances preserves general algorithms but not general hardness; a hardness bound transfers only when its gap reduction produces instances satisfying the restriction.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), it is NP-hard to distinguish unweighted Set Cover instances on a universe of size \(n\) whose optimum is at most \(a\) from instances whose optimum exceeds \((1-\varepsilon)(\ln n)a\), for the parameter range produced by the reduction. knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The weighted vertex-cover relaxation is \[\min\sum_{v\in V}w_vx_v\quad\text{s.t.}\quad x_u+x_v\ge1\ (uv\in E),\qquad x_v\ge0.\] It has an optimal solution with \(x_v\in\{0,\tfrac12,1\}\). \(w_v\ge0\) for every vertex.

Consequently, unless \(P=NP\), the problem admits no polynomial-time approximation scheme.

knowledge_statements.title: Worst-case family for maximum-degree greedy vertex cover

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Greedy vertex-cover construction using degrees in the residual graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a graph $G$, initialize $R:=\varnothing$. While $E(G)\ne\varnothing$, choose a vertex $v\in V(G)\setminus R$ of maximum current degree, set $R\leftarrow R\cup\{v\}$, and delete every edge incident with $v$. Upon termination, $R$ is a vertex cover of the original graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly choose a maximum-degree vertex in the current residual graph, add it to the cover, and delete its incident edges. When no edges remain, the selected vertices cover every original edge.

children.title: Feedback Vertex Set Frontier
children.top_down_role: Algorithmic guarantees and hardness limits for feedback vertex set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial separation for the exponential cycle family in the basic FVS relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given nonnegative vertex lengths \(x_v\), a minimum-weight simple cycle can be found in polynomial time. A cycle of weight below one supplies a violated constraint \(\sum_{v\in C}x_v\ge1\); if no such cycle exists, every cycle-covering constraint is satisfied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimum-weight-cycle computation separates the exponential family of FVS cycle constraints.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and undirected.
\(x_v\ge0\) for every vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{C\in\mathcal C(G)}\sum_{v\in C}x_v<1\iff\text{a cycle-covering inequality is violated}.
knowledge_statements.title: Separation of Cycle-Covering Constraints

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Excludes directed feedback vertex set from the undirected factor-two frontier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The factor-two theorem for undirected Feedback Vertex Set does not transfer merely by replacing undirected cycles with directed cycles. Directed Feedback Vertex Set is a distinct approximation problem, and no directed factor-two guarantee follows from the undirected result.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The undirected factor-two theorem does not imply a factor-two approximation for Directed Feedback Vertex Set.
assumptions_latex: The directed problem requires hitting every directed cycle.
knowledge_statements.title: Directed Variant Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical covering formulation for weighted undirected Feedback Vertex Set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal C(G)\) be the simple cycles of \(G\). Weighted Feedback Vertex Set is \[\min\sum_{v\in V}w_vx_v\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\sum_{v\in C}x_v\ge1\ (C\in\mathcal C(G)),\qquad x_v\in\{0,1\}.\] Replacing integrality by \(x_v\ge0\) gives an LP whose dual fractionally packs cycles subject to vertex capacities \(w_v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feedback Vertex Set is cycle hitting, and its basic LP is dual to fractional cycle packing under vertex capacities.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and undirected.
\(w_v\ge0\) for every vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\text{ is a feedback vertex set}\iff S\cap C\ne\varnothing\text{ for every }C\in\mathcal C(G).

notation.meaning: family of simple cycles of G

knowledge_statements.title: Cycle-Hitting Formulation and Packing Dual

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted extension of the undirected approximation frontier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every finite undirected graph with nonnegative vertex weights, a polynomial-time algorithm returns a feedback vertex set \(S\) satisfying \[w(S)\le2\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{WFVS}}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted undirected Feedback Vertex Set has a polynomial-time factor-two approximation.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and undirected.
Vertex weights are nonnegative.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph.
A feedback vertex set is a set \(S\subseteq V\) for which \(G-S\) is acyclic.
The objective is to minimize \(|S|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Undirected Feedback Vertex Set has a polynomial-time factor-\(2\) approximation but no PTAS unless \(P=NP\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undirected, unweighted Feedback Vertex Set; directed variants have different frontiers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There is a polynomial-time algorithm which, for every finite undirected graph \(G\), returns a feedback vertex set \(S\) satisfying \[|S|\leq 2\operatorname{fvs}(G).\] On the hardness side, the problem is APX-hard: some constant \(\delta>0\) exists such that a polynomial-time \((1+\delta)\)-approximation would imply \(P=NP\). Hence the undirected problem has a constant-factor approximation, but it has no polynomial-time approximation scheme unless \(P=NP\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Undirected Feedback Vertex Set admits a factor-two approximation, while APX-hardness rules out a PTAS unless P equals NP.
knowledge_statements.title: Feedback Vertex Set Frontier

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement consistently concerns unweighted undirected Feedback Vertex Set and fits the frontier container, but the factor-2 theorem and APX-hardness claim require authoritative citations.

children.title: Obstruction-Set Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Structural contrasts between edge-covering and cycle-breaking vertex selections.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial Verification for Explicit and Implicit Obstructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of feasibility and separation for edge and cycle obstruction systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(X\subseteq V\), Vertex Cover feasibility is decided by scanning for an uncovered edge. Feedback Vertex Set feasibility is decided by testing whether \(G-X\) is acyclic. Both tests take \(O(|V|+|E|)\) time; an uncovered edge or residual cycle is a violated obstruction constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Both edge hitting and cycle hitting have linear-time feasibility tests, despite the implicit exponential cycle family.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite undirected graph.
\(X\subseteq V\) is explicitly given.
knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Verification for Explicit and Implicit Obstructions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explains why generic hitting-set rank arguments apply to edges but not to cycles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an unweighted hitting-set instance of rank \(q\), the union of a maximal pairwise-disjoint obstruction packing is a hitting set of size at most \(q\) times optimum. Edge obstructions have rank two, yielding the generic factor two for Vertex Cover. Cycle obstructions have unbounded cardinality, so this argument gives no constant factor for Feedback Vertex Set; its factor-two theorem uses additional graph structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded-rank hitting set explains Vertex Cover's factor two but not Feedback Vertex Set's factor two.
assumptions_latex: The obstruction family is finite or supports construction of a maximal disjoint packing.
The generic approximation statement is unweighted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: q=2\text{ for edges, while }\sup_{C\in\mathcal C(G)}|C|\text{ is unbounded}.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Rank Transfer Boundary

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite simple undirected graph.
A hitting-set instance consists of a universe \(U\) and a family \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Vertex Cover is rank-\(2\) hitting set, whereas Feedback Vertex Set is hitting set for an unbounded family of cycles.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares exact hitting-set representations rather than asserting identical approximation behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\mathcal E_G=\{\{u,v\}:uv\in E\}\) and let \(\mathcal C_G\) be the family of vertex sets of all simple cycles of \(G\). Then \[C\text{ is a vertex cover}\iff C\cap F\neq\varnothing\quad\text{for every }F\in\mathcal E_G,\] while \[S\text{ is a feedback vertex set}\iff S\cap F\neq\varnothing\quad\text{for every }F\in\mathcal C_G.\] The first obstruction family has rank \(2\); the second can contain sets of arbitrarily large cardinality and may have exponentially many members.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vertex Cover hits two-vertex edge obstructions; Feedback Vertex Set hits an implicit, potentially exponential family of cycles of unbounded size.
knowledge_statements.title: Obstruction-Set Comparisons

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two hitting-set equivalences are precise, and representation is the correct kind for this comparison leaf. A source with a specific locator is nevertheless required for the nontrivial cycle-family representation and size claims.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact small-budget regime for explicitly represented Maximum Coverage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an explicit family of \(m\) sets and fixed budget \(k\), enumerating all subfamilies of size at most \(k\) computes an optimum in time \(m^{O(k)}\operatorname{poly}(|U|)\). This is polynomial for each fixed constant \(k\), but not polynomial in general when \(k\) is part of the input.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximum Coverage is exactly solvable by m-to-the-k enumeration for fixed k, but not thereby for variable k.
assumptions_latex: The set system is explicitly represented.
\(k\) is fixed for the polynomial-time claim.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local diminishing-returns structure of coverage objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonnegative element weights, \(f(A)=w(\bigcup_{S\in A}S)\) is normalized, monotone, and submodular. Thus, for \(A\subseteq B\) and \(T\notin B\), \[f(A\cup\{T\})-f(A)\ge f(B\cup\{T\})-f(B).\] Negative element weights can destroy monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coverage with nonnegative element weights is normalized, monotone, and submodular.
assumptions_latex: Element weights are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is normalized, monotone, and submodular}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonnegative element-weight extension under a cardinality budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p_u\ge0\) and \(f(A)=\sum_{u\in\cup_{S\in A}S}p_u\). Repeatedly adding a set of maximum marginal gain for \(k\) iterations returns \(A_k\) satisfying \[f(A_k)\ge\left(1-\left(1-\frac1k\right)^k\right)\operatorname{OPT}_k\ge(1-1/e)\operatorname{OPT}_k.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Greedy retains the one-minus-one-over-e guarantee for nonnegative weighted coverage.
assumptions_latex: The universe and family are finite.
Element weights are nonnegative.
At most \(k\) sets may be selected.

assumptions_latex: \(U\) is finite and \(\mathcal S=\{S_1,\ldots,S_m\}\subseteq 2^U\).
The budget satisfies \(1\leq k\leq m\).
Approximation ratios compare covered cardinality with the optimum using at most \(k\) sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Greedy achieves at least \(1-1/e\), and any factor exceeding \(1-1/e\) by a constant would imply \(P=NP\).

notation.meaning: elements covered after the greedy choices

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cardinality Maximum Coverage under a cardinality budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Starting with \(C_0=\varnothing\), at iteration \(i\) choose a set maximizing \(|S_j\setminus C_{i-1}|\) and put \(C_i=C_{i-1}\cup S_j\). After \(k\) iterations, \[|C_k|\geq \left(1-\left(1-\frac1k\right)^k\right)\mathrm{OPT}_k\geq (1-1/e)\mathrm{OPT}_k.\] Conversely, for every constant \(\varepsilon>0\), a polynomial-time \((1-1/e+\varepsilon)\)-approximation for Maximum Coverage would imply \(P=NP\). Thus the diminishing-returns guarantee meets the standard hardness boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Greedy Maximum Coverage attains at least one minus one over e, and improving this ratio by any fixed amount is NP-hard.
knowledge_statements.title: Maximum Coverage Frontier

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The greedy guarantee and matching hardness boundary are stated consistently for cardinality Maximum Coverage, and theorem is an appropriate kind, but neither result has a cited source.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A valid inequality determined by disjoint handles and teeth satisfying parity and connectivity conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H_1,\ldots,H_r\) be pairwise disjoint subsets and let \(T_1,\ldots,T_s\), where \(s\ge1\), be pairwise disjoint nonempty proper subsets. children.title: Metric TSP Frontier
children.top_down_role: Tree, matching, circulation, and APX-hardness regimes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical LP lower bound for symmetric metric TSP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The subtour-elimination relaxation is \[\min\sum_ec_ex_e\quad\text{s.t.}\quad x(\delta(v))=2\ (v\in V),\quad x(\delta(S))\ge2\ (\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V),\quad x_e\ge0.\] Its optimum \(\operatorname{HK}\) satisfies \(\operatorname{HK}\le\operatorname{OPT}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Degree-two equations and subtour cuts define the standard Held–Karp lower bound.
assumptions_latex: The instance is a complete undirected graph with nonnegative edge costs.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence frontier for randomized polynomial-time approximation of symmetric metric TSP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There is a universal constant \(\epsilon_0>0\) and a randomized polynomial-time algorithm returning a tour \(H\) with \[\mathbb E[c(H)]\le(3/2-\epsilon_0)\operatorname{OPT}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Symmetric metric TSP admits a randomized polynomial-time approximation strictly better than three halves.
assumptions_latex: Costs are nonnegative, symmetric, and satisfy the triangle inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Improvement over Three Halves

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is complete and undirected.
Edge costs \(c:E\to\mathbb R_{\geq0}\) satisfy the triangle inequality.
The objective is a minimum-cost Hamiltonian cycle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Metric TSP has a factor-\(3/2\) approximation and is APX-hard.

notation.meaning: tour returned by the tree-and-matching construction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical symmetric metric TSP benchmark; factor three-halves is not asserted to be the exact threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The tree-and-matching algorithm computes a minimum spanning tree, adds a minimum-cost perfect matching on its odd-degree vertices, takes an Euler tour, and shortcuts repeated vertices. Triangle inequality preserves feasibility without increasing cost, and the resulting Hamiltonian cycle \(H\) satisfies \[c(H)\leq \frac32\mathrm{OPT}.\] Metric TSP is also APX-hard: there is a constant \(\delta>0\) such that a polynomial-time \((1+\delta)\)-approximation would imply \(P=NP\). Therefore it has constant-factor approximation but no PTAS unless \(P=NP\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tree, matching, Euler traversal, and shortcutting give a three-halves approximation; APX-hardness excludes a PTAS unless P equals NP.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric TSP Frontier

assumptions_latex: The dimension \(d\geq2\) is fixed.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fixed-dimensional Euclidean TSP admits a PTAS returning a tour of length at most \((1+\varepsilon)\mathrm{OPT}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed dimension; polynomial degree may depend on dimension and accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every fixed \(d\geq2\) and fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), there is an algorithm that, on every finite \(P\subset\mathbb R^d\), returns a Hamiltonian cycle \(T_\varepsilon\) satisfying \[\operatorname{length}(T_\varepsilon)\leq(1+\varepsilon)\mathrm{OPT}(P).\] Its running time is polynomial in \(|P|\) when \(d\) and \(\varepsilon\) are fixed. The algorithmic basis is a geometric decomposition with a bounded interface state, so this scheme depends essentially on fixed-dimensional Euclidean structure rather than only the abstract triangle inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In every fixed Euclidean dimension, geometric decomposition yields a polynomial-time approximation scheme for TSP.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A local geometric modification bound for reducing a tour's crossings of a segment disjoint from the input points.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Steiner Tours and Light Tours in a Shifted Dissection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definitions are relative to the previously fixed shifted grids, portal construction, and crossing bound \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\subseteq[0,2^N]\times[0,2^N]\) be a well-rounded Euclidean TSP instance, let \(a,b\in\{0,2,\ldots,2^N-2\}\), and fix the associated shifted grids, \(C\), \(P\), and portals. A Steiner tour is a closed walk of straight-line segments containing \(V\) whose intersection with every grid line is a subset of the portals. It is light if, for every \(i\) and every region of \(G_i^{(a,b)}\), it crosses each edge of that region at most \(C\) times.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Steiner tour is a closed polygonal walk containing all input points and meeting grid lines only at portals. It is light when it crosses each edge of every region at every dissection level at most C times.

G_i^{(a,b)},C,P\text{, and the portals are fixed by the preceding shifted-grid construction}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\text{ is a Steiner tour iff it is a closed straight-segment walk containing }V\text{ and meeting every grid line only at portals; it is light if each region edge is crossed at most }C\text{ times.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the scaled, translated odd-integer-grid instance used in Euclidean TSP approximation schemes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2\) be finite, \(n=|V|\), \(L=\max_{v,w\in V}\|v-w\|_2>0\), \(v_x^{\min}=\min\{v_x:(v_x,v_y)\in V\}\), \(v_y^{\min}=\min\{v_y:(v_x,v_y)\in V\}\), and \(\epsilon>0\). The corresponding well-rounded instance is \[V'=\left\{\left(1+2\left\lfloor\frac{5n(v_x-v_x^{\min})}{\epsilon L}\right\rfloor,1+2\left\lfloor\frac{5n(v_y-v_y^{\min})}{\epsilon L}\right\rfloor\right):(v_x,v_y)\in V\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Translate each coordinate by its coordinatewise minimum, scale by 5n/(epsilon L), round down, then double and add one. The resulting point set is the well-rounded instance corresponding to V.
assumptions_latex: V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2\text{ is finite}
n=|V|
L=\max_{v,w\in V}\|v-w\|_2>0
\epsilon>0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cycle-Cover Relaxation Does Not Enforce a Tour
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Connectivity boundary of the directed assignment relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Removing the directed cut constraints leaves the unit in-degree and out-degree assignment system, whose integral feasible points may consist of several vertex-disjoint directed cycles. Thus assignment feasibility alone does not certify a Hamiltonian tour.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed assignment solution can be a disconnected cycle cover, so subtour connectivity constraints are essential.
assumptions_latex: The loopless complete directed instance has at least four vertices.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical circulation-and-cut lower bound for metric ATSP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The directed subtour relaxation minimizes \(\sum_ac_ax_a\) subject to \[x(\delta^+(v))=x(\delta^-(v))=1\ (v\in V),\qquad x(\delta^+(S))\ge1\ (\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V),\qquad x_a\ge0.\] Its optimum \(\operatorname{HK}_{\rm ATSP}\) satisfies \(\operatorname{HK}_{\rm ATSP}\le\operatorname{OPT}_{\rm ATSP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unit in/out degree constraints and directed subtour cuts give the standard ATSP lower bound.
assumptions_latex: \(D=(V,A)\) is complete and directed.
Arc costs are nonnegative.

assumptions_latex: \(D=(V,A)\) is a complete directed graph.
Costs \(c:A\to\mathbb R_{\geq0}\) satisfy the directed triangle inequality.
The objective is a minimum-cost directed Hamiltonian cycle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Metric ATSP has a polynomial-time constant-factor approximation and is APX-hard.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete directed metrics; the existence frontier is stated without fixing the best published constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exists a universal constant \(C<\infty\) and a polynomial-time algorithm which returns, for every directed metric instance, a tour \(H\) satisfying \[c(H)\leq C\,\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{ATSP}}.\] Thus asymmetry does not destroy constant-factor approximability when the directed triangle inequality is retained. However, metric ATSP is APX-hard: for some constant \(\delta>0\), a polynomial-time \((1+\delta)\)-approximation would imply \(P=NP\). Consequently, unless \(P=NP\), this regime has no PTAS.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directed triangle inequality still permits a constant-factor ATSP approximation, but APX-hardness rules out a PTAS unless P equals NP.
knowledge_statements.title: Asymmetric TSP Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The directed-metric regime is clearly separated from symmetric and nonmetric TSP, and the property kind fits this regime summary. The constant-factor theorem and APX-hardness claim require sources.

children.title: Nonmetric TSP Regimes
children.top_down_role: Approximation behavior without metric cost structure.

assumptions_latex: The input is a complete weighted graph with arbitrary nonnegative integer edge costs.
The cost encoding is binary.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without triangle inequality, no polynomial-time approximation with any prescribed polynomially bounded ratio exists unless \(P=NP\).

notation.meaning: claimed approximation factor on size n

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General symmetric TSP with unrestricted binary-encoded costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix any polynomial-time computable, polynomially bounded function \(\rho(n)\geq1\). Given an \(n\)-vertex graph \(G\), assign cost \(1\) to its edges and cost \(M>n\rho(n)\) to its nonedges in the complete graph. If \(G\) is Hamiltonian, the optimum is \(n\); otherwise every tour costs at least \(M+n-1\). Hence a polynomial-time \(\rho(n)\)-approximation would decide Hamiltonicity. Therefore, unless \(P=NP\), unrestricted nonmetric TSP admits no such approximation guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arbitrary nonmetric costs create an unbounded Hamiltonicity gap, excluding every polynomially bounded approximation ratio unless P equals NP.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonmetric TSP Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The binary-encoded Hamiltonicity gap is mathematically coherent and failure_boundary appropriately captures the nonmetric frontier, but the inapproximability formulation has no supporting citation.

children.title: Metric-Structure Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Loss of bounded approximability when metric assumptions are removed.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is an \(n\)-vertex graph used to encode Hamiltonicity.
The completed instance assigns cost \(1\) to edges of \(G\) and cost \(M\) to nonedges.
The parameter satisfies \(M>n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The triangle inequality can fail by factor \(M/2\), and the resulting tour-cost gap can be made arbitrarily large.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete gap family showing why metric shortcutting and bounded approximation fail together.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) contain vertices \(u,v,w\) with \(uv,vw\in E\) and \(uw\notin E\), and define \(c_M(e)=1\) for \(e\in E\) and \(c_M(e)=M\) otherwise. Then \[c_M(uw)=M>2=c_M(uv)+c_M(vw),\] so shortcutting the path through \(v\) can increase cost by a factor \(M/2\). In the associated complete TSP instance, a Hamiltonian cycle of \(G\) costs \(n\), while every tour using a nonedge costs at least \(M+n-1\). The gap diverges with \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replacing missing edges by cost M violates triangle inequality and makes shortcutting and approximation gaps arbitrarily bad as M grows.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Structure Failure Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The construction explicitly exhibits triangle-inequality failure and an unbounded tour-cost gap, and counterexample is the correct kind for this leaf. A source with a specific locator is still required.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Compute shortest-path distances among terminals, take a minimum spanning tree in that metric closure, expand its edges to paths in \(G\), and delete cycles. The resulting Steiner tree \(T\) satisfies \[c(T)\leq2\mathrm{OPT}_{\rm ST}.\] The bound follows from doubling an optimum tree, traversing it, and shortcutting in the terminal metric. Graph Steiner Tree is also APX-hard: some constant \(\delta>0\) exists for which a polynomial-time \((1+\delta)\)-approximation would imply \(P=NP\). Hence no PTAS exists unless \(P=NP\).

children.title: Steiner Forest Frontiers
children.top_down_role: Approximation guarantees and hardness limits for pairwise Steiner connectivity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Steiner Forest Cut Relaxation and Dual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard cut-packing lower bound for mandatory pair connectivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal S=\{S\subset V:\exists i,\ |S\cap\{s_i,t_i\}|=1\}\). The relaxation \[\min\{\sum_ec_ex_e:x(\delta(S))\ge1\ (S\in\mathcal S),\ x\ge0\}\] has dual \[\max\{\sum_{S\in\mathcal S}y_S:\sum_{S\in\mathcal S:e\in\delta(S)}y_S\le c_e\ (e\in E),\ y\ge0\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Packing weights on demand-separating cuts within edge costs gives the standard Steiner Forest lower bound.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and undirected with \(c_e\ge0\).
Demands are terminal pairs \((s_i,t_i)\).

notation.meaning: Sets separating at least one demand pair

knowledge_statements.title: Steiner Forest Cut Relaxation and Dual

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is an undirected graph with nonnegative edge costs.
The demands are terminal pairs \((s_i,t_i)\) for \(1\leq i\leq k\).
A feasible forest connects each \(s_i\) to its corresponding \(t_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Steiner Forest has a polynomial-time factor-\(2\) approximation and is APX-hard.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undirected pair-connectivity Steiner Forest with nonnegative costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There is a polynomial-time primal-dual algorithm that grows dual variables for cuts separating an unsatisfied demand pair, buys tight edges, and prunes redundant edges. Its output \(F\) connects every required pair and satisfies \[c(F)\leq2\mathrm{OPT}_{\rm SF}.\] Moreover, Steiner Forest is APX-hard: there is a constant \(\delta>0\) such that a polynomial-time \((1+\delta)\)-approximation would imply \(P=NP\). Thus the general problem admits a constant-factor guarantee but no PTAS unless \(P=NP\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal-dual cut growth gives a factor-two Steiner Forest approximation, and APX-hardness rules out a PTAS unless P equals NP.
knowledge_statements.title: Steiner Forest Frontiers

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The demand-pair formulation and factor-2 frontier are internally consistent, and property is suitable for this frontier leaf. The primal-dual guarantee and APX-hardness claim lack citations.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prize-Collecting Steiner Forest buys edges and pays for each demand pair left disconnected.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and undirected.
Edge costs and pair penalties are nonnegative.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pair-penalty cut LP crosses every cut separating a demand pair or fractionally pays that pair's penalty; its dual packs separating cuts under edge-cost and penalty budgets.

\(c_e\ge0\) and \(\pi_i\ge0\).

Rent-or-Buy Frontier
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Offline undirected, unsplittable multicommodity rent-or-buy network-design model and its approximation frontier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A feasible solution chooses an \(s_i\)-to-\(t_i\) path \(P_i\) for every commodity \(i\), inducing load \(x_e=\sum_{i:e\in P_i}d_i\) on edge \(e\). With rental rate \(r_e\ge 0\) and purchase price \(B_e\ge 0\), the edge charge is \(f_e(x_e)=\min\{r_ex_e,B_e\}\). The network objective is \(\min_{(P_i)}\sum_{e\in E}c_ef_e(x_e)\). For a fixed class of such instances, the rent-or-buy approximation frontier is the upward closure of the ratios to this optimum attained by polynomial-time algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rent-or-buy routing charges each edge the smaller of its load-proportional rental cost and fixed purchase cost, and its frontier records attainable polynomial-time approximation ratios.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointwise Decomposition Is Not an Approximation Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary on transferring approximation ratios through the seed's atom decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The identity \(f(x)=\sum_m a_m\min\{x,m\}\) is pointwise and edge-local. A guarantee for instances having one rent-or-buy charge per edge transfers to such sums only through an algorithm or reduction that preserves the common routing decisions and controls their combined objective. Independently optimizing the atoms may select incompatible paths and need not yield one feasible routing of comparable cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Algebraically decomposing edge costs does not by itself preserve approximation ratios because all atoms share one routing.
assumptions_latex: All edge-cost components are evaluated on the same routing loads.

Concave-Cost Model Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-load decomposition into nonnegative rent-or-buy atoms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\{0,1,\ldots,D\}\to[0,\infty)\) be nondecreasing and discretely concave, with \(f(0)=0\). Define \(\Delta_m=f(m)-f(m-1)\) for \(1\le m\le D\), set \(\Delta_{D+1}=0\), and let \(a_m=\Delta_m-\Delta_{m+1}\). Then \(a_m\ge 0\) and \[f(x)=\sum_{m=1}^{D}a_m\min\{x,m\}\] for every \(x\in\{0,1,\ldots,D\}\). Conversely, every nonnegative combination of the functions \(x\mapsto\min\{x,m\}\) is nonnegative, nondecreasing, discretely concave, and zero at \(x=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nondecreasing discrete concave edge cost on a bounded integer load domain is exactly a nonnegative sum of rent-or-buy cost atoms, and every such sum has the same properties.
assumptions_latex: The load domain is \(\{0,1,\ldots,D\}\) for an integer \(D\ge 1\).
The function \(f\) is nonnegative, nondecreasing, discretely concave, and satisfies \(f(0)=0\).

children.title: Semidefinite Rounding Regime
children.top_down_role: Vector-relaxation approaches to maximum cut.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Probability amplification for random-hyperplane Maximum Cut rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let one hyperplane round have value \(Z\), where \(0\le Z\le\operatorname{SDP}(G)\) and \(\mathbb E Z\ge\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}\operatorname{SDP}(G)\). For \(0<\delta<\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}\), \[\Pr\!\left[Z\ge(\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}-\delta)\operatorname{SDP}(G)\right]\ge\frac{\delta}{1-\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}+\delta}.\] Returning the best of \(O(\delta^{-1}\log(1/\eta))\) independent rounds therefore achieves this reduced factor with probability at least \(1-\eta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent repetition converts the expected Goemans-Williamson guarantee into a high-probability guarantee with arbitrarily small factor loss.
assumptions_latex: Edge weights are nonnegative.
The hyperplane rounds are independent.
\(0<\delta<\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}\) and \(0<\eta<1\).

notation.meaning: cut weight from one hyperplane round

knowledge_statements.title: High-Probability Hyperplane Rounding

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-precision interpretation of the SDP-based approximation algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), the standard Maximum Cut SDP can be solved to sufficient additive accuracy in time polynomial in the binary input length and \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\). Combining this with hyperplane rounding yields a randomized polynomial-time \((\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}-\varepsilon)\)-approximation; the exact irrational optimum of the SDP need not be computed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-precision SDP optimization suffices for a randomized polynomial-time approximation arbitrarily close to the Goemans-Williamson factor.
assumptions_latex: Edge weights are nonnegative rationals given in binary.
\(\varepsilon>0\) is fixed or represented to polynomial precision.
Standard polynomial-time approximate SDP optimization is available.
knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial-Time Precision Regime

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gram-Matrix Form of the Maximum Cut SDP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent vector and correlation-matrix representations of the standard relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The unit-vector relaxation \[\max\frac12\sum_{ij\in E}w_{ij}(1-\langle v_i,v_j\rangle),\qquad \|v_i\|_2=1,\] is equivalent, under \(X_{ij}=\langle v_i,v_j\rangle\), to \[\max\frac12\sum_{ij\in E}w_{ij}(1-X_{ij}),\qquad X\succeq0,\quad X_{ii}=1.\] Every cut sign vector \(s\in\{-1,1\}^V\) yields the feasible rank-one matrix \(X=ss^\top\), so \(\operatorname{OPT}(G)\le\operatorname{SDP}(G)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Maximum Cut vector SDP is equivalently a positive-semidefinite correlation-matrix relaxation containing every cut as a rank-one point.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and undirected.
Each edge is summed once.
knowledge_statements.title: Gram-Matrix Form of the Maximum Cut SDP

assumptions_latex: The graph \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and has nonnegative edge weights \(w_{ij}\).
The semidefinite relaxation assigns a unit vector \(v_i\) to every vertex.
The rounding hyperplane has a uniformly random normal direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The rounded cut has expected weight at least \(\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}\operatorname{SDP}(G)\ge\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}\operatorname{OPT}(G)\).

notation.meaning: Value of the maximum-cut SDP relaxation
Angle between vectors assigned to two vertices

review_flags: authoritative_source_required: Goemans-Williamson rounding theorem and constant
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Goemans-Williamson vector relaxation and random-hyperplane rounding for weighted maximum cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maximize \(\frac12\sum_{ij\in E}w_{ij}(1-\langle v_i,v_j\rangle)\) subject to \(\lVert v_i\rVert_2=1\). Given an optimal vector solution, choose a uniformly random hyperplane through the origin and separate vertices according to the signs of their vector projections. Edge \(ij\) is cut with probability \(\theta_{ij}/\pi\), where \(\theta_{ij}=\arccos\langle v_i,v_j\rangle\). Therefore the expected cut weight is at least \(\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}\operatorname{SDP}(G)\), where \(\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}=\min_{0\le\theta\le\pi}\frac{2\theta}{\pi(1-\cos\theta)}\approx0.87856\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Random-hyperplane rounding of the maximum-cut SDP achieves the Goemans-Williamson approximation factor, approximately 0.87856.
knowledge_statements.title: Semidefinite Rounding Regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated Goemans–Williamson theorem and constant are plausible and internally consistent, but the source-dependent theorem has no inspectable citation or locator.

children.title: Integrality-Gap Regime
children.top_down_role: Approximation limits witnessed by the relaxation formulation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domain conditions for the multiplicative value gap of the standard Maximum Cut SDP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The ratio \(\operatorname{SDP}(G)/\operatorname{OPT}(G)\) is defined only for \(\operatorname{OPT}(G)>0\). All-zero nonnegative weights give \(0/0\). If negative weights are allowed, the edgewise nonnegative comparison used in Goemans-Williamson rounding no longer implies the standard gap bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The standard multiplicative SDP gap requires nonnegative weights and a positive integral optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{OPT}(G)>0\text{ and }w_e\ge0\text{ are required for this gap regime}.
knowledge_statements.title: Integrality-Gap Ratio Domain

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Asymptotic Tightness of the Standard SDP Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matching lower-bound instances for the standard Maximum Cut SDP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\varepsilon>0\), there is a finite nonnegatively weighted Maximum Cut instance \(G\), with \(\operatorname{OPT}(G)>0\), such that \(\operatorname{OPT}(G)/\operatorname{SDP}(G)\le\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}+\varepsilon\). Together with the universal rounding bound, this gives \[\sup_G\frac{\operatorname{SDP}(G)}{\operatorname{OPT}(G)}=\frac1{\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}}.\] This is a supremum statement and does not assert attainment by one finite instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The reciprocal Goemans-Williamson factor is the exact worst-case value gap of the standard Maximum Cut SDP in the asymptotic-supremum sense.
assumptions_latex: The standard unit-vector Maximum Cut SDP is used.
Edge weights are nonnegative.
Only instances with positive integral optimum enter the ratio.
review_flags: authoritative_source_required: asymptotically tight standard-SDP gap construction
knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Tightness of the Standard SDP Gap

assumptions_latex: The maximum-cut SDP is the unit-vector relaxation used by random-hyperplane rounding.
Graph edge weights are nonnegative.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Upper integrality-gap consequence of Goemans-Williamson rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an instance \(G\), define \(g(G)=\operatorname{SDP}(G)/\operatorname{OPT}(G)\). Since random-hyperplane rounding produces a cut of expected weight at least \(\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}\operatorname{SDP}(G)\), and no cut exceeds \(\operatorname{OPT}(G)\), one has \(\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}\operatorname{SDP}(G)\le\operatorname{OPT}(G)\). Consequently, \(g(G)\le1/\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}\) and the worst-case gap \(g^*=\sup_G g(G)\) obeys \(g^*\le1/\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}\). Equality requires a separate asymptotic gap construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Goemans-Williamson rounding bounds the vector SDP's worst-case value gap by the reciprocal of its approximation factor.
knowledge_statements.title: Integrality-Gap Regime

knowledge_statements.scope_note: UGC-conditional hardness threshold for weighted maximum cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assuming the Unique Games Conjecture, for every constant \(\varepsilon>0\) it is NP-hard to distinguish maximum-cut instances whose optimum is at least the completeness value of the canonical noise-stability test from instances whose optimum is at most the corresponding soundness value. Optimizing the ratio of these values yields \(\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}\). Hence no polynomial-time algorithm can guarantee a cut of weight greater than \((\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}+\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(G)\) on every instance, unless the conjectured hardness fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the Unique Games Conjecture, no polynomial-time maximum-cut algorithm can improve the Goemans-Williamson factor by any fixed positive amount.
knowledge_statements.title: Hardness Regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The UGC-conditional threshold requires an authoritative theorem citation. The final algorithmic impossibility must also preserve the standard complexity qualification, such as “unless P=NP,” rather than attributing every escape solely to failure of the conjecture.

children.title: Gap–Hardness Alignment
children.top_down_role: Cases where relaxation gaps match or diverge from computational hardness.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes exact frontier alignment from hardness at one isolated ratio.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a maximization problem, an algorithmic guarantee \(\alpha\) and hardness at one ratio \(\beta>\alpha\) establish only \(\alpha\le\rho^*<\beta\). Equality \(\rho^*=\alpha\) follows when, under the same stated conjecture and input regime, hardness excludes every \(\alpha+\varepsilon\) for all fixed \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact alignment requires hardness against every fixed improvement over the achieved factor, not merely one larger factor.
assumptions_latex: All guarantees concern the same problem variant, objective convention, and complexity model.
knowledge_statements.title: Quantifier Requirement for Threshold Alignment

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integrality Gaps Do Not Establish Computational Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical boundary between the two sibling regimes compared by alignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An integrality gap \(g\) for a specified relaxation limits guarantees certified solely by comparing integral solutions with that relaxation's value. It does not imply that the underlying problem is hard to approximate beyond \(g\), because a polynomial-time algorithm may use a stronger relaxation or another method. Computational hardness requires an independent reduction under an explicit complexity assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relaxation gap limits that formulation, not every polynomial-time algorithm; matching hardness needs an independent reduction.
assumptions_latex: The integrality gap is measured for a specified relaxation and objective convention.

notation.meaning: integrality-gap factor of a specified relaxation

knowledge_statements.title: Integrality Gaps Do Not Establish Computational Hardness

assumptions_latex: A polynomial-time algorithm guarantees approximation ratio \(\alpha\) for a maximization problem.
Under an explicitly stated complexity conjecture, achieving ratio \(\alpha+\varepsilon\) is hard for every \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The conditional polynomial-time approximation threshold equals \(\alpha\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal criterion for alignment of an approximation guarantee with conditional hardness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\rho^*\) be the supremum approximation ratio guaranteed by polynomial-time algorithms for a maximization problem. If an algorithm attains \(\alpha\), then \(\rho^*\ge\alpha\). If, under a stated complexity conjecture, no polynomial-time algorithm attains \(\alpha+\varepsilon\) for any \(\varepsilon>0\), then \(\rho^*\le\alpha\) conditional on that conjecture. Together these bounds imply \(\rho^*=\alpha\). For maximum cut, the SDP-rounding and Unique-Games hardness regimes align at \(\alpha=\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An approximation frontier is aligned when an algorithm attains a factor and conditional hardness excludes every fixed improvement over it.
knowledge_statements.title: Gap–Hardness Alignment

children.title: Multiway Cut Frontier
children.top_down_role: Approximation regimes for separating a prescribed terminal set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical combinatorial approximation for undirected multiway cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each terminal \(t_i\), compute a minimum cut separating \(t_i\) from \(T\setminus\{t_i\}\). Discard the most expensive of these \(k\) isolating cuts and take the union of the remaining cut edge sets. The union is a feasible multiway cut of cost at most \((2-2/k)\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{MWC}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The union of all but the most expensive minimum isolating cuts is a 2 minus 2/k approximation for multiway cut.
assumptions_latex: The graph is finite, undirected, and nonnegatively weighted.

notation.meaning: union of the retained isolating-cut edge sets

knowledge_statements.title: Isolating-Cut Approximation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical prescribed-terminal separation objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given distinct terminals \(T=\{t_1,\ldots,t_k\}\), a multiway cut is an edge set whose deletion leaves no two terminals in the same connected component. With nonnegative weights, it is equivalently induced by a labeling \(\ell:V\to[k]\) satisfying \(\ell(t_i)=i\), with cost \(\sum_{uv\in E:\ell(u)\ne\ell(v)}w_{uv}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiway cut separates every pair of prescribed terminals, equivalently labeling vertices by terminals and paying for edges crossing labels.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and undirected.
Edge weights are nonnegative.
The terminals are distinct.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiway Cut and Terminal-Labeling Form

assumptions_latex: The graph is undirected with nonnegative edge weights and has \(k\ge 2\) distinct terminals.
A feasible solution deletes edges so that every pair of terminals becomes disconnected.
The CKR simplex relaxation is used as the lower bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Polynomial-time simplex rounding returns a multiway cut of expected cost at most \((3/2-1/k)\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}\).

notation.meaning: Simplex vector assigned to vertex v

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical CKR relaxation frontier for undirected weighted multiway cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assign each vertex \(v\) a point \(x_v\) in the simplex \(\Delta_k\), fix terminal \(t_i\) at the vertex \(e_i\), and minimize \(\frac12\sum_{uv\in E}w_{uv}\lVert x_u-x_v\rVert_1\). The Calinescu-Karloff-Rabani rounding scheme maps all vertices to terminals and cuts edges whose endpoints receive different labels. Its expected cut cost is at most \((3/2-1/k)\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}\), and therefore at most \((3/2-1/k)\operatorname{OPT}\). For \(k=2\), the factor specializes to \(1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The classical simplex relaxation and CKR rounding give a 3/2 minus 1/k approximation for k-terminal multiway cut.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiway Cut Frontier

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical deletion and partition formulations of undirected minimum k-cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(2\le k\le|V|\), minimum \(k\)-cut minimizes the weight of an edge set \(F\subseteq E\) for which \((V,E\setminus F)\) has at least \(k\) connected components. With nonnegative weights, this equals \[\min_{V=V_1\dot\cup\cdots\dot\cup V_k\atop V_i\ne\varnothing}w(\delta(V_1,\ldots,V_k)),\] where \(\delta(V_1,\ldots,V_k)\) contains edges whose endpoints lie in different parts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimum k-cut removes minimum total edge weight to create at least k components, equivalently selecting a minimum crossing-edge k-partition.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and undirected.
Edge weights are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimum k-Cut and Partition Form

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact specialization of minimum k-cut at k equal to two.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(k=2\), minimum \(k\)-cut is the undirected global minimum-cut problem and is solvable in polynomial time. Accordingly, the general approximation factor \(2-2/k\) specializes to \(1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At k equal to two, minimum k-cut is ordinary global minimum cut and is exactly polynomial-time solvable.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite, undirected, and nonnegatively weighted.

k-Cut Frontier
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial-time approximation frontier for undirected minimum \(k\)-cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected graph with nonnegative edge weights and let \(2\le k\le |V|\). If \(\operatorname{OPT}_k(G)\) is the minimum weight of edges whose deletion leaves at least \(k\) connected components, then a polynomial-time algorithm can output a feasible \(k\)-cut \(F\) satisfying \[w(F)\le \left(2-\frac{2}{k}\right)\operatorname{OPT}_k(G).\] The running time is polynomial in the encoded input size when \(k\) is part of the input.

children.title: Terminal-Count Transition Regimes

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-complexity transition for prescribed-terminal multiway cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Undirected multiway cut with \(k=2\) is an ordinary minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut and is polynomial-time solvable. It is NP-hard already for the fixed value \(k=3\). Consequently, fixing the number of prescribed terminals does not generally yield tractability once \(k\ge3\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiway cut is polynomial for two terminals but NP-hard already for three fixed terminals.
assumptions_latex: The graph is finite, undirected, and nonnegatively weighted.
The terminals are distinct.
Exact optimization is considered.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiway-Cut Terminal-Count Dichotomy

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison between component-count and prescribed-terminal parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For undirected minimum \(k\)-cut, fixing \(k\) permits an \(n^{O(k)}\operatorname{poly}(L)\) exact algorithm, while prescribed-terminal multiway cut is NP-hard already at fixed \(k=3\). Thus the number of requested components and the number of prescribed terminals are not interchangeable parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed component count makes minimum k-cut polynomial, whereas a fixed set of three prescribed terminals does not make multiway cut polynomial.
assumptions_latex: The standard binary encoding model is used.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tight Asymptotic Gap of the Path Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case strength of the canonical undirected-multicut LP as the number of demands grows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the path relaxation of undirected edge multicut with \(r\) terminal pairs, the worst-case integrality gap is \(\Theta(\log(r+1))\): region-growing gives an \(O(\log(r+1))\) upper bound, and families of instances attain an \(\Omega(\log(r+1))\) gap.

knowledge_statements.title: Tight Asymptotic Gap of the Path Relaxation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical LP pair for nonnegative-cost undirected edge multicut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For terminal pairs \((s_i,t_i)_{i=1}^r\), the path relaxation is \[\min\sum_{e\in E}c_ex_e\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\sum_{e\in P}x_e\ge1\quad(P\text{ an }s_i\text{-}t_i\text{ path}),\qquad x_e\ge0.\] Its dual maximizes \(\sum_{i,P}y_{i,P}\) subject to \(y_{i,P}\ge0\) and \(\sum_{i,P\ni e}y_{i,P}\le c_e\) for every edge. Hence \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}=\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{dual}}\le\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{MC}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The standard multicut LP covers every terminal-connecting path; its dual fractionally packs such paths under edge-cost capacities.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and undirected.
\(c_e\ge0\) for all edges.
The terminal-pair list is finite.

A polynomial-time region-growing rounding algorithm applied to the path-distance relaxation returns a multicut \(F\) with \[c(F)\le O(\log(r+1))\operatorname{OPT}.\] Thus the guarantee is logarithmic in the number of separation demands, without assuming that the pairs share a common terminal.

Its LP dual is maximum concurrent multicommodity flow, and \[\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{flow}}=\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{metric}}\le\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{SC}}.\]

Some cut separates positive demand.

Sparsest-Cut Frontier
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonuniform undirected sparsest cut with weighted capacities and pair demands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have capacities \(c_{uv}\ge 0\), and let symmetric demands \(d_{uv}\ge 0\) be given for unordered vertex pairs. For every nonempty proper set \(S\subset V\), define \(\delta(S)=\{uv\in E:|\{u,v\}\cap S|=1\}\) and \(D(S)=\sum_{u\in S,\,v\notin S}d_{uv}\). The sparsity of \(S\) is \[\phi(S)=\frac{\sum_{e\in\delta(S)}c_e}{D(S)},\] provided \(D(S)>0\). The nonuniform sparsest-cut optimum is the minimum of \(\phi(S)\) over all such eligible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sparsest cut minimizes crossing edge capacity divided by the separated pair demand over all nontrivial cuts with positive separated demand.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite.
Capacities and demands are nonnegative.
At least one proper nonempty cut has positive separated demand.

notation.meaning: edges crossing the cut induced by S

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits on converting metric distortion into a normalized cut guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An \(L_1\) decomposition alone does not imply a bounded normalized cut if the demand normalization can vanish, has negative coefficients, or the embedding controls only pairs unrelated to the objective or normalization. The transfer requires a common positive scale and distortion inequalities for every pair having a nonzero coefficient in either functional.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric-to-cut transfer requires positive normalization, nonnegative pair functionals, and distortion control on every relevant pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{positive normalization, nonnegative coefficients, and matching pairwise quantifiers are required}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite L1 Metrics as the Cut Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact cut decomposition underlying metric-to-cut transfer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A semimetric \(d\) on a finite set \(V\) is isometrically embeddable in \(L_1\) if and only if there are coefficients \(\lambda_S\ge0\) such that \[d(u,v)=\sum_{\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V}\lambda_S\,|\mathbf1_S(u)-\mathbf1_S(v)|.\] Thus finite \(L_1\) semimetrics are exactly the cut cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite L1 semimetrics are exactly nonnegative combinations of cut semimetrics.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite.
\(d\) is a semimetric.

notation.meaning: indicator that cut S separates u and v

knowledge_statements.title: Finite L1 Metrics as the Cut Cone

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic distortion bound for arbitrary finite metrics and its cut-rounding consequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every \(n\)-point metric space admits an embedding \(f\) into \(L_1\) and a scale \(a>0\) such that \[a d(u,v)\le\|f(u)-f(v)\|_1\le O(\log n)\,a d(u,v)\] for all \(u,v\). A randomized embedding with this guarantee is constructible in polynomial time. Under the deferred v58 transfer principle's nonnegative objective and positive-normalization hypotheses, this yields an \(O(\log n)\)-factor cut rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bourgain's theorem embeds every finite metric into L1 with logarithmic distortion, yielding logarithmic cut rounding when the transfer hypotheses hold.
assumptions_latex: \(d\) is a metric on an n-element finite set.
The downstream objective and normalization satisfy the transfer principle's positivity conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c_1(V,d)=O(\log n)\Longrightarrow\text{ an }O(\log n)\text{-factor metric-to-cut transfer}.

notation.meaning: least distortion of an embedding into L1

knowledge_statements.title: Bourgain Logarithmic Embedding Transfer
Metric-Embedding Transfer Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfer from metric-relaxation embeddings into distributions over graph cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a cut problem whose relaxation assigns a semimetric \(d\) to \(V\), with objective \(\sum_{u<v}c_{uv}d(u,v)\), and whose normalization is a nonnegative linear demand functional. Suppose every feasible \(d\) admits an embedding \(f:V\to L_1\) and a scaling \(\alpha>0\) such that \[\alpha d(u,v)\le \|f(u)-f(v)\|_1\le D\alpha d(u,v)\] for all \(u,v\). Decomposing the finite \(L_1\) metric into cut semimetrics then yields a polynomially samplable cut whose normalized objective is at most \(D\) times the relaxation optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A distortion-D embedding of a feasible metric into L1 transfers to a D-factor cut rounding when objective and normalization are nonnegative linear pair functionals.
assumptions_latex: The relaxation objective and normalization are nonnegative linear pair-distance functionals.
The stated \(L_1\) embedding is computable in polynomial time.
The relaxation has positive normalization.

children.title: Minimum Bisection Frontier

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-complexity boundary for unweighted balanced partitioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Computing a minimum bisection is NP-hard for unweighted undirected graphs. Thus, unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), no polynomial-time algorithm always finds an optimal exactly balanced cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimum bisection is NP-hard even without edge weights.
assumptions_latex: For even-order graphs, balance means \(|S|=|V|/2\).
knowledge_statements.title: NP-Hardness of Minimum Bisection

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Essential interpretation boundary for approximation results.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An algorithm returning \(S\) with \(\beta n\le|S|\le(1-\beta)n\) for fixed \(0<\beta<1/2\) solves a weaker balanced-separator problem, not necessarily minimum bisection. Even if \(w(\delta(S))\le\rho\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{bis}}\), it is not a \(\rho\)-approximation for minimum bisection unless the prescribed bisection cardinality is also satisfied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A low-cost roughly balanced cut is only a bicriteria result unless it has the required bisection size.
assumptions_latex: The target problem requires exact bisection balance.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Balance versus Bicriteria Balance

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Collapse of the Direct Bisection LP Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary for the direct continuous relaxation of the binary cut formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the direct LP relaxation, setting \(x_v=1/2\) for every vertex and \(z_{uv}=0\) for every edge satisfies \(\sum_vx_v=n/2\) and all absolute-difference inequalities. Its optimum is therefore zero for every nonnegatively weighted instance, even when every integral bisection has positive cost. Consequently the relaxation has an unbounded multiplicative integrality gap, for example on connected positive-weight graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The naive LP relaxation collapses to zero at the all-half solution and cannot certify a multiplicative approximation.
assumptions_latex: \(n\) is even.
Edge weights are nonnegative.
For the unbounded-gap conclusion, the integral optimum is positive.
knowledge_statements.title: Collapse of the Direct Bisection LP Relaxation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Binary Cut Formulation for Exact Bisection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact integer formulation and its direct continuous relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For even \(n\), introduce \(x_v\in\{0,1\}\) with \(\sum_vx_v=n/2\) and variables satisfying \(z_{uv}\ge x_u-x_v\) and \(z_{uv}\ge x_v-x_u\) for every \(uv\in E\). Minimizing \(\sum_{uv}w_{uv}z_{uv}\) exactly models minimum bisection, since at optimum \(z_{uv}=|x_u-x_v|\). Replacing \(x_v\in\{0,1\}\) by \(0\le x_v\le1\) gives the direct LP relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary side indicators plus absolute-difference variables exactly formulate minimum bisection.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and undirected.
\(n\) is even.
Edge weights are nonnegative.

notation.meaning: Indicator that vertex v lies on one side.
Indicator or relaxation of whether edge uv is cut.

knowledge_statements.title: Binary Cut Formulation for Exact Bisection

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Logarithmic Approximation for Exact Minimum Bisection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General weighted-graph approximation preserving the exact bisection cardinality; the implementation theorem requires a direct locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There is a randomized polynomial-time algorithm for weighted undirected minimum bisection that returns an exactly balanced cut and has expected cost at most \(O(\log n)\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{bis}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact minimum bisection admits a randomized logarithmic-factor approximation that preserves exact balance.
assumptions_latex: The graph is finite, undirected, and has nonnegative edge weights.
\(n\) is even.
The returned side has exactly \(n/2\) vertices.
