intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The independent AND-repetition calculation is mathematically precise and the property kind fits the leaf, but no inspectable authoritative source is cited.

children.title: Composition–Amplification Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Interactions among gap strength, alphabet size, query structure, and instance growth.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary on combining headline PCP parameters from incompatible models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Completeness, soundness, and query counts alone do not determine the parameters of a composition–amplification pipeline. Bounds can fail to compose when the inner proof lacks a global decoding or agreement guarantee, repetitions share correlated randomness, alphabets or encodings differ, or proof and reduction size grow superpolynomially.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Headline gap and query parameters cannot be combined safely without compatible decoding, independence, alphabet, and size assumptions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (c,s,q)\text{ summaries alone do not determine a valid composed-and-amplified PCP}.
knowledge_statements.title: Noncomposable Parameter Summaries

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint parameter accounting when a robust composed verifier is subsequently amplified by independent repetition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a composed verifier has completeness \(c'\), soundness \(s'\), randomness \(r'\), queries \(q'\), proof length \(L'\), and alphabet \(\Sigma'\). Applying \(t\) independent repetitions with acceptance predicate \(A_t\) transforms \((c',s')\) according to the tail probabilities of \(A_t\), uses at most \(tr'\) random bits and \(tq'\) queries, and may require up to \(tL'\) proof locations unless queries share a common encoded proof. Thus soundness improvement is meaningful only together with randomness, query, alphabet, proof-length, and reduction-size growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After composition, repetition trades lower soundness for larger randomness, query, proof, alphabet, and reduction resources; all parameters must be accounted for in the same verifier model.
assumptions_latex: The repeated random strings are independent.
The acceptance predicate and proof-sharing convention are fixed.

notation.meaning: acceptance predicate on the t repetition outcomes

knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Composition–Repetition Accounting
Composition–Amplification Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract resource and error accounting for blockwise PCP composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an outer verifier using \(r_o\) random bits and reading \(q_o\) symbols, with soundness \(s_o\). Suppose each outer symbol is tested by an inner verifier using \(r_i\) fresh random bits and \(q_i\) queries. If the composed verifier independently tests all \(q_o\) requested symbols, then its query and randomness costs are at most \(q_oq_i\) and \(r_o+q_or_i\). If the inner analysis supplies an additional inconsistency error \(\delta\), the usual soundness decomposition is \(s_{\mathrm{comp}}\le s_o+\delta\). Thus reducing \(\delta\) through stronger amplification must be balanced against the resulting alphabet, randomness, and query blowups.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Composition replaces outer symbols by inner tests: resources multiply or add, while soundness consists of outer error plus an inner inconsistency term.
assumptions_latex: Inner random strings are fresh conditional on the outer random string.
The inner soundness analysis bounds inconsistent outer answers by \(\delta\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated resource accounting is plausible for the specified blockwise construction, but the additive soundness decomposition depends on a particular composition and decoding theorem that is not cited or fully specified.

children.title: Projection-Game Hardness Representation
children.top_down_role: Canonical intermediate representations for transferring PCP hardness.

children.title: Projection-Game Representations
children.top_down_role: Bipartite constraint games used as hardness intermediates.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rational Weights as Parallel Unweighted Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between rationally weighted games and unweighted bipartite multigraph games.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If all normalized edge weights are rational, choose a common positive denominator \(D\) and replace edge \(e\) by \(Dw(e)\) parallel copies carrying the same projection. The fraction of satisfied copies under every labeling equals its satisfied weight in the original game, so the games have identical value. This explicit expansion is polynomial-size only when the total multiplicity \(D\) is polynomially bounded in the original encoding length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rational edge weights can be represented by parallel unweighted constraints without changing value, subject to an encoding-size boundary.
assumptions_latex: \(w(e)\in\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\) and \(\sum_e w(e)=1\).
\(D\) is a common denominator with \(Dw(e)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\).

notation.meaning: common denominator and total replication scale

knowledge_statements.title: Rational Weights as Parallel Unweighted Constraints

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent one-sided optimization formula for a weighted projection game.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed left labeling \(\ell_U\), right vertices optimize independently. Therefore \[\operatorname{val}(G)=\max_{\ell_U:U\to\Sigma_U}\sum_{v\in V}\max_{b\in\Sigma_V}\sum_{e=(u,v)\in E}w(e)\mathbf 1[\pi_e(\ell_U(u))=b].\] An optimal right labeling chooses a maximizing label independently at every \(v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After the left labels are fixed, each right vertex independently chooses its best response, yielding an equivalent one-sided value formula.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite weighted projection game as in the immutable definition.
knowledge_statements.title: Best-Response Elimination of Right Labels
Projection-Game Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite bipartite projection games in their weighted Label-Cover form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A projection game is a tuple \(G=(U,V,E,\Sigma_U,\Sigma_V,(\pi_e)_{e\in E},w)\), where \((U,V,E)\) is a finite bipartite multigraph, \(\Sigma_U,\Sigma_V\) are finite alphabets, each edge \(e=(u,v)\) carries a projection \(\pi_e:\Sigma_U\to\Sigma_V\), and \(w:E\to[0,1]\) satisfies \(\sum_{e\in E}w(e)=1\). A labeling \((\ell_U,\ell_V)\) satisfies \(e=(u,v)\) when \(\pi_e(\ell_U(u))=\ell_V(v)\). The value \(\operatorname{val}(G)\) is the maximum total weight of satisfied edges over all labelings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A projection game is a weighted bipartite constraint system in which each left label uniquely determines the required right label on an edge.
assumptions_latex: \(U,V,E,\Sigma_U,\Sigma_V\) are finite.
\(w(e)\ge0\) and \(\sum_{e\in E}w(e)=1\).

notation.meaning: Projection constraint attached to edge e.
Labelings of the two vertex classes.

children.title: Label-Cover Gap-Transfer Interface
children.top_down_role: Interfaces transporting label consistency and gap structure to target problems.

children.title: Label-Cover Gadgets
children.top_down_role: Gadget interfaces transferring label consistency to target optimization problems.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gap Consequence of Extension and Decoding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Threshold transfer implied by the immutable extension-and-decoding gadget interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a gadget reduction is \((\alpha,\beta)\)-gap transferring in the stated extension-and-decoding sense and \(\beta\) is nondecreasing. Then \[\operatorname{val}(R(G))\ge 1-\alpha(1-\operatorname{val}(G)).\] Moreover, if \(\operatorname{val}(G)\le s\) and \(\beta(1-z)<1-s\), then \(\operatorname{val}(R(G))<z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extension transfers completeness, while monotone decoding loss transfers any target threshold whose decoded quality would contradict source soundness.
assumptions_latex: The immutable universal extension and polynomial-time decoding conditions hold.
\(\beta\) is nondecreasing.
review_flags: Builder statement repaired by adding the monotonicity assumption needed to compare decoding losses at target values at least z.
knowledge_statements.title: Gap Consequence of Extension and Decoding
Label-Cover Gadgets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Completeness and decoding conditions for a gap-transferring constraint gadget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a finite weighted Label-Cover instance, and let \(R(G)\) be a finite weighted constraint instance obtained by replacing each edge constraint with a gadget. Let \(\alpha,\beta:[0,1]\to[0,1]\). The gadget family is \((\alpha,\beta)\)-gap transferring if: (i) every labeling of \(G\) satisfying edge weight \(p\) extends to an assignment of \(R(G)\) satisfying weight at least \(1-\alpha(1-p)\); and (ii) every assignment of \(R(G)\) satisfying weight \(z\) can be decoded in polynomial time to a labeling of \(G\) satisfying weight at least \(1-\beta(1-z)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Label-Cover gadget transfers a gap when every good source labeling extends to a controlled-quality target assignment and every good target assignment efficiently decodes to a controlled-quality source labeling.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) and \(R(G)\) are finite weighted constraint instances.
The extension and decoding requirements hold for every source labeling and target assignment, respectively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{val}(R(G))\ge 1-\alpha\!\left(1-\operatorname{val}(G)\right),\] and every target assignment of value \(z\) decodes to a source labeling of value at least \(1-\beta(1-z)\).

notation.meaning: Constraint instance produced by the gadget reduction.
Satisfied weights of a source labeling and a target assignment, respectively.

children.title: Label-Cover Gap Amplification
children.top_down_role: Mechanisms strengthening the approximation gap in Label Cover instances.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Iteration Blowup of a Gap Amplifier
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Size accounting for repeated amplification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If one amplification round maps every instance of size \(N\) to size at most \(B(N)\), then after \(t\) rounds the size is at most \(B^{\circ t}(N)\). If \(B(N)\le C N^a\) for fixed \(C\ge1\) and \(a\ge1\), then \[|A^t(G)|\le C^{1+a+\cdots+a^{t-1}}|G|^{a^t}.\] Hence every fixed number of rounds preserves polynomial size, while a growing number of rounds requires separate blowup analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Amplification composes its size blowup; fixedly many rounds of a polynomial-blowup amplifier remain polynomial-size.
assumptions_latex: One-round output size is bounded by \(B\).
For the explicit formula, \(B(N)\le C N^a\) for fixed constants \(C,a\).

notation.meaning: t-fold composition of the size-blowup map

knowledge_statements.title: Iteration Blowup of a Gap Amplifier

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict One-Step Contraction Does Not Ensure Uniform Amplification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary separating pointwise value decrease from a uniform iterated gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The condition \(F(s)<s\) for every \(s\in(0,1)\) does not give a uniform fixed number of rounds for reaching a soundness threshold over all starting values below one. For \(F(s)=s^2\), every fixed \(t\) satisfies \(\sup_{s<1}F^{\circ t}(s)=1\). A uniform claim therefore requires an initial bound \(s\le s_0<1\) or a quantitative contraction estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pointwise strict contraction is insufficient for a uniform soundness bound when initial values may approach one.
assumptions_latex: \(F:[0,1]\to[0,1]\) is nondecreasing.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict One-Step Contraction Does Not Ensure Uniform Amplification
Label-Cover Gap Amplification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract value-shrinking transformation for Label-Cover instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polynomial-time transformation \(A\) is a Label-Cover gap amplifier with soundness map \(F\) and size blowup \(B\) if, for every projection game \(G\), the output \(A(G)\) is a projection game satisfying three conditions: perfect completeness is preserved, \(\operatorname{val}(G)=1\Rightarrow\operatorname{val}(A(G))=1\); soundness contracts, \(\operatorname{val}(G)\le s\Rightarrow\operatorname{val}(A(G))\le F(s)\); and \(|A(G)|\le B(|G|)\). It is a strict amplifier on an interval \(I\subset(0,1)\) when \(F(s)<s\) for every \(s\in I\). Iteration then yields the bound \(\operatorname{val}(A^t(G))\le F^{\circ t}(s)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Label-Cover amplifier preserves satisfiable instances, decreases the value of unsatisfiable instances, and controls the resulting instance-size blowup.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) maps finite projection games to finite projection games in polynomial time.
\(F:[0,1]\to[0,1]\) is nondecreasing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{val}(G)\le s\Rightarrow\operatorname{val}(A^t(G))\le F^{\circ t}(s)\), with perfect completeness preserved.

notation.meaning: The t-fold composition of the soundness map.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition accurately defines an abstract value-shrinking projection-game transformation, and monotonicity of the soundness map supports iteration, but no authoritative source is supplied.

children.title: Consistency-Preservation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on preserving projection structure and label consistency through transfers.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global Consistency on an Acyclic Bijective Instance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive boundary complementing the cyclic inconsistency witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a connected projection-game instance whose constraint graph is a tree and whose edge projections are bijections between their endpoint alphabets. Choosing a label at one root and propagating it through each projection or inverse projection determines a labeling satisfying every edge. Thus every acyclic system of bijective projection constraints is globally consistent; incompatible composition can arise only when constraints meet around a cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bijective projection constraints on a tree are globally satisfiable by propagating a root label.
assumptions_latex: The constraint graph is a finite tree.
Every edge projection is a bijection between its endpoint alphabets.
The alphabets are nonempty.
knowledge_statements.title: Global Consistency on an Acyclic Bijective Instance
Consistency-Preservation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local satisfiability does not imply a globally consistent Label-Cover labeling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4\in\{0,1\}\), with bipartition \(U=\{x_1,x_3\}\) and \(V=\{x_2,x_4\}\). Impose the projection constraints \(x_1=x_2\), \(x_3=x_2\), \(x_3=x_4\), and \(x_4=1-x_1\). Every proper edge subinstance is satisfiable, because deleting any edge breaks the cycle. Nevertheless, no labeling satisfies all four constraints: the first three imply \(x_1=x_4\), contradicting \(x_4=1-x_1\). Thus consistency on proper local subinstances does not by itself ensure global consistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bipartite cycle of projection constraints can be satisfiable after deleting any edge yet globally inconsistent, so proper local checks alone do not guarantee a global Label-Cover labeling.
assumptions_latex: The constraint graph has bipartition \(U=\{x_1,x_3\}\) and \(V=\{x_2,x_4\}\).
Each equality or complementation constraint is interpreted as a projection from its endpoint in \(U\) to its endpoint in \(V\).

notation.meaning: The two vertex classes of the bipartite projection game.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit finite bipartite counterexample directly checkable

children.title: Code-Based Soundness Test Family
children.top_down_role: Test families underlying sharp constraint-satisfaction hardness.

children.title: Dictatorship Tests
children.top_down_role: Test families distinguishing dictator-like functions from pseudorandom alternatives.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixes the influence convention used by the immutable dictatorship-test definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the uniform measure on \(\{-1,1\}^n\), write \(f(x)=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}\widehat f(S)\chi_S(x)\), where \(\chi_S(x)=\prod_{j\in S}x_j\). The degree-at-most-\(d\) influence of coordinate \(i\) is \[\operatorname{Inf}^{\le d}_i(f)=\sum_{\substack{S\ni i\\|S|\le d}}\widehat f(S)^2.\] For the dictator \(f(x)=x_i\), this equals one at coordinate \(i\) and zero at every other coordinate whenever \(d\ge1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Low-degree influence is the Fourier mass on degree-at-most-d sets containing the coordinate; a dictator concentrates it on one coordinate.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A \((c,s,\tau,d)\)-dictatorship test is a distribution over a finite tuple of query points \(X^{(1)},\ldots,X^{(k)}\in\{-1,1\}^n\), together with an acceptance predicate \(P:\{-1,1\}^k\to\{0,1\}\). Given oracle access to \(f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\}\), it accepts with probability \(\mathbb E[P(f(X^{(1)}),\ldots,f(X^{(k)}))]\). knowledge_statements.title: Unique Games Conjecture
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard completeness–soundness formulation for finite-alphabet unique label-cover instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A unique game consists of a finite graph \(G=(V,E)\), an alphabet \([q]\), and, for every oriented edge \((u,v)\), a permutation \(\pi_{uv}:[q]\to[q]\). A labeling \(L:V\to[q]\) satisfies \((u,v)\) when \(L(v)=\pi_{uv}(L(u))\). The Unique Games Conjecture asserts that for every \(\varepsilon,\delta>0\), some alphabet size \(q=q(\varepsilon,\delta)\) makes it NP-hard to distinguish instances with optimum at least \(1-\varepsilon\) from instances with optimum at most \(\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For suitable alphabet size, distinguishing almost satisfiable unique games from games having only a small satisfiable fraction is conjectured NP-hard.

Each edge constraint is a permutation of the alphabet.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete strengthening obtained by requiring fully satisfiable completeness instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The perfect-completeness Unique Games Conjecture asserts that for every \(\delta>0\) there exists an alphabet size \(q\) such that it is NP-hard, given a unique game \(U\) over \([q]\), to distinguish \(\operatorname{val}(U)=1\) from \(\operatorname{val}(U)\le\delta\). This statement implies the corresponding ordinary UGC gap with completeness \(1-\varepsilon\), while the converse is not part of ordinary UGC's formulation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical schema for hypotheses strictly stronger than ordinary UGC.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A strengthened unique-games hypothesis is a family \(H\) of NP-hardness assertions for unique-game promise problems that implies the ordinary Unique Games Conjecture and additionally requires a sharper gap or a structural guarantee not supplied by ordinary UGC. Formally, \(H\Rightarrow\operatorname{UGC}\), while the extra assertion may prescribe expansion, small-set behavior, alphabet growth, completeness, or soundness. Any hardness theorem derived using the extra assertion is conditional on \(H\), not merely on UGC, unless an independent implication from UGC is established.

children.title: Conditionality Caveats

knowledge_statements.title: Conditionality Caveats
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical boundary on interpreting UGC-based inapproximability results.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a reduction proves \(\operatorname{UGC}\Rightarrow H_P(\rho)\), where \(H_P(\rho)\) states that optimization problem \(P\) cannot be approximated beyond threshold \(\rho\) in polynomial time unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\). This implication alone neither proves \(H_P(\rho)\) unconditionally nor proves UGC from \(H_P(\rho)\). If UGC is false, the implication places no restriction on the approximability of \(P\); and if the reduction uses a strengthened variant \(H\), its conclusion is only \(H\)-conditional.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: UGC-based hardness is an implication: it is not unconditional, reversible, or transferable from a strengthened variant without another theorem.
assumptions_latex: A hardness result has the form \(A\Rightarrow B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\Rightarrow B\) does not entail \(B\), \(B\Rightarrow A\), or \(\neg A\Rightarrow\neg B\).

Such a reduction proves, assuming only \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), that no polynomial-time algorithm always distinguishes these cases. knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits exact recovery when the necessary inverse accuracy is not polynomially bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The exact-recovery argument excludes an FPTAS only when the minimum relevant objective separation can be resolved using \(1/\varepsilon\) polynomial in the input length. If the needed objective bound is exponential or feasible values can differ by exponentially small amounts, the required inverse accuracy may be exponential, and the FPTAS running-time guarantee no longer yields a polynomial-time exact algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact recovery gives no polynomial-time contradiction when resolving the objective gap requires exponentially large inverse accuracy.
assumptions_latex: The hypothetical scheme runs in time polynomial in the input length and \(1/\varepsilon\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximization analogue of the integral-objective FPTAS-exclusion argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be an NP-hard maximization problem with nonnegative integral feasible objective values and \(1\le\operatorname{OPT}(I)\le B(n)\) on the hard instance family, where \(B\) is polynomially bounded. If an FPTAS returned a feasible value \(A(I)\ge(1-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(I)\), choosing \(0<\varepsilon<1/B(n)\) would force \(A(I)>\operatorname{OPT}(I)-1\), and integrality and feasibility would imply \(A(I)=\operatorname{OPT}(I)\). Hence such an FPTAS would imply \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For polynomially bounded integral maximization objectives, sufficiently accurate fully polynomial approximation recovers the exact optimum.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard integer-objective obstruction to an FPTAS through exact recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be an NP-hard minimization problem whose feasible objective values are nonnegative integers. Suppose a polynomial-time reduction produces instances of encoding length \(n\) with \(1\le\operatorname{OPT}(I)\le B(n)\), where \(B\) is polynomially bounded. If \(P\) admitted an FPTAS returning a feasible solution of value at most \((1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) in time polynomial in \(n\) and \(1/\varepsilon\), then running it with \(\varepsilon<1/B(n)\) would recover the exact optimum in polynomial time. Hence no such FPTAS exists unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: NP-Hardness Alone Does Not Exclude a PTAS
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates exact NP-hardness from fixed-gap approximation hardness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Binary-encoded \(0\)-\(1\) Knapsack maximization is NP-hard and nevertheless admits an FPTAS, hence also a PTAS. Therefore exact NP-hardness alone does not exclude a polynomial-time approximation scheme; a gap-preserving hardness argument is required.

assumptions_latex: The standard binary encoding of \(0\)-\(1\) Knapsack is used.
knowledge_statements.title: NP-Hardness Alone Does Not Exclude a PTAS

knowledge_statements.scope_note: PTAS exclusion obtained from APX-hardness under a PTAS-preserving reduction notion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If an optimization problem \(P\) is APX-hard under reductions that transform a PTAS for \(P\) into a PTAS for every problem in APX, then a PTAS for \(P\) would yield a PTAS for an APX problem with an NP-hard fixed approximation gap. Consequently, unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\), such an APX-hard problem has no PTAS.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: APX-hardness under PTAS-preserving reductions excludes a PTAS unless P equals NP.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimization counterpart of fixed-gap PTAS exclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a minimization problem for which it is NP-hard to distinguish \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\le c\) from \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\ge s\), where \(0<c<s\) are fixed constants. A PTAS run with fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) satisfying \((1+\varepsilon)c<s\) would return a value below \(s\) in the completeness case, whereas every feasible solution has value at least \(s\) in the soundness case. Therefore \(P\) has no PTAS unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed multiplicative minimization gap rules out a PTAS unless P equals NP.
assumptions_latex: The promise gap \(\operatorname{OPT}\le c\) versus \(\operatorname{OPT}\ge s\) is NP-hard for fixed \(0<c<s\).

Polynomial-Time Scheme Exclusion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constant-gap NP-hardness excludes a PTAS.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a maximization problem with normalized objective in \([0,1]\). Suppose it is NP-hard to distinguish instances satisfying \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\ge c\) from those satisfying \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\le s\), for fixed constants \(c>s\ge0\). A PTAS with guarantee \(A(I)\ge(1-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(I)\), run at any fixed \(\varepsilon<1-s/c\), would output more than \(s\) in the completeness case and at most \(s\) in the soundness case. Therefore \(P\) has no PTAS unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any fixed NP-hard approximation gap rules out arbitrarily accurate polynomial-time approximation unless P equals NP.

The \((c,s)\) promise gap is NP-hard for fixed \(c>s\).

children.title: Efficient Scheme Exclusion

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary reduction properties for deriving EPTAS exclusion from parameterized hardness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: W[1]-hardness alone does not exclude an EPTAS for a target optimization problem. The contradiction requires a fixed-parameter reduction whose requested accuracy is a computable function of the source parameter alone and whose target size is \(h(k)|x|^{O(1)}\). Without these properties, substituting the selected accuracy into \(f(1/\varepsilon)n^{O(1)}\) need not yield an FPT algorithm for the source problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bare W[1]-hardness is insufficient; the reduction must convert a hypothetical EPTAS into an FPT source algorithm.
assumptions_latex: The proposed obstruction uses the hypothesis \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne\mathrm{W[1]}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{EPTAS exclusion requires a compatible parameter-to-accuracy gap reduction.}\)
knowledge_statements.title: Parameterized-Hardness Sufficiency Boundary

assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is W[1]-hard under fixed-parameter reductions.
The reduction runs in time \(h_0(k)|x|^{O(1)}\), produces an instance of size at most \(h_1(k)|x|^{O(1)}\), and selects a computable accuracy \(\varepsilon=g(k)>0\).
A solution satisfying the specified approximation guarantee at accuracy \(\varepsilon=g(k)\) decides \((x,k)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne\mathrm{W[1]}\Rightarrow\text{the target optimization problem has no EPTAS compatible with the reduction}.\)

notation.meaning: EPTAS running-time form, where the exponent of n is independent of the accuracy.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameterized-complexity obstruction to efficient polynomial-time approximation schemes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume a parameterized problem \(Q\) is W[1]-hard. Suppose an approximation-preserving reduction maps each instance \((x,k)\), in time \(h_0(k)|x|^{O(1)}\), to an optimization instance \(I\) of size \(n\le h_1(k)|x|^{O(1)}\) and a computable accuracy \(\varepsilon=g(k)>0\), such that a solution satisfying the specified approximation guarantee at accuracy \(\varepsilon\) decides \((x,k)\). If the optimization problem had an EPTAS with running time \(f(1/\varepsilon)n^{O(1)}\), composition would decide \(Q\) in time \(h(k)|x|^{O(1)}\). Consequently, under \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne\mathrm{W[1]}\), no such EPTAS exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameterized gap reduction rules out an EPTAS because the scheme would make a W[1]-hard problem fixed-parameter tractable.
knowledge_statements.title: Efficient Scheme Exclusion

children.title: Subexponential Scheme Exclusion
children.top_down_role: Barriers excluding approximation schemes within subexponential running time.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hypotheses needed to transfer a subexponential decision lower bound to approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Exact ETH alone supplies no fixed approximation gap. A subexponential approximation-scheme exclusion therefore requires a gap hypothesis or gap-producing reduction, and the transferred exponent depends on the reduction blowup. If \(n\le N^a\), target time \(2^{o(n^{1/a})}\operatorname{poly}(n)\) composes to subexponential time in \(N\); without a fixed detectable gap or quantitative size bound, the conclusion does not follow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subexponential scheme exclusion requires both a preserved approximation gap and a quantitative reduction-size bound.
assumptions_latex: The intended contradiction is to a \(2^{o(N)}\) source lower bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{Exact ETH alone or an unquantified reduction does not imply the stated approximation-time lower bound.}\)
knowledge_statements.title: Gap and Blowup Requirements
Subexponential Scheme Exclusion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gap-ETH template excluding subexponential-time approximation schemes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume Gap-ETH: some constant-gap bounded-width SAT problem on \(N\) variables cannot be distinguished in time \(2^{o(N)}\). Suppose a reduction maps such formulas to optimization instances of size \(n\le N^a\), preserves a fixed gap detectable by accuracy \(\varepsilon_0>0\), and is computable in \(2^{o(N)}\) time. Then an approximation scheme running at \(\varepsilon_0\) in time \(2^{o(n^{1/a})}\operatorname{poly}(n)\) would violate Gap-ETH. Thus the target problem admits no scheme with that subexponential dependence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under Gap-ETH, a polynomial-size gap reduction transfers a quantitative subexponential lower bound to any approximation scheme at the preserved accuracy.
assumptions_latex: Gap-ETH holds.
The reduction has size bound \(n\le N^a\).
Accuracy \(\varepsilon_0\) distinguishes the reduced gap.

children.title: Accuracy–Time Tradeoff Barriers
children.top_down_role: Lower-bound regimes relating achievable accuracy to running-time growth.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions for converting a reduction-indexed bound into an explicit accuracy–time curve.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A reduction establishing only \(T(r(N),\varepsilon(N))+R(N)\ge L(N)\) gives a parametric lower bound on pairs realized by the reduction. Converting it into a bound for independently specified \((n,\varepsilon)\) requires compatible monotonicity and generalized-inverse or envelope bounds for the size and accuracy maps. Otherwise separate inversion can assert hardness at parameter pairs that no reduced instance realizes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reduction gives a parametric tradeoff; a global accuracy–time curve requires justified monotonicity and inverse-envelope conditions.
assumptions_latex: \(T(r(N),\varepsilon(N))+R(N)\ge L(N)\) is known only for parameter pairs generated by the reduction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{Separate inversion of }r\text{ and }\varepsilon\text{ is unjustified without compatible inverse-envelope conditions.}\)
knowledge_statements.title: Parametric Lower-Bound Elimination Boundary
Accuracy–Time Tradeoff Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction-based conversion of source hardness into an accuracy-dependent time lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a source gap problem of size \(N\) require time at least \(L(N)\). Suppose a reduction produces an optimization instance of size \(n\le r(N)\) and an accuracy parameter \(\varepsilon(N)\) such that any \(\varepsilon(N)\)-approximate solution decides the source gap. Every approximation algorithm with running time \(T(n,\varepsilon)\) must then satisfy \(T(r(N),\varepsilon(N))+R(N)\ge L(N)\) for infinitely many \(N\), where \(R(N)\) is the reduction time. Inverting \(r\) and \(\varepsilon\) yields the corresponding accuracy–time lower-bound curve.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quantitative gap reduction converts source decision-time hardness into a lower bound coupling target instance size and requested accuracy.
assumptions_latex: The source gap problem has lower bound \(L(N)\).
The reduction has size \(r(N)\), time \(R(N)\), and distinguishing accuracy \(\varepsilon(N)\).

assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a maximization problem with a nonnegative objective and feasible solutions whose values can be evaluated in polynomial time.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gap formulation of hardness beyond a fixed approximation threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a maximization problem \(P\) with a nonnegative objective, constant-threshold hardness at ratio \(\rho\in(0,1)\) means that fixed constants \(c>s\ge 0\) satisfy \(s/c=\rho\) and that it is NP-hard to distinguish instances with \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\ge c\) from instances with \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\le s\). If a polynomial-time algorithm guaranteed approximation ratio \(r>\rho\), then on a completeness instance it would return a feasible solution of value at least \(r\operatorname{OPT}(I)\ge rc>s\), while on a soundness instance every feasible solution would have value at most \(s\). Thus such an algorithm would decide the NP-hard gap, so it cannot exist unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An NP-hard fixed objective gap with ratio s divided by c rules out every polynomial-time maximization approximation ratio strictly greater than that threshold, unless P equals NP.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimization–Maximization Asymmetry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of conventional guarantees for nonnegative minimization and maximization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\alpha\ge1\), a nonnegative minimization guarantee is \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\min}\le f(x_A)\le\alpha\operatorname{OPT}_{\min}\), whereas a nonnegative maximization guarantee is \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\max}/\alpha\le f(x_A)\le\operatorname{OPT}_{\max}\). Consequently the minimization relative excess is at most \(\alpha-1\), while the maximization relative deficit is at most \(1-1/\alpha\). The two conventions coincide only after reciprocal reparameterization: a maximization factor \(\alpha\) corresponds to retained fraction \(1/\alpha\), not to retained fraction \(1-(\alpha-1)\).

children.title: Absolute–Asymptotic Guarantee Mismatch
children.top_down_role: The boundary between uniform and large-instance guarantees.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform versus additive-slack asymptotic guarantees for nonnegative maximization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let A(I) and \operatorname{OPT}(I) be nonnegative values. An absolute \alpha-approximation satisfies A(I)\ge \operatorname{OPT}(I)/\alpha. An asymptotic guarantee may instead satisfy A(I)\ge \operatorname{OPT}(I)/\alpha-\beta for an instance-independent \beta\ge0. For \operatorname{OPT}(I)>0, this yields A(I)/\operatorname{OPT}(I)\ge 1/\alpha-\beta/\operatorname{OPT}(I), which supplies no uniform positive retained fraction when positive optima can approach zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For maximization, additive asymptotic loss can eliminate every uniform retained-value guarantee on small-optimum instances.
assumptions_latex: A(I),\operatorname{OPT}(I)\ge0.
\alpha\ge1 and \beta\ge0 are instance-independent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A(I)\ge \operatorname{OPT}(I)/\alpha-\beta does not imply A(I)\ge \operatorname{OPT}(I)/\alpha' for any uniform finite \alpha' when positive optima can approach zero.
review_flags: Added missing maximization counterpart to the minimization seed.
Uses the conventional reciprocal-factor maximization parameterization.
knowledge_statements.title: Maximization Absolute–Asymptotic Mismatch
Absolute–Asymptotic Guarantee Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform versus additive-slack asymptotic guarantees for minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A(I)\) and \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) be nonnegative costs. An absolute \(\alpha\)-approximation satisfies \(A(I)\le\alpha\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) for every instance \(I\). An asymptotic \(\alpha\)-approximation permits a constant \(\beta\ge0\) with \(A(I)\le\alpha\operatorname{OPT}(I)+\beta\) for every \(I\). The latter implies the ratio bound \(A(I)/\operatorname{OPT}(I)\le\alpha+\beta/\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) only when \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)>0\); it gives no uniform finite factor as the optimum approaches zero. Thus an asymptotic guarantee does not, without a positive lower bound or separate treatment of small instances, imply an absolute guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An additive constant is negligible for large optima but can destroy every uniform ratio bound on instances whose optimum is small or zero.
assumptions_latex: \(A(I),\operatorname{OPT}(I)\ge0\).
\(\alpha\ge1\) and \(\beta\ge0\) are instance-independent constants.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A(I)\le\alpha\operatorname{OPT}(I)+\beta\) does not imply \(A(I)\le\alpha'\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) for any uniform finite \(\alpha'\) when positive optima can approach zero.

children.title: Structural Regime Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Loss of guarantees outside required combinatorial, geometric, or numerical regimes.

children.title: Metric-Geometric Structural Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Failure of routing, clustering, and geometric schemes outside their structural regimes.

children.title: Metricity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Applicability of approximation guarantees under metric, near-metric, or nonmetric input structure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Near-metric shortcut bounds under a multiplicatively relaxed triangle inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\beta\ge1\), suppose \(d\) is symmetric, nonnegative, zero on the diagonal, and satisfies \(d(u,w)\le\beta(d(u,v)+d(v,w))\) for all \(u,v,w\). Replacing one two-edge subwalk \(u,v,w\) by \(u,w\) increases the total nonnegative walk cost by at most a factor \(\beta\). If \(q\) shortcuts are compared successively with the current walk, the generic bound is \(C_q\le\beta^q C_0\). Thus \(\beta>1\) does not preserve the nonincreasing-shortcut argument available at \(\beta=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A beta-relaxed triangle inequality bounds one shortcut by beta, but repeated generic comparisons may compound, so metric shortcut proofs do not transfer unchanged.
assumptions_latex: \(\beta\ge1\).
Walk costs are nonnegative sums of edge distances.
Each shortcut is compared with the current walk.

notation.meaning: walk cost after i analyzed shortcuts

review_flags: The compounded estimate is a generic guarantee bound and need not be tight for a particular near metric or shortcut sequence.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxed-Triangle Shortcut Regime
Metricity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Triangle inequality as the boundary for shortcut-based metric approximation arguments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be a finite set. A function \(d:V\times V\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\) is a metric when \(d(u,v)=0\) if and only if \(u=v\), \(d(u,v)=d(v,u)\), and \(d(u,w)\le d(u,v)+d(v,w)\) for all \(u,v,w\in V\). Any approximation argument that shortcuts the two-edge subwalk \(u,v,w\) by replacing it with the edge \(u,w\) relies on the triangle inequality. Without it, shortcut cost can increase without bound: for three distinct vertices, set \(d(u,v)=d(v,w)=1\) and \(d(u,w)=M\), with symmetric values and zero diagonal. Replacing the two-edge path by the direct edge multiplies its cost by \(M/2\), which tends to infinity as \(M\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The triangle inequality makes metric shortcutting nonincreasing; without it, one shortcut can increase cost by an arbitrarily large factor.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite and \(d:V\times V\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\).
The counterexample uses three distinct vertices and \(M>2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without the triangle inequality, shortcut inflation can satisfy \(d(u,w)/(d(u,v)+d(v,w))=M/2\to\infty\).

notation.meaning: three distinct vertices in the counterexample

review_flags: Supplied graph-theory locator does not specifically certify the approximation boundary.

children.title: Dimensional Regimes
children.top_down_role: Dependence of approximation schemes on fixed, bounded, growing, or unrestricted dimension.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Slice-Wise, XP, FPT, and Uniform Dimensional Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameterized classification of algorithms whose complexity depends on dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\) be total input length and \(d\) the dimension parameter. A bound \(m^{g(d)}\) is slice-wise polynomial and belongs to XP with parameter \(d\), because each fixed-\(d\) slice has a polynomial bound. A bound \(f(d)m^c\), with \(c\) independent of \(d\), is fixed-parameter tractable. Neither form alone is uniformly polynomial in the combined input: uniform polynomiality requires a constant \(C\), independent of \(d\), such that the actual running time is at most \(m^C\) on all admissible inputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed-dimensional polynomiality gives an XP guarantee; a dimension-independent exponent gives FPT, but combined-input polynomiality requires one uniform polynomial bound over all dimensions.
assumptions_latex: \(m\) includes the complete encoding of the instance and its dimension.
\(f\) and \(g\) are computable and \(c\) is independent of \(d\).
review_flags: FPT does not by itself imply ordinary polynomial time when the parameter is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.title: Slice-Wise, XP, FPT, and Uniform Dimensional Complexity
Dimensional Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed geometric dimension versus dimension supplied as part of the input.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a geometric optimization algorithm on \(n\) objects in dimension \(d\) have running time \(n^{g(d)}p(L,1/\varepsilon)\), where \(L\) is encoding length and \(g\) is unbounded. For every fixed \(d\), this is polynomial in \(n\), \(L\), and \(1/\varepsilon\). If \(d\) is part of the input, however, the exponent is not bounded by a universal constant, so the same bound does not establish polynomial time in the combined input size. Consequently a fixed-dimensional approximation scheme does not automatically transfer to variable or unbounded dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A running time polynomial for each fixed dimension need not be polynomial when dimension is input, so fixed-dimensional schemes do not automatically transfer.
assumptions_latex: \(g:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}\) is unbounded.
\(p\) is polynomial in its displayed arguments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(n^{g(d)}p(L,1/\varepsilon)\) is polynomial for fixed \(d\) but not uniformly polynomial in \((n,d,L,1/\varepsilon)\).
review_flags: Exact parameterized-geometric approximation source is absent.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixed-versus-input-dimension complexity boundary is correctly stated and failure_boundary fits the container, but no parameterized geometric-approximation source is supplied.

children.title: Geometric Representation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits imposed by the availability or fidelity of geometric representations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of multiplicative representation distortion on nonnegative pair-distance objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((V,d)\) be a finite metric space and let \(\phi:V\to\mathbb R^k\) satisfy \(s d(u,v)\le \|\phi(u)-\phi(v)\|_2\le Ds d(u,v)\) for all \(u,v\), where \(s>0\) and \(D\ge1\). For every feasible object \(X\) whose cost is a nonnegative weighted sum of selected pair distances, \(s c_d(X)\le c_\phi(X)\le Ds c_d(X)\). Hence a \(\rho\)-approximation under the represented distances is a \(D\rho\)-approximation under \(d\). Without a uniform finite distortion bound, representation fidelity supplies no uniform transferred factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A distortion-D representation changes nonnegative pair-distance objectives by at most D and multiplies a represented-space approximation factor by at most D.
assumptions_latex: Every coefficient multiplying a selected pair distance is nonnegative.
The original and represented problems have the same feasible objects.
The distortion inequalities hold uniformly over all pairs.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Distortion Representation Fidelity
Geometric Representation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact criterion for finite Euclidean distance representation in bounded dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(d_{ij})\) be a symmetric \(n\times n\) matrix with zero diagonal, let \(D^{(2)}=(d_{ij}^{2})\), and set \(J=I-\frac1n\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf T}\). There exist points \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\) satisfying \(d_{ij}=\lVert x_i-x_j\rVert_2\) for all \(i,j\) if and only if \(B=-\frac12JD^{(2)}J\) is positive semidefinite and \(\operatorname{rank}(B)\le d\). Thus positive semidefiniteness determines Euclidean representability, while rank determines the minimum required dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite distance matrix embeds exactly in Euclidean dimension d precisely when its centered Gram matrix is positive semidefinite and has rank at most d.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is finite, symmetric, entrywise nonnegative, and has zero diagonal.
\(d\in\mathbb{N}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D\) is realizable in \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\iff B\succeq0\) and \(\operatorname{rank}(B)\le d\).
review_flags: Supplied geometric locator does not identify the Euclidean distance-matrix criterion.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The centered-Gram-matrix criterion is a substantive Euclidean distance-matrix theorem and fits a condition record, but it has no source or exact theorem locator.

children.title: Cross-Regime Transfer Failures
children.top_down_role: Breakdown of routing, clustering, or geometric guarantees when transferred outside their intended structural regime.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additional efficiency conditions required to transfer an approximation algorithm, rather than only its objective guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the seed's distortion and feasibility hypotheses, if the instance map \(T\), reconstruction map \(R\), and the \(\alpha\)-approximation algorithm for \(T(I)\) all run in time polynomial in the source-instance encoding length, and \(|T(I)|\le \operatorname{poly}(|I|)\), their composition is a polynomial-time \(ab\alpha\)-approximation for the source class. Without these encoding-size and computation bounds, the approximation inequality still transfers but polynomial-time approximability need not.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Objective guarantees and polynomial running time transfer separately: the transformation, transformed instance, reconstruction, and target algorithm must all be polynomially bounded.
assumptions_latex: The feasibility and objective-distortion assumptions of the immutable transfer record hold.
\(|T(I)|\le \operatorname{poly}(|I|)\).
\(T\), \(R\), and the target approximation algorithm are polynomial-time under the chosen encoding model.
knowledge_statements.title: Efficient Approximation Transfer
Cross-Regime Transfer Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions required to transfer a multiplicative guarantee through an instance transformation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) map minimization instances in class \(\mathcal C_1\) to class \(\mathcal C_2\), and let \(R\) map feasible solutions back. Suppose positive constants \(a,b\) satisfy \(f_I(R(y))\le a f_{T(I)}(y)\) for every feasible \(y\) and \(\operatorname{OPT}(T(I))\le b\operatorname{OPT}(I)\). Then an \(\alpha\)-approximation on \(T(I)\) transfers as an \(a b\alpha\)-approximation on \(I\). If either uniform comparison is absent, the source-regime factor alone implies no target-regime factor; objective distortion or infeasible reconstruction may be unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximation factors transfer between structural regimes only when instance transformation and solution reconstruction uniformly control objective distortion and feasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(T(I)\in\mathcal C_2\) for every \(I\in\mathcal C_1\).
\(R(y)\) is feasible for \(I\) whenever \(y\) is feasible for \(T(I)\).
\(a,b>0\) are independent of the instance.
