intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sufficient transfer calculation is internally correct and matches the cross-regime failure container, but the reduction criterion and its failure claim lack an inspectable source.

children.title: Graph Structure Regime Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Dependence of schemes on density, separators, excluded minors, or bounded width.

children.title: Density Regimes
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity of approximation guarantees to dense input structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Density Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Edge-density regimes for finite simple undirected graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(n=|V|\ge2\) and \(m=|E|\), define its edge density by \(\delta(G)=m/\binom n2=2m/(n(n-1))\). A graph family \((G_n)\) lies in a uniformly dense regime when there exists a constant \(\rho>0\), independent of \(n\), such that \(\delta(G_n)\ge\rho\) for all sufficiently large \(n\). Equivalently, \(|E(G_n)|=\Omega(|V(G_n)|^2)\). Guarantees requiring this regime need not apply when \(\delta(G_n)\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph family is uniformly dense when a fixed positive fraction of all possible edges is present; vanishing density leaves that regime.
assumptions_latex: Every \(G_n\) is finite, simple, and undirected.
\(|V(G_n)|\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((G_n)\) is uniformly dense \(\iff\exists\rho>0\ \exists n_0\ \forall n\ge n_0:\delta(G_n)\ge\rho\).
review_flags: Locator is provisional and must be checked for the density convention.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary on reusing a global density hypothesis in induced or recursive subinstances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every fixed \(0<\rho<1\), there is a constant \(c>0\) and, for all sufficiently large \(n\), an \(n\)-vertex simple graph \(G_n\) with \(\delta(G_n)\ge\rho\) containing an independent set of size at least \(cn\). Hence a positive density lower bound for the whole graph does not imply a positive density lower bound for every linear-size induced subgraph. Recursive use of a dense-instance lemma requires density to be assumed or re-established for each encountered subinstance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A globally dense graph can contain a linear-size induced subgraph with no edges.
assumptions_latex: Graphs are finite, simple, and undirected.
\(0<\rho<1\) is independent of n.
knowledge_statements.title: Whole-Graph Density Is Not Hereditary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact structural correspondence under simple graph complementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every finite simple graph \(G\) with at least two vertices, \(\delta(\overline G)=1-\delta(G)\). Thus density approaching one is equivalent to the complement having \(o(n^2)\) edges. This structural identity alone does not transfer an approximation ratio unless feasible solutions and objectives also correspond under complementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complementation exchanges edge density with missing-edge density, but objective transfer needs an additional problem-specific correspondence.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and simple.
review_flags: Approximation transfer itself is owned by the complement-transfer boundary topic.
knowledge_statements.title: Density and Missing-Edge Density

children.title: Sparsity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Guarantees supported by sparse graphs or sparse incidence structure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear Total Edge Count Does Not Imply Hereditary Sparsity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation between a whole-graph edge count and bounded arboricity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G_n\) be the disjoint union of a clique on \(t=\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor\) vertices and \(n-t\) isolated vertices. Then \(|E(G_n)|=\Theta(n)\), while \(a(G_n)=\lceil t/2\rceil=\Theta(\sqrt n)\). Thus a linear total edge count for each whole graph does not imply uniformly bounded arboricity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph can have only linearly many edges overall while containing a clique whose arboricity grows with graph size.
assumptions_latex: Graphs are finite, simple, and undirected.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear Total Edge Count Does Not Imply Hereditary Sparsity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Sparse Analyses Require Hereditary Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applicability boundary for arguments using sparse edge bounds on generated subgraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An analysis that invokes \(|E(H)|\le k(|V(H)|-1)\) for every encountered subgraph \(H\) requires a hereditary sparsity hypothesis such as arboricity at most \(k\). A bound only on \(|E(G)|\) for the original graph does not justify the same inequality with \(|V(H)|\) for recursively selected or induced subgraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sparse-graph reasoning applied locally needs sparsity throughout the relevant subgraphs, not just a linear edge count for the original graph.
assumptions_latex: The analysis applies an edge bound to subgraphs produced during its execution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |E(G)|=O(|V(G)|)\not\Rightarrow\exists k\ \forall H\subseteq G:\ |E(H)|\le k(|V(H)|-1)\text{ uniformly over a family}.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Sparse Analyses Require Hereditary Control

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent constant-parameter formulations of hereditary graph sparsity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every finite loopless undirected graph with at least one edge, arboricity \(a(G)\) and degeneracy \(d(G)\) satisfy \(a(G)\le d(G)\le2a(G)-1\). Consequently, bounded arboricity and bounded degeneracy define the same graph-family regime, although their numerical values may differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded arboricity and bounded degeneracy are equivalent hereditary sparsity regimes, within a factor of two.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite, loopless, undirected, and has at least one edge.

notation.meaning: maximum over subgraphs of their minimum degree

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Arboricity and Bounded Degeneracy
Sparsity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform graph sparsity expressed through bounded arboricity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), define its arboricity by \(a(G)=\max_{H\subseteq G,\,|V(H)|\ge2}\left\lceil |E(H)|/(|V(H)|-1)\right\rceil\). A graph family \(\mathcal G\) lies in a bounded-arboricity sparsity regime when there exists a constant \(k\) such that \(a(G)\le k\) for every \(G\in\mathcal G\). Equivalently, every subgraph \(H\) of every member satisfies \(|E(H)|\le k(|V(H)|-1)\). In particular, every \(n\)-vertex member has at most \(k(n-1)\) edges, though linear total edge count alone does not control all subgraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded-arboricity families are uniformly sparse because every subgraph, not merely the whole graph, has only linearly many edges.
assumptions_latex: Graphs are finite and undirected.
The constant \(k\in\mathbb{N}\) is independent of graph size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{G\in\mathcal G}a(G)\le k\iff\forall G\in\mathcal G\ \forall H\subseteq G:\ |E(H)|\le k(|V(H)|-1)\) for \(|V(H)|\ge2\).
review_flags: The supplied graph-theory locators do not identify the arboricity theorem.
Exact source is required for the equivalence.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bounded-arboricity characterization is mathematically appropriate and correctly distinguishes hereditary sparsity from linear total edge count, but the Nash-Williams-type formula and equivalence require an exact source locator.

children.title: Width Parameter Regimes
children.top_down_role: Applicability boundaries associated with bounded treewidth, pathwidth, or related width measures.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional runtime threshold for decomposition algorithms that enumerate every bag state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a supplied decomposition has polynomially many bags and an algorithm explicitly processes \(q^{w+1}\) states at a bag of width \(w\), where \(q>1\) is constant. That bag requires \(\Omega(q^w)\) work. If every bag has at most \(q^{w+1}\) states and polynomial transition work, total time is \(q^{O(w)}n^{O(1)}\). Thus this explicit enumeration is polynomial for \(w=O(\log n)\), while actual widths satisfying \(w/\log n\to\infty\) force superpolynomial state processing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For algorithms that really enumerate exponentially many bag states, logarithmic width is the polynomial-time threshold.
assumptions_latex: A supplied decomposition has polynomially many bags.
All stated states are explicitly processed.
\(q>1\) is constant and transition work is polynomial.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T(n,w)=q^{\Theta(w)}n^{O(1)}\text{ under the stated enumeration hypotheses}.
review_flags: The lower bound requires actual enumeration, not merely an upper bound on possible states.
knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Bag-State Enumeration versus Width

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical tree-decomposition width parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A tree decomposition of \(G=(V,E)\) is a tree \(T\) with bags \((B_t)\) such that every graph vertex occurs in a nonempty connected set of bags and every graph edge has both endpoints in some bag. Its width is \(\max_t|B_t|-1\), and \(\operatorname{tw}(G)\) is the minimum width. A family has bounded treewidth when one constant bounds \(\operatorname{tw}(G)\) for every member.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Treewidth minimizes maximum bag size minus one; bounded treewidth means one uniform constant works for the graph family.
assumptions_latex: Graphs are finite and undirected.
knowledge_statements.title: Treewidth and Bounded-Treewidth Regimes

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bounded Width Alone Gives No Optimization Guarantee
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between structural width and a problem-specific algorithm exploiting it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bound on treewidth, pathwidth, or another decomposition width does not by itself imply exact solvability or an approximation ratio for an unspecified optimization problem. A transfer requires a problem-specific finite-state representation or other structural theorem, correct transitions, and states encoding every constraint and objective interaction across the interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Small width is algorithmically useful only when the optimization problem admits a correct bounded-interface formulation.
assumptions_latex: The optimization problem and its encoding are otherwise unspecified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{bounded width}\not\Rightarrow\text{a problem-independent approximation or runtime guarantee}.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Width Alone Gives No Optimization Guarantee

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pathwidth as a Stronger Width Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relationship between the treewidth and pathwidth variants named by this leaf.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A path decomposition is a tree decomposition whose decomposition tree is a path. Hence \(\operatorname{tw}(G)\le\operatorname{pw}(G)\) for every graph. Bounded pathwidth implies bounded treewidth, but the converse fails for graph families: trees have treewidth at most one while their pathwidth is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pathwidth restricts the decomposition tree to a path, so bounded pathwidth is stronger than bounded treewidth.
assumptions_latex: Graphs are finite and undirected.
knowledge_statements.title: Pathwidth as a Stronger Width Regime

assumptions_latex: The input is a graph \(G\) with \(n\) vertices and treewidth \(w=\operatorname{tw}(G)\).
A dynamic program stores at most \(q^w\) states per bag for a constant \(q>1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The bounded-width regime has polynomial running time, whereas unrestricted width permits exponential state growth.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard tree-decomposition dynamic-programming state-count boundary
source needed for a problem-specific approximation interpretation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: State-complexity boundary for tree-decomposition dynamic programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a tree-decomposition dynamic program whose table has at most \(q^w\) states per bag and polynomial transition cost, the running time is \(q^w n^{O(1)}\). Consequently, if \(w\leq W\) for a fixed constant \(W\), the algorithm is polynomial in \(n\); if \(w=O(\log n)\), it remains polynomial because \(q^w=n^{O(1)}\). Once \(w/\log n\to\infty\), this state enumeration is superpolynomial, and for \(w=\Theta(n)\) it is exponential. Thus the applicability boundary of this decomposition method lies at logarithmic width, unless additional state compression is proved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decomposition algorithm with exponentially many states in treewidth is polynomial through logarithmic width, but becomes superpolynomial beyond that regime.
knowledge_statements.title: Width Parameter Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind fits the width-regime leaf, but no inspectable source is cited. More importantly, an upper bound of at most q^w states supports the stated running-time upper bound but does not imply superpolynomial state enumeration when w is superlogarithmic; a matching lower bound or an assumption that all q^w states are enumerated is required.

children.title: Separator-Based Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Dependence of approximation schemes on the existence or quality of structural separators.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional runtime threshold for methods that explicitly process every separator labeling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a recursive method has polynomially many subproblems, explicitly processes all \(q^{|S|}\) labelings of every encountered separator \(S\), where \(q>1\) is constant, and performs polynomial work per labeling. If all encountered separators have size \(O(s(n))\), its total time is \(q^{O(s(n))}n^{O(1)}\). An encountered sequence with \(|S|=\omega(\log n)\) forces \(q^{|S|}=n^{\omega(1)}\) work for this enumeration; an upper bound \(|S|\le s(n)\) alone does not establish that such large separators occur.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicit exhaustive boundary processing is polynomial for logarithmic separators; actual superlogarithmic separators force superpolynomial enumeration.
assumptions_latex: The recursion creates polynomially many subproblems.
Every one of the \(q^{|S|}\) labelings is processed.
Per-labeling work is polynomial and \(q>1\) is constant.

notation.meaning: number of boundary states per separator vertex
upper bound on encountered separator size

review_flags: The lower bound uses actual encountered separator size, not merely an upper bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Boundary-State Enumeration versus Separator Size

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separator notion used by recursive graph decompositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0<\alpha<1\), an \(\alpha\)-balanced vertex separator of \(G=(V,E)\) is a set \(S\subseteq V\) such that every component of \(G-S\) has at most \(\alpha|V|\) vertices. If \(\alpha\) is fixed and the condition is maintained recursively, every root-to-leaf recursion path has depth \(O(\log n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A balanced separator leaves only constant-factor-smaller components and therefore supports logarithmic recursion depth.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and undirected.
\(0<\alpha<1\) is independent of n.
knowledge_statements.title: Balanced Vertex Separators

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Balance Does Not Bound Interface Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary on deriving approximation guarantees solely from component-size balance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The condition that every component of \(G-S\) has at most \(\alpha n\) vertices controls recursive size but does not bound the objective value incident with or crossing \(S\). Deleting, guessing, or independently solving across \(S\) therefore needs an additional bound on separator cost, lost profit, crossing interactions, or boundary-state error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A balanced separator controls subproblem sizes but not the optimization loss at its interface.
assumptions_latex: Objective weights or interaction costs may be nonuniform.
knowledge_statements.title: Balance Does Not Bound Interface Loss

assumptions_latex: A recursive algorithm enumerates \(q^{|S|}\) boundary assignments for each separator \(S\), where \(q>1\) is constant.
Every recursive subproblem has at most a fixed fraction \(\alpha<1\) of its parent's vertices after deleting \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Polynomial-time enumeration requires logarithmic separators; larger separators yield superpolynomial overhead for this method.

notation.meaning: number of boundary states per separator vertex

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct enumeration and balanced-recursion calculation
source needed for placement within approximation-frontier theory
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Enumeration boundary for balanced-separator recursion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose every \(m\)-vertex recursive subproblem admits a separator \(S\) with \(|S|\leq s(m)\), and deleting \(S\) leaves components of size at most \(\alpha m\). If the method enumerates \(q^{|S|}\) assignments and performs polynomial work per assignment, its overhead is \(q^{O(s(n))}n^{O(1)}\), up to the logarithmic recursion depth. Hence \(s(n)=O(\log n)\) gives polynomial time, while \(s(n)=\omega(\log n)\) makes this enumeration superpolynomial. A separator theorem alone therefore does not imply a polynomial-time approximation method when its boundary states must all be enumerated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Balanced separators support polynomial exhaustive boundary processing only when their size is logarithmic, absent further compression or approximation.
knowledge_statements.title: Separator-Based Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind fits the separator leaf, but no source is supplied. The bound |S|<=s(m) yields an overhead upper bound; s(n)=omega(log n) alone does not show that the actual separators or their enumeration are superpolynomial. A lower bound on encountered separator sizes, or a formulation limited to loss of a polynomial-time guarantee, is required.

children.title: Excluded-Minor Restrictions
children.top_down_role: Guarantee changes caused by excluding fixed graph minors or leaving minor-closed classes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifier boundary for runtime guarantees whose constants depend on the forbidden minor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bound \(T(G;H)\le f(H)|V(G)|^c\), with constant exponent \(c\), is polynomial in \(|V(G)|\) for every fixed \(H\). If \(H\) is supplied with the input or varies with \(n\), the displayed bound is not a uniform polynomial-time bound unless \(f(H)\) is itself bounded polynomially in the total input length and the exponent remains uniform. Variation of \(H\) alone does not prove superpolynomial runtime; the dependence \(f\) must be examined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arbitrary dependence on H is harmless only when H is fixed; varying H requires an explicit uniform bound on that dependence.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm has runtime at most \(f(H)|V(G)|^c\).
\(c\) is independent of both G and H.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H\text{ fixed}\Rightarrow T=n^{O(1)};\quad H\text{ variable requires a uniform bound on }f(H).
review_flags: No superpolynomial conclusion is asserted without a lower bound on f.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Minor versus Varying-Minor Uniformity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical fixed-parameter graph class used by excluded-minor approximation results.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed finite undirected graph \(H\), let \(\mathcal G_H=\{G:H\not\preccurlyeq G\}\), where the minor relation is generated by vertex deletion, edge deletion, and edge contraction. The class is minor-closed: if \(G\in\mathcal G_H\) and \(G'\preccurlyeq G\), then \(G'\in\mathcal G_H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An H-minor-free class excludes one fixed graph under deletion and contraction and is closed under taking minors.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is fixed independently of the input.
Graphs are finite and undirected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\in\mathcal G_H\land G'\preccurlyeq G\Rightarrow G'\in\mathcal G_H.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed Excluded-Minor Regime

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Class Membership Alone Is Not an Approximation Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applicability boundary for guarantees proved only on a fixed minor-free class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a theorem assumes \(G\in\mathcal G_H\), then an input containing \(H\) as a minor lies outside its scope, so its approximation and runtime conclusions do not follow. Conversely, membership in \(\mathcal G_H\) alone supplies no problem-independent approximation ratio; a problem-specific algorithm and analysis are also required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed-minor-free theorem does not apply outside its class, and minor exclusion alone supplies no approximation ratio.
assumptions_latex: The referenced theorem explicitly assumes \(H\not\preccurlyeq G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H\preccurlyeq G\Rightarrow\text{the class-restricted theorem is inapplicable}.
knowledge_statements.title: Class Membership Alone Is Not an Approximation Theorem

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a fixed finite graph.
Inputs belong to the class \(\mathcal G_H=\{G:H\not\preccurlyeq G\}\), where \(\preccurlyeq\) denotes the minor relation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fixed-minor exclusion is a nonuniform structural restriction and does not by itself specify an approximation guarantee.

notation.meaning: class of graphs excluding H as a minor

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: definition of fixed excluded-minor classes and its quantifier boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifier boundary between fixed and input-dependent excluded minors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The excluded-minor regime is defined with \(H\) fixed independently of the input size: an admissible graph \(G\) satisfies \(H\not\preccurlyeq G\). Structural constants and algorithmic running-time factors may depend arbitrarily on this fixed \(H\). If \(H\) is instead supplied as part of the input or varies with \(n=|V(G)|\), those constants are not uniform polynomial bounds. Moreover, minor exclusion alone supplies only structural information; an approximation ratio follows only after a problem-specific decomposition, dynamic program, or charging argument is established. The frontier therefore cannot be transferred automatically from each fixed \(\mathcal G_H\) to a varying-minor family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Excluded-minor algorithms apply with the forbidden graph fixed; varying it with the input destroys uniformity, and exclusion alone gives no approximation ratio.
knowledge_statements.title: Excluded-Minor Restrictions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind is appropriate, but the graph-minor claim lacks an authoritative citation. Allowing H to vary does not by itself prove that no uniform polynomial bound exists; that depends on the algorithm's explicit dependence on H. The fixed-parameter versus varying-parameter distinction needs a sourced and more carefully qualified statement.

children.title: Capacity-Degree-Connectivity Constraint Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Additional constraints that disrupt rounding or decomposition methods.

children.title: Capacity Constraint Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Failures of rounding or decomposition guarantees under binding capacity restrictions.

assumptions_latex: A state-indexed algorithm for an instance of encoded length \(L\) runs in \(O(nB)\) time.
The integer capacity \(B\) is represented in binary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The capacity-indexed algorithm is pseudopolynomial rather than polynomial in the encoded input length.
review_flags: problem-specific capacity algorithm source remains desirable
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary-encoding boundary for capacity-indexed state spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For binary-encoded capacity \(B\), its contribution to the input length is \(\Theta(\log(B+1))\). An algorithm using \(B+1\) capacity states and running in \(O(nB)\) time is polynomial in the numerical value \(B\), but may take \(2^{\Theta(L)}\) time when \(B=2^{\Theta(L)}\). It is therefore pseudopolynomial, not polynomial in the standard bit model. A capacity restriction restores polynomiality only when \(B\leq L^{O(1)}\), capacities are unary encoded, or scaling removes the dependence on their exact magnitude while preserving the stated approximation guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A runtime polynomial in a binary-encoded capacity can be exponential in input length; polynomial applicability requires bounded capacities, unary encoding, or scaling.
knowledge_statements.title: Capacity Constraint Boundaries

children.title: Degree Constraint Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Approximation limits introduced by bounded, prescribed, or heterogeneous degree requirements.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Immediate local tests for a proposed degree-constrained subgraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a selected subgraph \(H=(V,F)\) must satisfy \(\ell_v\le d_H(v)\le b_v\), then any vertex with \(d_H(v)<\ell_v\) or \(d_H(v)>b_v\) certifies infeasibility of \(H\). Moreover, \(\ell_v>b_v\) or \(\ell_v>d_G(v)\) certifies infeasibility of the instance, although passing these local necessary tests need not establish global feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A violating vertex certifies solution failure, while contradictory or unattainable local bounds certify instance failure.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite undirected graph.
Degree bounds are integral.

notation.meaning: degree of v in the selected subgraph

review_flags: The instance-level conditions are necessary certificates, not a complete global characterization.
knowledge_statements.title: Vertex Certificates for Degree-Bound Violations

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degree dependence of a unit-charge approximation analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a packing analysis assigns at most one unit charge for each rejected object and every object charged to a selected vertex \(v\) lies in \(N[v]\). In a graph of maximum degree \(\Delta\), this counting argument bounds the charge to \(v\) by \(\Delta+1\), yielding only a \((\Delta+1)\)-dependent certificate. It is constant when \(\Delta\) is uniformly bounded; if \(\Delta\) is unbounded, this argument alone does not prove a uniform constant factor. Weighted charges or additional structure require separate bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A unit conflict-charging proof based only on closed-neighborhood size yields a degree-dependent, not uniformly constant, factor.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) has maximum degree \(\Delta\).
Each rejected object contributes at most one unit charge.
All objects charged to \(v\) lie in \(N[v]\).
review_flags: The conclusion is limited to the stated unit-charge analysis and is not a hardness claim.
knowledge_statements.title: Boundary of Closed-Neighborhood Conflict Charging

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Additive Degree Violation Is Bicriteria Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between additive, exact, and multiplicative satisfaction of upper degree bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A guarantee \(d_H(v)\le b_v+\beta\) with \(\beta>0\) does not imply exact feasibility \(d_H(v)\le b_v\). It implies \(d_H(v)\le(1+\varepsilon)b_v\) uniformly only when \(\beta\le\varepsilon b_v\) for every relevant vertex. In particular, \(b_v=1\) and \(\beta=1\) permit degree two, a factor-two violation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed additive degree excess is a genuine bicriteria relaxation and may be a large relative violation for small bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(b_v\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\).
\(\beta>0\) is the allowed additive excess.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d_H(v)\le b_v+\beta\not\Rightarrow d_H(v)\le b_v;\qquad \beta\le\varepsilon b_v\text{ is required for the displayed relative bound}.
knowledge_statements.title: Additive Degree Violation Is Bicriteria Feasibility

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) has maximum degree \(\Delta\).
Each selected vertex conflicts only with vertices in its closed neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any guarantee derived by charging conflicts to one selected vertex degrades with \(\Delta\) and is nonconstant when \(\Delta\) is unbounded.
review_flags: source and specific optimization problem required for a sharper frontier
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of degree-based conflict charging arguments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a packing analysis in which every object rejected because of a selected vertex \(v\) is charged to \(v\), and all such conflicts lie in \(N[v]\). Since \(|N[v]|\leq\Delta+1\), this argument can certify at best a factor depending on \(\Delta+1\), unless it uses additional structure. For a fixed bound \(\Delta\leq D\), the resulting factor is constant. If \(\Delta\) grows with \(|V|\), the same proof yields a nonconstant bound and cannot establish a uniform constant-factor approximation. Bounded degree is thus an applicability hypothesis of this charging method, not a harmless input normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conflict-charging guarantees are constant only under fixed degree bounds; when maximum degree grows, the same analysis yields a growing approximation factor.
knowledge_statements.title: Degree Constraint Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind fits the degree-regime leaf, but no source or specific packing model is given. The neighborhood cardinality bound can yield a Delta-dependent charging upper bound under suitable unit or bounded-charge assumptions; it does not establish that every guarantee derived from conflict charging must degrade with Delta, especially for weighted objectives or analyses using additional structure.

children.title: Connectivity Requirement Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity of guarantees to global, local, survivable, or multiway connectivity requirements.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact feasibility test for undirected spanning edge-connectivity requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite undirected spanning subgraph \(H=(V,F)\) and integer \(k\ge1\), \(H\) is \(k\)-edge-connected if and only if \(|\delta_F(S)|\ge k\) for every \(\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V\). Thus any \(S\) with \(|\delta_F(S)|<k\) certifies violation; for \(k=1\), an empty proper cut certifies disconnection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every proper cut must contain at least k selected edges; a deficient cut certifies failure of k-edge-connectivity.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is finite, undirected, and spanning.
\(k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\).

notation.meaning: selected edges with exactly one endpoint in S

knowledge_statements.title: Cut Certificates for Edge-Connectivity Requirements

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Connectivity Guarantees Require Feasible Bounded Repair
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximation-transfer boundary when connectivity strengthens an otherwise unchanged feasible family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F_Q\subseteq\mathcal F_0\) impose a connectivity requirement \(Q\) on a minimization problem. Then \(\operatorname{OPT}_0\le\operatorname{OPT}_Q\), but an \(\alpha\)-approximate solution in \(\mathcal F_0\) need not satisfy \(Q\). A transfer to \(\mathcal F_Q\) requires a polynomial-time repair or construction that preserves every other constraint and has a proved cost bound relative to \(\operatorname{OPT}_Q\). Independent connected solutions on disjoint clusters fail the global requirement unless feasible intercluster connections are supplied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An approximation does not survive a stronger connectivity requirement without a repair that preserves feasibility and has a quantified cost.
assumptions_latex: The objective is a minimization objective finite on both feasible families.
\(\mathcal F_Q\subseteq\mathcal F_0\) differs by an added global, terminal, or survivable connectivity requirement.
knowledge_statements.title: Connectivity Guarantees Require Feasible Bounded Repair

assumptions_latex: Feasible solutions are edge sets satisfying a global connectivity requirement.
A method optimizes independently over vertex-disjoint components or clusters.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Independent local feasibility does not imply globally connected feasibility, and arbitrary repair can invalidate the approximation bound.

notation.meaning: union of independently selected local edge sets

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: connectivity is not closed under disjoint union of local solutions
source needed for a problem-specific approximation theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of componentwise decomposition under global connectivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let local subproblems return feasible edge sets \(F_1,\ldots,F_r\) on disjoint clusters, and let \(F=\bigcup_{i=1}^r F_i\). Even when every \(F_i\) is connected within its cluster, \(F\) has at least \(r\) connected components unless intercluster edges are selected. Hence \(F\) violates any requirement \(\kappa(F)=1\) when \(r>1\). Adding connector edges after local optimization is valid only if their existence, feasibility under the remaining constraints, and total objective loss are bounded. Without such a repair lemma, an approximation guarantee proved for componentwise solutions does not extend to the connected variant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Connected local pieces need not form a connected global solution; approximation transfers only with a feasible, quantitatively bounded connection repair.
knowledge_statements.title: Connectivity Requirement Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind fits the connectivity leaf, but the claim lacks a source and needs a precise ambient vertex set for kappa(F). The assertion of at least r components also requires every local edge set to be nonempty and the clusters to have no selected intercluster edges. A problem-specific repair statement is needed for the approximation conclusion.

children.title: Constraint Interaction Failures
children.top_down_role: Breakdowns arising when multiple structural constraints apply simultaneously.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Composition Condition for Sequential Repairs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient preservation and objective-loss conditions for composing two repairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R_i\) repair membership in \(\mathcal F_i\). If \(R_1(S)\in\mathcal F_1\), \(R_2(T)\in\mathcal F_2\), and \(R_2(T)\in\mathcal F_1\) for every relevant \(T\in\mathcal F_1\), then \(R_2(R_1(S))\in\mathcal F_1\cap\mathcal F_2\). If a nonnegative minimization objective also satisfies \(f(R_i(X))\le\beta_i f(X)\), then the composed loss is at most \(\beta_1\beta_2\). Without the preservation condition, sequential repair is not a joint-feasibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The second repair must preserve the first constraint; under multiplicative loss bounds, the two losses multiply.
assumptions_latex: Both repair maps are defined on every intermediate solution used.

notation.meaning: repair map for constraint family i

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Composition Condition for Sequential Repairs

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Separate Guarantees Do Not Compose under Constraint Intersection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical boundary for approximation guarantees proved over separate feasible families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\mathcal F=\mathcal F_1\cap\mathcal F_2\), separate algorithms returning approximate solutions in \(\mathcal F_1\) and \(\mathcal F_2\) do not imply that either output belongs to \(\mathcal F\), nor do their approximation factors alone imply a factor for optimization over \(\mathcal F\). Such a conclusion requires a joint-feasibility invariant or a quantitatively bounded map into \(\mathcal F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximation guarantees for two separate constraint systems do not automatically combine for their intersection.
assumptions_latex: The combined problem requires simultaneous membership in \(\mathcal F_1\) and \(\mathcal F_2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Separate guarantees on }\mathcal F_1,\mathcal F_2\not\Rightarrow\text{a guarantee on }\mathcal F_1\cap\mathcal F_2.

notation.meaning: feasible families defined by the constituent constraints

knowledge_statements.title: Separate Guarantees Do Not Compose under Constraint Intersection

assumptions_latex: Feasible sets must satisfy two partition-matroid constraints arising from the endpoints of a bipartite matching.
A greedy rule processes edges by nonincreasing weight and accepts each feasible edge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Intersecting individually tractable constraints can invalidate greedy optimality; the displayed family approaches a factor-two loss.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit weighted bipartite-matching instance is directly checkable
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Greedy failure under intersection of two partition constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the bipartite vertex classes be \(\{a_1,a_2\}\) and \(\{b_1,b_2\}\), with edges \(e_0=a_1b_1\), \(e_1=a_1b_2\), and \(e_2=a_2b_1\). Assign \(w(e_0)=1+\varepsilon\) and \(w(e_1)=w(e_2)=1\), where \(0<\varepsilon<1\). Weight-ordered greedy first accepts \(e_0\), after which both remaining edges violate an endpoint-capacity constraint, so its value is \(1+\varepsilon\). The feasible matching \(\{e_1,e_2\}\) has value \(2\). Thus two separately simple degree constraints interact so that greedy is not optimal, with ratio \(2/(1+\varepsilon)\to2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two endpoint-capacity constraints make weighted greedy choose one slightly heavier edge instead of two compatible edges, producing an asymptotic factor-two loss.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Interaction Failures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample kind exactly fits the interaction-failure leaf, and the displayed weighted bipartite-matching instance is internally correct. However, the record supplies no inspectable citation; the standard-field rationale alone does not satisfy this review layer's citation check for the claimed canonical constraint-intersection phenomenon.

children.title: Numerical-Encoding Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Dependence of schemes and running times on encoded numerical magnitude.

assumptions_latex: All numerical data are integers or rationals encoded in binary.
Running time is measured in bit operations as a function of total encoding length \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Polynomial dependence on numerical magnitude is not polynomial-time dependence on binary input length.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bit-model distinction between polynomial and pseudopolynomial schemes.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 1. Complexity, Oracles, and Numerical Computation p. 21; Encoding p. 23; Encoding Length of Numbers p. 29

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a positive integer \(M\) is binary encoded, it occupies \(\Theta(\log(M+1))\) bits. Consequently, a scheme with running time \(T(n,M,1/\varepsilon)=\operatorname{poly}(n,M,1/\varepsilon)\) need not be polynomial in the input length \(L\), because \(M\) may equal \(2^{\Theta(L)}\). It is polynomial-time in the bit model only when the magnitude dependence is \(\operatorname{poly}(\log(M+1))\), or when an explicit restriction gives \(M\leq L^{O(1)}\). Thus a pseudopolynomial approximation construction cannot be classified as an FPTAS until its dependence on encoded magnitudes is removed or bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary magnitudes can be exponential in their bit length, so magnitude-polynomial schemes are not automatically polynomial-time or fully polynomial approximation schemes.
knowledge_statements.title: Numerical-Encoding Boundaries

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 1. Complexity, Oracles, and Numerical Computation p. 21; Encoding p. 23; Encoding Length of Numbers p. 29

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Why a polynomial arithmetic-operation count need not imply polynomial bit complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the Turing bit model, a polynomial arithmetic-operation count implies polynomial time only when operand and intermediate-result encodings remain polynomially bounded. Starting with \(z_0=2\) and setting \(z_{i+1}=z_i^2\) uses \(k\) multiplications but produces \(z_k=2^{2^k}\), whose ordinary binary encoding has \(2^k+1\) bits. Thus polynomially many unit-cost arithmetic operations may require exponential bit time or produce an exponentially long explicit result.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomially many arithmetic operations do not imply polynomial bit complexity when intermediate numbers acquire exponentially many bits.
assumptions_latex: Integers are represented explicitly in ordinary binary notation.
Bit complexity includes reading and writing intermediate values.

notation.meaning: ordinary binary encoding length of z

knowledge_statements.title: Intermediate Bit-Length Boundary

children.title: Method-Specific Obstructions
children.top_down_role: Failure modes limiting particular paradigms without establishing general hardness.

children.title: Greedy-Locality Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Instances defeating local selection or a chosen neighborhood.

children.title: Greedy Selection Traps
children.top_down_role: Instance patterns where locally attractive selections lead to poor global approximation quality.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbounded failure of 0–1 knapsack density greedy without a best-single-item safeguard.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\), consider a unit-capacity knapsack with item \(a\) of size \(\varepsilon\) and value \(2\varepsilon\), and item \(b\) of size \(1\) and value \(1\). Decreasing-density greedy selects \(a\) because \(v_a/s_a=2>1=v_b/s_b\); then \(b\) no longer fits. Its value is \(2\varepsilon\), whereas the optimum selects \(b\) and has value \(1\). Hence \(\operatorname{OPT}/\operatorname{GREEDY}=1/(2\varepsilon)\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tiny high-density item can block a full-size valuable item, making unguarded density greedy arbitrarily bad for 0–1 knapsack.
assumptions_latex: 0<\varepsilon<1/2.
Items are processed by nonincreasing value-to-size ratio and accepted whenever they fit.
Accepted items are never removed and no best-single-item comparison is performed.
knowledge_statements.title: Density-Greedy Knapsack Trap

assumptions_latex: A deterministic greedy algorithm orders candidates by earliest finishing time.
Feasibility means selecting pairwise nonoverlapping intervals, and the objective is total weight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The earliest-finish greedy rule has an unbounded approximation ratio for weighted interval scheduling.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit two-interval counterexample is directly checkable
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted interval-scheduling trap for earliest-finish greedy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any \(M>1\), consider two overlapping intervals \(I_s=[0,1]\) and \(I_\ell=[0,2]\), with weights \(w(I_s)=1\) and \(w(I_\ell)=M\). The earliest-finish greedy rule selects \(I_s\) first and then rejects \(I_\ell\), returning value \(1\). The optimum selects \(I_\ell\) and has value \(M\). Therefore the approximation ratio \(\operatorname{OPT}/\operatorname{GREEDY}=M\) is unbounded. The selection rule is valid for unweighted interval cardinality but crosses its applicability boundary when arbitrary weights replace unit profits.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Earliest-finish greedy can choose a unit-weight short interval over an overlapping interval of arbitrary weight, so its weighted approximation ratio is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.title: Greedy Selection Traps

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample kind fits the greedy-trap leaf, and the two-interval construction correctly gives an unbounded ratio for earliest-finish greedy on weighted interval scheduling. No inspectable source is cited, so canonical attribution and the stated boundary between weighted and unweighted variants remain unsupported at this review layer.

children.title: Locality Gaps
children.top_down_role: Separation between locally optimal solutions and globally competitive solutions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimization counterpart of the immutable maximization locality-gap definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization problem, a feasible solution \(S\) is \(N\)-locally optimal when \(f_I(T)\ge f_I(S)\) for every feasible \(T\in N_I(S)\). On instances with \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)>0\), define \[\operatorname{gap}_{\min}(N)=\sup_I\ \sup_{S\text{ is }N\text{-locally optimal}}\frac{f_I(S)}{\operatorname{OPT}(I)}.\] A finite value \(\alpha\) is exactly a uniform \(\alpha\)-approximation bound for all such local optima; an unbounded value precludes a uniform multiplicative guarantee based solely on \(N\)-local optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For minimization, the locality gap is the worst local-optimum-to-global-optimum ratio.
assumptions_latex: I\text{ ranges over minimization instances with }\operatorname{OPT}(I)>0.
N_I(S)\text{ is the specified feasible neighborhood.}
knowledge_statements.title: Minimization Locality Gap

assumptions_latex: \(I\) ranges over instances of a maximization problem.
\(N_I(S)\) is the specified neighborhood of a feasible solution \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A finite locality gap bounds the approximation quality of every local optimum for that neighborhood; an infinite gap precludes such a guarantee.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard worst-case ratio definition for local search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximization-form locality gap with positive local value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A feasible solution \(S\) is \(N\)-locally optimal when \(f_I(T)\leq f_I(S)\) for every feasible \(T\in N_I(S)\). For instances with positive local-optimum value, the locality gap is \[\operatorname{gap}(N)=\sup_I\ \sup_{S\text{ is }N\text{-locally optimal}}\frac{\operatorname{OPT}(I)}{f_I(S)}.\] If a local-search algorithm terminates at an \(N\)-local optimum, the definition certifies the approximation factor \(\operatorname{gap}(N)\) whenever this supremum is finite. If the ratios are unbounded, local optimality under \(N\) alone cannot certify any uniform multiplicative approximation factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The locality gap is the worst optimum-to-local-optimum ratio over all instances; an unbounded gap rules out a neighborhood-based approximation guarantee.
knowledge_statements.title: Locality Gaps

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind is the correct role for the Locality Gaps leaf, and the maximization-form definition is precise after restricting to positive local-optimum values. Plain text and LaTeX agree, but no authoritative local-search source with a section, definition, or page locator is supplied.

children.title: Neighborhood-Choice Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Dependence of local-search guarantees on the permitted move family or neighborhood radius.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Incomparable Neighborhoods Have No Gap Ordering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Neighborhood inclusion is essential for generic locality-gap monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the feasible states be \(O,A,B\). Let symmetric neighborhood \(N_1\) contain only the edge \(\{A,O\}\), and \(N_2\) contain only \(\{B,O\}\). For maximization values \(f(O)=M>2\), \(f(A)=1\), and \(f(B)=2\), the worst local optimum under \(N_1\) has value \(2\), while under \(N_2\) it has value \(1\); their single-instance gaps are \(M/2\) and \(M\). Interchanging the values of \(A\) and \(B\) reverses the ordering. Hence incomparable neighborhoods admit no universal locality-gap ordering from neighborhood choice alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two incomparable neighborhoods can rank either way; swapping two objective values reverses which neighborhood has the better locality gap.
assumptions_latex: Neighborhood adjacency is symmetric.
Neither neighborhood contains the other.

notation.meaning: objective value of the global optimum

knowledge_statements.title: Incomparable Neighborhoods Have No Gap Ordering

children.title: Rounding Dependence Failures
children.top_down_role: Dependence structures invalidating naive rounding choices.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Independent Rounding Violates a Packing Constraint
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A feasible fractional packing inequality need not survive independent marginal rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the feasible fractional point \(x_1=x_2=1/2\) satisfying \(x_1+x_2\le1\), independently round \(X_i\in\{0,1\}\) with \(\Pr(X_i=1)=x_i\). Then \(\Pr(X_1+X_2>1)=\Pr(X_1=X_2=1)=1/4\). Thus marginal preservation and feasibility in expectation do not imply almost-sure packing feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent rounding of a feasible two-variable packing point violates the constraint with probability one quarter.
assumptions_latex: X_1,X_2\text{ are independent Bernoulli variables with the specified marginals.}
knowledge_statements.title: Independent Rounding Violates a Packing Constraint

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Arbitrary Dependence Invalidates Independent Tail Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perfect positive correlation can destroy concentration while preserving all Bernoulli marginals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)\) and set \(X_1=\cdots=X_n=Y\). Every coordinate has marginal \(p\), and \(S=\sum_iX_i\) has mean \(np\), but \(S\in\{0,n\}\) and \(\Pr(S=n)=p\). For fixed \(p\in(0,1)\), this upper-tail probability does not decay with \(n\). Therefore concentration conclusions valid for independent Bernoulli trials cannot be inferred from Bernoulli marginals under arbitrary dependence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Perfectly correlated Bernoulli variables preserve the desired marginals but do not exhibit independent-sum concentration.
assumptions_latex: Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p),\quad0<p<1.
X_i=Y\text{ for every }i.
knowledge_statements.title: Arbitrary Dependence Invalidates Independent Tail Bounds

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Marginals Determine Linear Expectation, Not Joint Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between conclusions determined by one-dimensional marginals and those requiring dependence information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\in\{0,1\}^n\) be any possibly dependent rounding satisfying \(\mathbb E[X_i]=x_i\). For every coefficient vector \(c\), \(\mathbb E[c^\top X]=c^\top x\) without an independence assumption. In contrast, the marginals alone do not determine \(\Pr(X\in\mathcal F)\), variances, tail probabilities, or expectations of nonlinear objectives. Preserved marginals may therefore certify expected linear value, but not joint feasibility or concentration without additional correlation properties, alteration, or direct analysis of the joint distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Preserved marginals suffice for expected linear objective value, but not for feasibility, concentration, or nonlinear performance.
assumptions_latex: \mathbb E[X_i]=x_i\text{ for every }i.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb E[c^\top X]=c^\top x,\quad\text{while joint feasibility and tail bounds do not follow from the marginals alone.}

notation.meaning: joint feasible set of integral outcomes

knowledge_statements.title: Marginals Determine Linear Expectation, Not Joint Guarantees
Rounding Dependence Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-cardinality feasibility can be destroyed by independent marginal rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix an integer \(k\ge 1\), let \(n=2k\), and consider the fractional point \(x_i=1/2\) satisfying \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i=k\). Independently round each coordinate to \(X_i\in\{0,1\}\) with \(\Pr(X_i=1)=x_i\). Although every marginal is preserved, the exact-cardinality constraint fails with probability
\[
\Pr\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_i\ne k\right)=1-\binom{2k}{k}4^{-k},
\]
which tends to \(1\) as \(k\to\infty\). Thus marginal preservation alone does not ensure joint feasibility; any rounding scheme that enforces exact cardinality with probability one must couple the coordinate choices rather than round them independently.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent rounding preserves each marginal but violates the exact-cardinality constraint with probability approaching one; enforcing that constraint requires coupled coordinate choices.
assumptions_latex: \(k\in\mathbb N\) and \(k\ge 1\).
The variables \(X_1,\ldots,X_{2k}\) are mutually independent Bernoulli variables with parameter \(1/2\).

children.title: Weak-Relaxation Failures
children.top_down_role: Large formulation gaps blocking strong guarantees from selected relaxations.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak-Relaxation Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An integrality gap limits guarantees obtainable by rounding a relaxation optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a minimization formulation with positive finite optima, define its integrality gap by
\[
g=\sup_{I}\frac{\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{IP}}(I)}{\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{R}}(I)}.
\]
Suppose a rounding procedure, applied to an optimal relaxed solution of every instance \(I\), always returns an integer-feasible solution of value at most \(\alpha\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{R}}(I)\). Integer optimality then gives \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{IP}}(I)\le\alpha\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{R}}(I)\) for every \(I\), hence \(\alpha\ge g\). Therefore a relaxation with gap \(g\) cannot by such rounding certify a uniform approximation factor below \(g\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The worst-case integrality gap is a lower bound on every approximation factor certified by rounding an optimal solution of that relaxation.
assumptions_latex: \(0<\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{R}}(I)\le\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{IP}}(I)<\infty\).
The rounded output is integer-feasible for every instance.

children.title: Hardness Interpretation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Distinctions required when translating lower bounds into algorithmic conclusions.

children.title: Hardness Assumption-Status Classes
children.top_down_role: Separation of established lower bounds from conjecture-dependent frontiers.

children.title: Conditional Hardness Frontiers
children.top_down_role: Approximation lower bounds whose force depends on unresolved complexity premises.

knowledge_statements.title: Conditional Hardness Frontiers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Frontier relative to an explicitly named complexity hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a minimization problem \(P\), algorithm class \(\mathcal A\), and complexity hypothesis \(H\), define the conditional hardness frontier
\[
\rho_H(P,\mathcal A)=\sup\!\left\{r\ge1: H\Longrightarrow \text{no algorithm in }\mathcal A\text{ has worst-case ratio strictly below }r\right\}.
\]
Every lower bound contributing to this supremum is an implication whose antecedent is \(H\). Consequently, the frontier records what is excluded under \(H\), not an unconditional nonexistence result. The algorithmic model, input encoding, and approximation convention are part of \(\mathcal A\) and must remain fixed when frontiers are compared.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conditional frontier is the supremum of approximation ratios ruled out under a fixed complexity hypothesis and algorithmic model.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a minimization problem with approximation ratios at least \(1\).
\(H\) and the algorithm class \(\mathcal A\) are fixed.

notation.meaning: fixed algorithm class and computational model

children.title: Unconditional Hardness Bounds
children.top_down_role: Lower bounds established without reliance on additional unproved complexity premises.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines unconditionality relative to a fully specified computational model, not independence from all modeling choices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a problem \(P\), algorithm class \(\mathcal A\), approximation convention, and input or oracle model \(\mathcal M\). A statement \(\neg E_{P,r}(\mathcal A,\mathcal M)\) is an unconditional approximation lower bound when it is established without an additional unresolved complexity hypothesis as an antecedent. Unconditionality is model-relative: changing \(\mathcal A\), \(\mathcal M\), the resource budget, or the performance convention changes the proposition being asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unconditional approximation lower bound uses no additional unresolved complexity premise but remains relative to its specified algorithmic, resource, and input model.
assumptions_latex: The problem, algorithm class, approximation convention, and computational model are fixed.
No additional unresolved complexity hypothesis is assumed.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Yao Distributional Transfer for Randomized Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfers a deterministic distributional lower bound to randomized algorithms in the same fixed resource model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal I\) be a finite instance set, let \(L(I,o)\) be the loss of output \(o\) on instance \(I\), and let \(\mathcal D\) be a distribution on \(\mathcal I\). If every deterministic algorithm \(A\) in a fixed resource-bounded class satisfies \[\mathbb E_{I\sim\mathcal D}[L(I,A(I))]>\rho,\] then every randomized algorithm \(R\) that is a distribution over algorithms in that deterministic class has some \(I\in\mathcal I\) satisfying \[\mathbb E[L(I,R(I))]>\rho.\] Thus the distributional deterministic lower bound gives a worst-case randomized lower bound in the same model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Yao's distributional principle converts a hard input distribution for every deterministic bounded-resource algorithm into a worst-case expected-loss lower bound for randomized algorithms.

Unconditional Hardness Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconditional query lower bound obtained through transcript indistinguishability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a deterministic oracle model and a query budget \(q\). Suppose two valid instances \(I_0,I_1\) can answer every sequence of at most \(q\) adaptive queries with the same transcript, while no single output is a \(\rho\)-approximate solution for both instances. Every deterministic algorithm using at most \(q\) queries receives identical information on \(I_0\) and \(I_1\), hence returns the same output and fails on at least one instance. Therefore no such algorithm guarantees approximation ratio \(\rho\). This lower bound is unconditional relative to the specified oracle model and query budget.

children.title: Assumption-Dependence Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Distinctions in lower-bound meaning caused by the strength or status of supporting premises.

knowledge_statements.title: Assumption-Dependence Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A conditional lower bound inherits the logical scope of its premise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a complexity hypothesis and let \(E_{P,r}\) denote existence of an allowed polynomial-time algorithm for problem \(P\) with approximation ratio at most \(r\). A conditional hardness result has the form
\[
H\Longrightarrow\neg E_{P,r}.
\]
It entails only \(E_{P,r}\Longrightarrow\neg H\) by contraposition. If the status of \(H\) is unresolved, neither \(\neg E_{P,r}\) nor \(E_{P,r}\) follows without additional information. Replacing \(H\) by a stronger, weaker, or incomparable premise therefore changes the justified hardness claim and may change the stated frontier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conditional inapproximability excludes an algorithm only under its premise; without resolving that premise, algorithm existence remains logically undecided.
assumptions_latex: The asserted lower bound is \(H\Rightarrow\neg E_{P,r}\).
No independent proof of \(H\) or \(\neg E_{P,r}\) is assumed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Only \(H\Rightarrow\neg E_{P,r}\) and \(E_{P,r}\Rightarrow\neg H\) are justified.

notation.meaning: existence of the specified approximation algorithm

children.title: Promise-Restriction Sensitivity Interface
children.top_down_role: Dependence of hardness on promises and instance subclasses.

children.title: Promise Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Changes in hardness caused by guarantees that inputs satisfy specified promises.

knowledge_statements.title: Promise Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximation thresholds may change after imposing an input promise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\) be a minimization problem on an instance set \(\mathcal I\), let \(\Pi\subseteq\mathcal I\) be a nonempty promise, and let \(\mathcal A\) be an algorithm class. For every nonempty domain \(D\subseteq\mathcal I\), let \(\mathcal A_D\) contain the algorithms in \(\mathcal A\) that return a feasible solution on every \(I\in D\), and define
\[
\alpha(P\mid D,\mathcal A)=\inf_{A\in\mathcal A_D}\sup_{I\in D}\frac{A(I)}{\operatorname{OPT}(I)},
\]
where \(A(I)\) denotes the objective value returned by \(A\), and where the infimum is \(+\infty\) if \(\mathcal A_D=\varnothing\). The approximation frontier is promise-sensitive when \(\alpha(P\mid\Pi,\mathcal A)\ne\alpha(P\mid\mathcal I,\mathcal A)\). Hardness or algorithms for the unrestricted domain therefore do not automatically characterize the promised domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Promise sensitivity occurs when restricting valid inputs changes the best worst-case approximation ratio achievable by algorithms that are feasible throughout the evaluated domain.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a minimization problem with positive optimum on every relevant instance.
\(\varnothing\ne\Pi\subseteq\mathcal I\), and \(\mathcal A\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Promise sensitivity means \(\alpha(P\mid\Pi,\mathcal A)\ne\alpha(P\mid\mathcal I,\mathcal A)\).

notation.meaning: algorithms feasible on every instance in the evaluation domain D
best worst-case ratio on domain D

children.title: Instance-Restriction Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Changes in lower bounds after restricting inputs to structured subclasses.

knowledge_statements.title: Instance-Restriction Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural subclasses can have strictly different approximation frontiers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal C_1\subseteq\mathcal C_2\) be two classes of instances of a minimization problem, and define
\[
\alpha(\mathcal C)=\inf_{A\in\mathcal A}\sup_{I\in\mathcal C}\frac{A(I)}{\operatorname{OPT}(I)}.
\]
Then \(\alpha(\mathcal C_1)\le\alpha(\mathcal C_2)\), because every algorithm is evaluated over a smaller worst-case domain on \(\mathcal C_1\). The restriction is frontier-sensitive when the inequality is strict. An algorithmic or hardness threshold established for \(\mathcal C_2\) consequently need not be tight for \(\mathcal C_1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricting the instance class cannot worsen the optimal worst-case ratio and may strictly improve the approximation frontier.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal C_1\subseteq\mathcal C_2\).
The same minimization objective and algorithm class \(\mathcal A\) are used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha(\mathcal C_1)\le\alpha(\mathcal C_2)\), with sensitivity when the inequality is strict.

notation.meaning: best worst-case approximation ratio on a class

children.title: Promise-Preserving Transfers
children.top_down_role: Whether hardness transfers retain the promises required by the target instance family.

knowledge_statements.title: Promise-Preserving Transfers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximation transfer between promise problems requires promise preservation in both maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let source and target minimization promise problems have valid-instance sets \(\Pi_P\) and \(\Pi_Q\), positive optimum values, and approximation ratios at least \(1\). An approximation transfer consists of a polynomial-time instance map \(f\), a polynomial-time solution map \(g\), and a nondecreasing function \(\phi:[1,\infty)\to[1,\infty)\). It is promise-preserving when
\[
I\in\Pi_P\Longrightarrow f(I)\in\Pi_Q
\]
and, for every \(I\in\Pi_P\), every \(r\ge1\), and every target-feasible solution \(y\) for \(f(I)\) having approximation ratio at most \(r\), the decoded solution \(g(I,y)\) is source-feasible for \(I\) and has approximation ratio at most \(\phi(r)\). Under these conditions, any \(r\)-approximation on \(\Pi_Q\) yields a \(\phi(r)\)-approximation on \(\Pi_P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transfer respects promises when every valid source instance maps to a valid target instance and every decoded approximate solution remains source-feasible with controlled ratio loss.
assumptions_latex: The source and target are minimization promise problems with positive optima.
The maps \(f\) and \(g\) are polynomial-time computable.
The function \(\phi:[1,\infty)\to[1,\infty)\) is nondecreasing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(r\ge1\), an \(r\)-approximation on \(\Pi_Q\) induces a \(\phi(r)\)-approximation on \(\Pi_P\).

children.title: Restriction Escape Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where a hardness construction leaves the subclass to which a claimed lower bound is meant to apply.

knowledge_statements.title: Restriction Escape Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A reduction cannot transfer restricted hardness after leaving the restricted domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a hardness claim concern a source restriction \(\Pi_P\) and a target restriction \(\Pi_Q\), with reduction maps \(f\) and \(g\). The restricted transfer fails if there exists \(I\in\Pi_P\) such that \(f(I)\notin\Pi_Q\), because a target algorithm guaranteed only on \(\Pi_Q\) need not process \(f(I)\). It also fails if some target-feasible approximate solution \(y\) decodes to \(g(I,y)\) outside the source feasible set. Either escape breaks the composition needed to infer a source approximation algorithm, so the claimed restricted lower bound does not follow from that reduction alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricted hardness does not transfer if the reduction leaves the target promise or its decoder leaves the source feasible set.
assumptions_latex: The target algorithm is guaranteed only for instances in \(\Pi_Q\).
The intended source conclusion is restricted to \(\Pi_P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Failure of promise or feasibility preservation invalidates the restricted transfer.

children.title: Reduction-Premise Sensitivity Interface
children.top_down_role: Changes in lower-bound meaning under different reductions or complexity premises.

children.title: Reduction-Type Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Changes in approximation lower bounds under different notions of reduction.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A decision reduction alone need not preserve optimization quality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polynomial-time many-one reduction from the decision version of \(P\) to the decision version of \(Q\) specifies only preservation of yes/no answers. Unless additional maps recover feasible source solutions and quantitatively relate their objective error to target objective error, the reduction alone does not imply that a \(\rho\)-approximation for the optimization version of \(Q\) yields any bounded-factor approximation for the optimization version of \(P\). Thus decision NP-hardness alone is not an approximation-hardness threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decision reduction transfers no approximation factor without an additional quantitative solution-decoding guarantee.
assumptions_latex: P\le_m^p Q\text{ is supplied only as a decision many-one reduction.
No quantitative solution decoder is assumed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\le_m^p Q\text{ alone implies no bounded approximation-ratio transfer between the optimization versions.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative error degradation under an L-reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For minimization problems with positive source optimum, suppose \(R,D\) satisfy \(\operatorname{OPT}_Q(R(x))\le\alpha\operatorname{OPT}_P(x)\) and \(|c_P(D(y))-\operatorname{OPT}_P(x)|\le\beta|c_Q(y)-\operatorname{OPT}_Q(R(x))|\). If \(c_Q(y)\le(1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}_Q(R(x))\), then \(c_P(D(y))\le(1+\alpha\beta\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}_P(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An L-reduction converts target relative error ε into source relative error at most αβε.
assumptions_latex: \alpha,\beta>0.
\operatorname{OPT}_P(x)>0.
y\text{ is feasible and }c_Q(y)\le(1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}_Q(R(x)).

knowledge_statements.title: L-Reduction Error Transfer
Reduction-Type Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The transferred approximation threshold depends on the reduction’s quantitative guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a reduction type \(R\), let \(\phi_R(r)\) be the guaranteed source approximation ratio obtained by decoding a target solution of ratio \(r\). If the source problem admits no allowed approximation algorithm with ratio strictly below \(a\), then this source bound and reduction certify the impossibility of every target ratio \(r\) satisfying \(\phi_R(r)<a\). No exclusion for a ratio with \(\phi_R(r)\ge a\) follows from that source bound and reduction alone. Consequently, two valid reduction types \(R_1\) and \(R_2\) with different degradation functions can transfer different target lower bounds from the same source theorem. A transferred hardness factor must therefore be interpreted together with the reduction type and its quantitative decoding inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Different reduction types can transfer different hardness factors because their decoding guarantees can degrade approximation ratios differently.
assumptions_latex: Each reduction is polynomial-time and feasibility-preserving.
Each \(\phi_R\) is a valid upper bound on the decoded source ratio.
The source excludes ratios strictly below \(a\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The exclusion region certified by the stated source bound and reduction is \(\{r:\phi_R(r)<a\}\).

children.title: Complexity-Premise Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Variation in hardness conclusions under alternative complexity premises.

knowledge_statements.title: Complexity-Premise Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A reduction yields contradiction only when composition enters the premise’s forbidden class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose a source hardness premise excludes source algorithms in a computational class \(\mathcal C_P\). Let the reduction and decoder use resources \(T_f(n)\) and \(T_g(n)\), let the target algorithm use \(T_A(m)\) on instances of size \(m\), and suppose \(|f(I)|=s(|I|)\). The transfer contradicts the premise only if the composed source algorithm
\[
I\longmapsto g\bigl(I,A(f(I))\bigr)
\]
belongs to \(\mathcal C_P\). Its resource use is bounded by
\[
T_f(n)+T_A(s(n))+T_g(n),
\]
so this bound must satisfy the resource requirement defining membership in \(\mathcal C_P\). Otherwise the composed algorithm lies outside the class excluded by the premise, and that premise supplies no lower bound against the proposed target algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hardness premise transfers only when the reduction, target algorithm, and decoder compose into an algorithm belonging to the computational class excluded by that premise.
assumptions_latex: The source premise excludes only algorithms in \(\mathcal C_P\).
The size expansion satisfies \(|f(I)|=s(|I|)\).
The displayed sum bounds the resources of the complete composition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Transfer requires \(g\circ A\circ f\in\mathcal C_P\), with the composition interpreted using the decoder’s source-instance argument.

notation.meaning: computational class excluded by the source premise
resource bounds for reduction, target algorithm, and decoding

children.title: Lower-Bound Transfer Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on carrying approximation hardness across problems, parameters, or instance classes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Instance-class boundary when a reduction reaches only part of the target domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let R map the source class \(\mathcal I_P\) into \(\mathcal J\subseteq\mathcal I_Q\), and suppose decoding a target guarantee on every instance of \(\mathcal J\) produces a source guarantee forbidden by premise \(\Pi\). Then \(\Pi\) excludes target algorithms whose guaranteed domain contains \(\mathcal J\). It does not, from this reduction alone, exclude an algorithm guaranteed only on \(\mathcal U\subseteq\mathcal I_Q\) when \(\mathcal J\nsubseteq\mathcal U\), or establish hardness specifically outside \(\mathcal J\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hardness transfers only to target guarantees covering the reduction image; it gives no conclusion by itself about target subclasses that do not cover that image.

knowledge_statements.title: Image-Class Transfer Boundary
Lower-Bound Transfer Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A ratio-degradation function determines the exact region transferred by a reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume a source minimization problem has no allowed approximation algorithm with ratio strictly below \(a\). Suppose a valid reduction converts every target algorithm of ratio \(r\) into a source algorithm of ratio at most \(\phi(r)\), where \(\phi\) is nondecreasing. Then every target ratio satisfying \(\phi(r)<a\) is impossible under the same premise. The transfer boundary is
\[
r^*=\sup\{r\ge1:\phi(r)<a\}.
\]
No target lower bound for a ratio with \(\phi(r)\ge a\) follows from this source bound and reduction alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Source hardness transfers exactly where the reduction’s decoded ratio remains below the source hardness threshold.
assumptions_latex: The source excludes approximation ratios strictly below \(a\).
The reduction is valid and has nondecreasing degradation function \(\phi\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The justified exclusion region is \(\{r\ge1:\phi(r)<a\}\), with boundary \(r^*\).

children.top_down_role: Interpretive constraints arising from the interaction between a reduction framework and its supporting complexity premise.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact logical condition for deriving a contradiction by composing a target approximation algorithm with a reduction and decoder.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Pi\) exclude every algorithm in computational model \(\mathcal C\) that attains source guarantee \(G_P\) on source domain \(\mathcal I_P\). A reduction-decoder pair \((R,D)\) transfers target guarantee \(G_Q\) compatibly with \(\Pi\) if: \(R\) and \(D\) use only resources allowed by \(\mathcal C\); \(R(x)\) satisfies the target promise for every \(x\in\mathcal I_P\); every target algorithm in \(\mathcal C\) attaining \(G_Q\) on all reduced instances yields, through \(x\mapsto D(x,A_Q(R(x)))\), a feasible source solution satisfying \(G_P\); and the composed runtime, randomness, advice, parameter dependence, oracle access, and success probability remain within \(\mathcal C\). Under these conditions, existence of such an \(A_Q\) contradicts \(\Pi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reduction is premise-compatible exactly when the full composed algorithm preserves promises and the forbidden source guarantee while remaining inside the computational model ruled out by the premise.
assumptions_latex: \Pi\text{ excludes guarantee }G_P\text{ on }\mathcal I_P\text{ within model }\mathcal C.
R\text{ maps every source instance into the promised target domain.
D\text{ transfers }G_Q\text{ to }G_P\text{ for every reduced instance.
The complete composition remains in }\mathcal C.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nexists A_Q\in\mathcal C\text{ attaining }G_Q\text{ on every reduced instance.}

knowledge_statements.title: Premise-Compatible Composition Criterion

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Error-budget condition for randomized reduction compositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the composed reduction, target algorithm, and decoder have failure events \(E_1,\ldots,E_t\), while \(\Pi\) excludes source algorithms in the resulting model with failure probability at most \(\delta\). The composition contradicts \(\Pi\) only if \(\Pr(\bigcup_{j=1}^tE_j)\le\delta\). Bounds \(\Pr(E_j)\le\delta_j\) with \(\sum_j\delta_j\le\delta\) suffice without independence. Amplification is valid only when its repetitions, verification requirements, and overhead remain allowed by the premise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Randomized hardness transfer must keep the total failure probability and amplification overhead within the model excluded by the premise.
assumptions_latex: \Pi\text{ excludes source algorithms with failure probability at most }\delta.
E_1,\ldots,E_t\text{ include every failure event in the composition.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pr\!\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^tE_j\right)\le\delta\text{ is required for the composition to invoke }\Pi.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A reduction-decoder pair \((R,D)\) from an optimization problem \(P\) to an optimization problem \(Q\) is compatible with a complexity premise \(\Pi\) relative to a model \(\mathcal C\) when: \(R\) and \(D\) are computable within \(\mathcal C\); \(R\) maps every source instance covered by \(\Pi\) to a valid target instance without violating either problem's promise; and there exist guarantees \(g_P\) and \(g_Q\) such that every feasible target solution satisfying \(g_Q\) is decoded by \(D\) into a feasible source solution satisfying \(g_P\). Any randomness, nonuniform advice, parameter dependence, or oracle access used by \(R\) or \(D\) must also be permitted by \(\Pi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hardness reduction is premise-compatible when it preserves promises and approximation guarantees while using only the computational resources, randomness, advice, parameters, and oracles allowed by the premise.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind “condition” fits this terminal container, and the statement is broadly aligned with premise-sensitive hardness transfer. However, the cited general sections on reductions and numerical approximation do not reliably support the specialized approximation-preserving formulation, including promises, randomness, nonuniform advice, parameters, and oracle access. Moreover, the assumptions do not explicitly identify the forbidden source guarantee as g_P or state that the reduction transfers g_Q to that forbidden guarantee, so the claimed contradiction does not follow as written. The meanings and quantification of g_P and g_Q also require a precise approximation framework and an authoritative locator.
